content.text:
The current application @src/lex.zig @macos/Lex.swift is working fine on macOS, but **sometime** I could not type on input in the website within Safari, while I could type on other application just fine. e.g. I'm typing "nguyee" but only see "nguye". If I observe carefully, I see the che "ê" briefly appear, then disappear. another case, I type "hoanx" and the result is "hoaã".

Find out the possible root cause. You'r on the sandbox environment on Linux.

I’ll trace the Zig state transitions and the macOS input-event bridge, focusing on cases where a composed replacement is emitted and then partially undone or reordered. I’ll keep this read-only and separate code-supported causes from Safari-specific hypotheses that cannot be reproduced on Linux.

input.command: git status --short && wc -l src/lex.zig macos/Lex.swift && sed -n '1,260p' macos/Lex.swift
sed -n '1,320p' src/lex.zig
find . -maxdepth 3 -type f | sort | sed -n '1,240p' && find . -maxdepth 3 -type f \( -name '*test*' -o -name '*.md' -o -name '*.h' \) -print | sort

- **gi/qu reclassification** means interpretation of earlier letters can change after later input

- **The backspace contract must be symmetric with normal input.**
- The engine must be able to say: “swallow this Backspace and replace the current composition with this new rendering.”

The engine state is only valid while the user is doing **linear typing at the same insertion point with no selection changes**.

- app switch
- Cmd/Ctrl/Alt-modified keyDown
- multi-char events
- tap disable events

- **mouse down / click** in a text area

- **double/triple click** word/line selection

Reset triggers are incomplete.** The Swift side resets on app switch, modifier keys, and tap disables — but misses **mouse clicks, arrow keys, forward delete, Home/End, and within-app focus changes**. ### 1. Can the bundle be lowercase `lex.app`?

**Technically yes**, but I'd recommend against it:

- macOS app bundles are just directories — `lex.app` works fine at the filesystem level.
- **However**, every macOS app uses UpperCamelCase (`Finder.app`, `Safari.app`, `Squirrel.app`). Lowercase would look out of place in `/Library/Input Methods/` and Finder.
- The display name shown to users is controlled by `CFBundleDisplayName` in `Info.plist`, which is independent of the filename. So you can have `Lex.app` on disk but display "lex" to users everywhere (menu bar, System Settings, etc.).

**Recommendation:** Use `Lex.app` as the bundle name, set `CFBundleDisplayName` to `lex` if you want the lowercase branding.

---

### 2. Directory structure analysis

Your current structure:

```
structure-app/
├── src/          ← shared Zig library (liblex)
├── macos/        ← platform integration (Swift)
├── build.zig
└── build.zig.zon
```

**This makes sense.** It's the standard "core + shell" pattern for cross-platform apps. Community references with very similar structures:

- **Ghostty** (Zig terminal emulator by Mitchell Hashimoto): core engine in Zig under `src/`, macOS shell in `macos/` with Swift/AppKit, single `build.zig` at root that builds both the library and the platform app.
- **librime / Squirrel**: C++ input method engine as a library, with `Squirrel` as a separate macOS frontend — same separation of concerns.

One thing to consider: when you add more platforms (e.g., `linux/`, `windows/`), this scales naturally. The `build.zig` at the root can conditionally build the right platform target.

   704	private func event_tap_callback(
   705	    proxy: CGEventTapProxy,
   706	    type event_type: CGEventType,
   707	    event: CGEvent,
   708	    userInfo: UnsafeMutableRawPointer?
   709	) -> Unmanaged<CGEvent>? {
   710	    // passthrough event when the event tap is inactive.
   711	    guard let userInfo else {
   712	        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
   713	    }
   714	
   715	    let app_delegate = Unmanaged<AppDelegate>
   716	            .fromOpaque(userInfo)
   717	            .takeUnretainedValue()
   718	
   719	    switch event_type {
   720	        case .tapDisabledByTimeout, .tapDisabledByUserInput:
   721	            // Reset engine.
   722	            app_delegate.engine.reset()
   723	            // Re-enable tap.
   724	            app_delegate.enable_event_tap()
   725	            // Pass through event.
   726	            return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
   727	
   728	        case .leftMouseDown, .rightMouseDown:
   729	            // Reset engine.
   730	            app_delegate.engine.reset()
   731	            // Pass through event.
   732	            return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
   733	
   734	        case .flagsChanged:
   735	            // Pass through event.
   736	            // Don't reset for plain Shift / Caps Lock.
   737	            return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
   738	
   739	        case .keyDown:
   740	            // Handle key down.
   741	
   742	            // Let the registered hot key handler lock or unlock the keyboard.
   743	            if let key_code = app_delegate.registered_keyboard_lock_key_code(),
   744	                    matches_keyboard_lock_hot_key(
   745	                        key_code: key_code,
   746	                        event_key_code: event.getIntegerValueField(.keyboardEventKeycode),
   747	                        event_flags: event.flags
   748	                    ) {
   749	                return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
   750	            }
   751	
   752	            if app_delegate.is_keyboard_locked() {
   753	                return nil
   754	            }
   755	
   756	            // passthrough event when in literal mode.
   757	            if app_delegate.is_literal() {
   758	                return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
   759	            }
   760	            
   761	            // Ignore Lex's synthetic events.
   762	            if event.getIntegerValueField(.eventSourceUserData) == synthetic_event_source_user_data {
   763	                return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
   764	            }
   765	
   766	            // Ignore hot key combination when holding either: Command, Option, Control.
   767	            let modifier_mask: CGEventFlags = [.maskCommand, .maskControl, .maskAlternate]
   768	            if !event.flags.intersection(modifier_mask).isEmpty {
   769	                // Reset the engine because user execute other action while typing.
   770	                app_delegate.engine.reset()
   771	                // Passthrough the action.
   772	                return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
   773	            }
   774	
   775	            // Get keycode to detect special key pressed.
   776	            let key_code = event.getIntegerValueField(.keyboardEventKeycode)
   777	            switch key_code {
   778	                case Int64(kVK_Space):
   779	                    // Reset the state to process new word.
   780	                    app_delegate.engine.reset()
   781	                    // Passthrough the space.
   782	                    return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
   783	
   784	                case Int64(kVK_Delete):
   785	                    // User input backspace.
   786	                    // Call backspace action to keep buffer in sync with real input.
   787	                    app_delegate.engine.backspace()
   788	                    // Passthrough backspace.
   789	                    return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
   790	
   791	                default:
   792	                        // Reset state for unhandled keycode.
   793	                        // app_delegate.engine.reset()
   794	                        // return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
   795	                        break
   796	            }
   797	
   798	            // Detect and handle alphabetic input.
   799	            var character_count = 0
   800	                event.keyboardGetUnicodeString(
   801	                        maxStringLength: 0,
   802	                        actualStringLength: &character_count,
   803	                        unicodeString: nil
   804	                        )
   805	                guard character_count == 1 else {
   806	                    // No character, could be a special key, could not handle this case.
   807	                    app_delegate.engine.reset()
   808	                        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
   809	                }
   810	
   811	            // Get Unicode character.
   812	            var character: UniChar = 0
   813	                event.keyboardGetUnicodeString(
   814	                        maxStringLength: 1,
   815	                        actualStringLength: &character_count,
   816	                        unicodeString: &character
   817	                        )
   818	                // Check if it's alphabetic.
   819	                let is_alphabetic = (character >= 65 && character <= 90)
   820	                || (character >= 97 && character <= 122)
   821	                guard is_alphabetic else {
   822	                    // No alphabitec, reset state.
   823	                    app_delegate.engine.reset()
   824	                        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
   825	                }
   826	                guard let input = UnicodeScalar(UInt32(character)) else {
   827	                    app_delegate.engine.reset()
   828	                    return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
   829	                }
   830	
   831	            // Valid input, safe to process with the engine.
   832	            if app_delegate.engine.buffer_full() {
   833	                // The state reach the limit, reset it before continue processing.
   834	                app_delegate.engine.reset()
   835	            }
   836	
   837	            if app_delegate.engine.buffer_effective_full() {
   838	                // The buffer effective is full, process literal input.
   839	                app_delegate.engine.add(input)
   840	                return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
   841	            } else {
   842	                // The buffer effective has room, process with synthetic backspace and replacement.
   843	                guard let synthetic_event_source = app_delegate.get_synthetic_event_source() else {
   844	                    // No event source to send synthetic event.
   845	                    app_delegate.engine.reset()
   846	                    return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
   847	                }
   848	                
   849	                // Send the input character to engine.
   850	                app_delegate.engine.add(input)
   851	
   852	                // Calculate synthetic backspaces.
   853	                let backspace_count = app_delegate.engine.synthetic_backspaces()
   854	
   855	                // Post synthetic backspaces to event tap.
   856	                if backspace_count > 0 {
   857	                    for _ in 0..<backspace_count {
   858	                        if let synthetic_backspace_down = CGEvent(
   859	                            keyboardEventSource: synthetic_event_source,
   860	                            virtualKey: CGKeyCode(kVK_Delete),
   861	                            keyDown: true
   862	                        ) {
   863	                            synthetic_backspace_down.tapPostEvent(proxy)
   864	                        }
   865	                        
   866	                        if let synthetic_backspace_up = CGEvent(
   867	                            keyboardEventSource: synthetic_event_source,
   868	                            virtualKey: CGKeyCode(kVK_Delete),
   869	                            keyDown: false
   870	                        ) {
   871	                            synthetic_backspace_up.tapPostEvent(proxy)
   872	                        }
   873	                    }
   874	                }
   875	                
   876	                // Compose replacement.
   877	                app_delegate.engine.compose_replacement { replacement in
   878	                    guard let replacement_base_address = replacement.baseAddress else {
   879	                        return
   880	                    }
   881	
   882	                    if let synthetic_characters_down = CGEvent(
   883	                        keyboardEventSource: synthetic_event_source,
   884	                        virtualKey: 0,
   885	                        keyDown: true
   886	                    ) {
   887	                        synthetic_characters_down.keyboardSetUnicodeString(
   888	                            stringLength: replacement.count,
   889	                            unicodeString: replacement_base_address
   890	                        )
   891	                        synthetic_characters_down.tapPostEvent(proxy)
   892	                    }
   893	
   894	                    
   895	                    if let synthetic_characters_up = CGEvent(
   896	                        keyboardEventSource: synthetic_event_source,
   897	                        virtualKey: 0,
   898	                        keyDown: false
   899	                    ) {
   900	                        synthetic_characters_up.keyboardSetUnicodeString(
   901	                            stringLength: replacement.count,
   902	                            unicodeString: replacement_base_address
   903	                        )
   904	                        synthetic_characters_up.tapPostEvent(proxy)
   905	                    }
   906	                }
   907	                return nil
   908	            }
   909	
   910	
   911	        default:
   912	            return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
   913	    }

Section Title: CGEvent
Content:
Defines an opaque type that represents a low-level hardware event.
Mac Catalyst macOS
```
class CGEvent
```
Section Title: CGEvent > Overview
Content:
Low-level hardware events of this type are referred to as Quartz events. A typical event in macOS originates when the user manipulates an input device such as a mouse or a keyboard. The device driver associated with that device, through the I/O Kit, creates a low-level event, puts it in the window server’s event queue, and notifies the window server. The window server creates a Quartz event, annotates the event, and dispatches the event to the appropriate run-loop port of the target process. There the event is picked up by the Carbon Event Manager and forwarded to the event-handling mechanism appropriate to the application environment. You can use event taps to gain access to Quartz events at several different steps in this process.
This opaque type is derived from CFType and inherits the properties that all Core Foundation types have in common. For more information, see doc://com.apple.documentation/documentation/corefoundation/cftype.

1386:                    "result": "### GõKey Bug Context
- **Issue**: Synthetic events (backspaces followed by replacement characters) arrive out of order at the target application when the user types quickly. This causes interleaving where a real user keystroke might be processed between the synthetic backspace and the synthetic character insertion.
- **Root Cause**: Using `CGEvent.post(tap: .cghidEventTap)` (or equivalent global posting) injects events into the global HID/session queue. The OS may reorder these relative to real user keystrokes arriving at the HID level.
- **Fix**: Switch from global posting to `CGEventTapPostEvent(proxy, event)`, which injects synthetic events directly into the tap's event stream, guaranteeing strict ordering relative to the triggering event.

### Analysis of `macos/Lex.swift` Implementation
In `Lex.swift`, the `applyDiff` method handles the generation of synthetic events:

```swift
// Lines 163-170: Emitting backspaces
for _ in 0..<numBackspaces {
    if let down = CGEvent(keyboardEventSource: source, virtualKey: 0x33, keyDown: true),
       let up = CGEvent(keyboardEventSource: source, virtualKey: 0x33, keyDown: false) {
        down.post(tap: .cgSessionEventTap)
        up.post(tap: .cgSessionEventTap)
    }
}

// Lines 172-182: Emitting replacement characters
if !replacementChars.isEmpty {
    var chars = replacementChars
    if let down = CGEvent(keyboardEventSource: source, virtualKey: 0, keyDown: true),
       let up = CGEvent(keyboardEventSource: source, virtualKey: 0, keyDown: false) {
        down.keyboardSetUnicodeString(stringLength: chars.count, unicodeString: &chars)
        up.keyboardSetUnicodeString(stringLength: chars.count, unicodeString: &chars)
        down.post(tap: .cgSessionEventTap)
        up.post(tap: .cgSessionEventTap)
    }
}
```

### Key Technical Questions Identified
1. **Current Method**: `Lex.swift` uses `CGEvent.post(tap: .cgSessionEventTap)`.
2. **The Proxy**: The `eventTapCallback` receives a `proxy: CGEventTapProxy` (Line 189), but it is currently unused.
3. **Ordering Risk**: Does `CGEvent.post(tap: .cgSessionEventTap)` suffer from the same out-of-order issue as `.cghidEventTap`? 
4. **Comparison**: What is the functional difference between posting to `.cgSessionEventTap` versus using `CGEventTapPostEvent(proxy, ...)` regarding event serialization and the prevention of interleaving with physical hardware events?",
1394:                "message": "**TL;DR:** Yes — Lex.swift is exposed to the same *class* of out-of-order synthetic-event bug. Using `CGEvent.post(tap: .cgSessionEventTap)` from inside the tap callback still posts into the global event stream at a location, not into the callback’s own in-flight stream, so it lacks the ordering guarantee that `CGEventTapPostEvent(proxy, ...)` is designed to provide.

### Analysis

1. **What Lex.swift is doing**
   - The tap is created at **`.cgSessionEventTap`** (`startEventTap`, lines 85–91).
   - On consumed keys, `applyDiff()` emits multiple synthetic events — backspace down/up pairs and replacement key down/up — using **`post(tap: .cgSessionEventTap)`** (lines 164–181).
   - The callback receives a **`proxy`** (line 189) but never uses it.
   - Synthetic events are tagged via `eventSourceUserData` and ignored on re-entry (lines 223–226), which prevents self-processing but does **not** affect ordering.

2. **Why this is the same fundamental bug**
   - Apple’s documented semantics for **`CGEvent.post(tap:)`** are about **where** the event is injected: it is posted “immediately before any event taps instantiated for that location.”
   - That is **not** the same as saying it is inserted **atomically in sequence with the current callback’s triggering event**.
   - So when Lex swallows a real key and then separately posts synthetic backspaces/replacement characters, those synthetic events are still entering a **global session-level stream** as new events.
   - A later real hardware keystroke can therefore race with that posted sequence and be observed between the synthetic events, exactly the failure mode GõKey hit.

3. **Why `.cgSessionEventTap` does not materially fix the ordering issue**
   - **`.cghidEventTap`** is the earlier injection point: where HID events enter the window server.
   - **`.cgSessionEventTap`** is a later injection point: where events enter the login session.
   - That difference affects **pipeline position**, but not the core issue here:
     - both are still **global injection points**
     - both create **new posted events** that are not intrinsically tied to the current callback’s return path
   - So posting to `.cgSessionEventTap` may change *where* the race happens and may narrow the window somewhat compared with `.cghidEventTap`, but it does **not** provide a strict no-interleaving guarantee.

4. **Why `CGEventTapPostEvent(proxy, ...)` is different**
   - Apple’s documented semantics for **`tapPostEvent`** are stronger and specifically callback-relative:
     - it posts “at the same point to which an event returned from an event tap callback function would be posted”
     - and “the new event enters the system **before** the event returned by the callback enters the system”
   - That is the key distinction: it is **tap-stream insertion**, not generic stream posting-at-a-location.
   - In other words, `post(tap:)` says “inject a new event at this global tap location,” while `tapPostEvent(proxy)` says “inject this from *this tap callback’s stream position*.”

5. **Why Lex’s implementation is especially sensitive**
   - `applyDiff()` emits a **sequence** of separate events, not one atomic unit:
     - multiple backspace key down/up pairs
     - then replacement key down/up
   - That creates multiple interleaving boundaries.
   - So if ordering is not guaranteed, the composition can be corrupted by a real keystroke arriving between any of those synthetic events.

6. **What the synthetic tag/source does and does not do**
   - `CGEventSource(.privateState)` plus `userData = syntheticTag` is useful for **identifying self-generated events**.
   - It prevents Lex from recursively processing its own synthetic events.
   - It does **not** serialize them relative to real user input and does **not** make `post(tap:)` callback-ordered.

### Bottom line

From a correctness standpoint, **Lex.swift should be considered affected by the same ordering bug family as GõKey**. The fact that it posts to **`.cgSessionEventTap`** instead of **`.cghidEventTap`** changes the reinjection point, but not the fundamental problem: it is still using **global event posting** rather than **tap-relative posting**, and therefore it does not have the strict ordering semantics that GõKey’s fix relied on.",

    func applyDiff(next: [UniChar]) {
        guard let source = syntheticSource else { return }

        // Find longest common prefix
        let minLen = min(currentRendered.count, next.count)
        var diverge = 0
        while diverge < minLen && currentRendered[diverge] == next[diverge] {
            diverge += 1
        }

        let numBackspaces = currentRendered.count - diverge
        let replacementChars = Array(next.suffix(from: diverge))

        // Emit backspaces
        for _ in 0..<numBackspaces {
            if let down = CGEvent(keyboardEventSource: source, virtualKey: 0x33, keyDown: true),
               let up = CGEvent(keyboardEventSource: source, virtualKey: 0x33, keyDown: false) {
                down.post(tap: .cgSessionEventTap)
                up.post(tap: .cgSessionEventTap)
            }
        }

        // Emit replacement characters in a single multi-char CGEvent
        if !replacementChars.isEmpty {
            var chars = replacementChars
            if let down = CGEvent(keyboardEventSource: source, virtualKey: 0, keyDown: true),
               let up = CGEvent(keyboardEventSource: source, virtualKey: 0, keyDown: false) {
                down.keyboardSetUnicodeString(stringLength: chars.count, unicodeString: &chars)
                up.keyboardSetUnicodeString(stringLength: chars.count, unicodeString: &chars)
                down.post(tap: .cgSessionEventTap)
                up.post(tap: .cgSessionEventTap)
            }
        }

        currentRendered = next
    }"

# How do I use CGEventKeyboardSetUnicodeString with multiple characters?
Ask Question
Asked 16 years, 5 months ago
Modified [9 years, 7 months ago](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/2123873/how-do-i-use-cgeventkeyboardsetunicodestring-with-multiple-characters?lastactivity "2016-11-06 12:50:18Z")
Viewed 2k times
2
I'm trying to use event taps to create an OS X program that will listen for Yiddish typed in transliteration and post the result in Hebrew characters. I made a very short program to test one things I'd have to do: http://pastie.org/791398
As is, the program successfully replaces every typed 'q' with 'w':
```
if(inputString[0] == 'q') { inputString[0] = 'w'; }
```
But how does one post a string of more than one character? For instance, if someone types 'sh' you'd presumably have to post a backspace (to delete the character that was posted for 's' alone) and then post the character that corresponds to 'sh'. However, this code results in only a backspace being posted:
```
else if(inputString[0] == 'm') { inputString[0] = '\b'; inputString[1] = 'n'; }
```
I apologize if these are basic questions; I have read all the documentation I could find, but I might not have understood it all. It's also possible that I'm going about this entirely the wrong way.
* macos
* quartz-graphics
* keypress
* cgeventtap

## 2 Answers 2

Ideally you should be using an input method instead of a program with event taps, most likely using [Input Method Kit](http://developer.apple.com/mac/library/documentation/Cocoa/Reference/InputMethodKitFrameworkRef/index.html#//apple_ref/doc/uid/<redacted:team-id>) if you don't need to support pre-10.5. Using event taps for this purpose is inherently a bad idea because the user can change where he/she is typing with the mouse as well as the keyboard. So if the user typed a "s" in one text field followed by a "h" in another, you wouldn't be able to tell the difference.
That said, here's a direct answer to your question.
The string is length-counted, so you can't just provide the incoming length (1); the second character will be ignored. However, most applications also don't like to get more than a single character per event, so they'll just discard the remaining characters. (Terminal is a notable exception.)
So what you can do is simply post a second event with the second character in it.
```
else if(inputString[0] == 'm') {
  inputString[0] = 'n';
  CGEventKeyboardSetUnicodeString(event, 1, inputString);
  CGEventPost(kCGSessionEventTap, event);
  inputString[0] = '\b';
}
```
In the general case (simulating > 2 keypresses) you'll need to create an event for each character you want to insert. [This mailing list post](http://www.mail-archive.com/<redacted:email>/msg23343.html) includes a simple example.

// 1 - Get the string length in bytes.        
NSUInteger l = [string lengthOfBytesUsingEncoding:NSUTF16StringEncoding];

// 2 - Get bytes for unicode characters
UniChar *uc = malloc(l);
[string getBytes:uc maxLength:l usedLength:NULL encoding:NSUTF16StringEncoding options:0 range:NSMakeRange(0, l) remainingRange:NULL];

// 3 - create an empty tap event, and set unicode string
CGEventRef tap = CGEventCreateKeyboardEvent(NULL,0, YES);
CGEventKeyboardSetUnicodeString(tap, string.length, uc);

// 4 - Send event and tear down
CGEventPost(kCGSessionEventTap, tap);
CFRelease(tap);
free(uc);
```

# Safari Web Content Guide
PDF Companion File
* Table of Contents

# Handling Events
This chapter describes the events that occur when the user interacts with a webpage on iOS. Forms and documents generate the typical events in iOS that you might expect on the desktop. Gestures handled by Safari on iOS emulate mouse events. In addition, you can register for iOS-specific multi-touch and gesture events directly. Orientation events are another example of an iOS-specific event. Also, be aware that there are some unsupported events such as cut, copy, and paste.
Gestures that the user makes—for example, a double tap to zoom and a flick to pan—emulate mouse events. However, the flow of events generated by one-finger and two-finger gestures are conditional depending on whether or not the selected element is clickable or scrollable as described in One-Finger Events and Two-Finger Events .
In addition, you can turn off the default Safari on iOS behavior as described in Preventing Default Behavior and handle your own multi-touch and gesture events directly. Handling multi-touch and gesture events directly gives developers the ability to implement unique touch-screen interfaces similar to native applications. Read Handling Multi-Touch Events and Handling Gesture Events to learn more about DOM touch events.
If you want to change the layout of your webpage depending on the orientation of iOS, read Handling Orientation Events .
See Supported Events for a complete list of events supported in iOS.
On iOS, emulated mouse events are sent so quickly that the down or active pseudo state of buttons may never occur. Read Highlighting Elements for how to customize a button to behave similar to the desktop.
It’s very common to combine DOM touch events with CSS visual effects. Read _Safari CSS Visual Effects Guide_ to learn more about CSS visual effects.

...

## One-Finger Events
**Figure 6-3** The double-tap gesture The double-tap gesture
Mouse events are delivered in the same order you'd expect in other web browsers illustrated in Figure 6-4 . If the user taps a nonclickable element, no events are generated. If the user taps a clickable element, events arrive in this order: `mouseover` , `mousemove` , `mousedown` , `mouseup` , and `click` . The `mouseout` event occurs only if the user taps on another clickable item. Also, if the contents of the page changes on the `mousemove` event, no subsequent events in the sequence are sent. This behavior allows the user to tap in the new content.
**Figure 6-4** One-finger gesture emulating a mouse One-finger gesture emulating a mouse

## Two-Finger Events
The pinch open gesture does not generate any mouse events as shown in Figure 6-5 .
**Figure 6-5** The pinch open gesture The pinch open gesture
Figure 6-6 illustrates the mouse events generated by using two fingers to pan a scrollable element. The flow of events is as follows:
* If the user holds two fingers down on a scrollable element and moves the fingers, `mousewheel` events are generated.
* If the element is not scrollable, Safari on iOS pans the webpage. No events are generated while panning.
* An `onscroll` event is generated when the user stops panning.
**Figure 6-6** Two-finger panning gesture Two-finger panning gesture

...

## Handling Multi-Touch Events
You can use JavaScript DOM touch event classes available on iOS to handle multi-touch and gesture events in a way similar to the way they are handled in native iOS applications.
If you register for multi-touch events, the system continually sends `TouchEvent` objects to those DOM elements as fingers touch and move across a surface. These are sent in addition to the emulated mouse events unless you prevent this default behavior as described in Preventing Default Behavior . A touch event provides a snapshot of all touches during a multi-touch sequence, most importantly the touches that are new or have changed for a particular target. The different types of multi-touch events are described in _[Touch Class Reference](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/webkitjs/touch)_ .

# CGEvent
Defines an opaque type that represents a low-level hardware event.
Mac Catalyst macOS
```
class CGEvent
```

## Overview
Low-level hardware events of this type are referred to as Quartz events. A typical event in macOS originates when the user manipulates an input device such as a mouse or a keyboard. The device driver associated with that device, through the I/O Kit, creates a low-level event, puts it in the window server’s event queue, and notifies the window server. The window server creates a Quartz event, annotates the event, and dispatches the event to the appropriate run-loop port of the target process. There the event is picked up by the Carbon Event Manager and forwarded to the event-handling mechanism appropriate to the application environment. You can use event taps to gain access to Quartz events at several different steps in this process.
This opaque type is derived from CFType and inherits the properties that all Core Foundation types have in common. For more information, see `CFType Ref` .

# How do I use CGEventKeyboardSetUnicodeString with multiple characters?

Ask Question

Asked 16 years, 5 months ago

I'm trying to use event taps to create an OS X program that will listen for Yiddish typed in transliteration and post the result in Hebrew characters. I made a very short program to test one things I'd have to do: <http://pastie.org/791398>

As is, the program successfully replaces every typed 'q' with 'w':

```
if(inputString[0] == 'q') { inputString[0] = 'w'; }
```

But how does one post a string of more than one character? For instance, if someone types 'sh' you'd presumably have to post a backspace (to delete the character that was posted for 's' alone) and then post the character that corresponds to 'sh'. However, this code results in only a backspace being posted:

```
else if(inputString[0] == 'm') { inputString[0] = '\b'; inputString[1] = 'n'; }
```

I apologize if these are basic questions; I have read all the documentation I could find, but I might not have understood it all. It's also possible that I'm going about this entirely the wrong way.

## 2 Answers 2

Ideally you should be using an input method instead of a program with event taps, most likely using [Input Method Kit](http://developer.apple.com/mac/library/documentation/Cocoa/Reference/InputMethodKitFrameworkRef/index.html#//apple_ref/doc/uid/<redacted:team-id>) if you don't need to support pre-10.5. Using event taps for this purpose is inherently a bad idea because the user can change where he/she is typing with the mouse as well as the keyboard. So if the user typed a "s" in one text field followed by a "h" in another, you wouldn't be able to tell the difference.

That said, here's a direct answer to your question.

The string is length-counted, so you can't just provide the incoming length (1); the second character will be ignored. However, most applications also don't like to get more than a single character per event, so they'll just discard the remaining characters. (Terminal is a notable exception.)

So what you can do is simply post a second event with the second character in it.

```
else if(inputString[0] == 'm') {
  inputString[0] = 'n';
  CGEventKeyboardSetUnicodeString(event, 1, inputString);
  CGEventPost(kCGSessionEventTap, event);
  inputString[0] = '\b';
}
```

In the general case (simulating > 2 keypresses) you'll need to create an event for each character you want to insert. [This mailing list post](http://www.mail-archive.com/<redacted:email>/msg23343.html) includes a simple example.

// 2 - Get bytes for unicode characters
UniChar *uc = malloc(l);
[string getBytes:uc maxLength:l usedLength:NULL encoding:NSUTF16StringEncoding options:0 range:NSMakeRange(0, l) remainingRange:NULL];

// 3 - create an empty tap event, and set unicode string
CGEventRef tap = CGEventCreateKeyboardEvent(NULL,0, YES);
CGEventKeyboardSetUnicodeString(tap, string.length, uc);

// 4 - Send event and tear down
CGEventPost(kCGSessionEventTap, tap);
CFRelease(tap);
free(uc);

2: 
3: A playground prototype for a Vietnamese Telex input method on macOS. The core engine (`liblex`) is a Zig static library that models each rendered character as a **span** (base + modifier + tone), handling the full Telex input set: all vowels with diacritics (â, ă, ê, ô, ơ, ư), tones (sắc, huyền, hỏi, ngã, nặng), đ, cancellation logic, `gi`/`qu` onset reclassification, and `ươ` auto-fill. The shell (`Lex.swift`) is a macOS menubar app that intercepts keystrokes via `CGEventTap`, feeds them to the engine, and applies a **diff** against the currently rendered text — emitting only the minimal sequence of synthetic backspaces followed by a single multi-character insertion event to update the active application.
4: 
5: ## Architecture
6: 
7: The system is split into two layers communicating through a C ABI:
8: 
9: - **Core (`src/liblex.zig`)** — A span-based composition engine. Each keystroke mutates an array of `Span` structs (base letter, modifier, tone, flags). The engine handles modifier application (doubled vowels `aa`→`â`, `w`→`ơ`/`ư`/`ă`, `dd`→`đ`), tone placement following Vietnamese linguistic rules (region analysis: onset → nucleus → coda, with semi-vowel coda detection), cancellation (repeating a filled modifier/tone strips it and enters literal mode), `gi`/`qu` onset binding, and `ươ` auto-fill. Unicode output is produced via lookup tables covering all 12 vowel bases × 6 tone variants in both cases. The engine exposes `add`, `backspace`, `reset`, `get_composed_utf16`, `init_state`, and `state_size`.
10: 
11: - **Shell (`macos/Lex.swift`)** — A menubar-only macOS app (`LSUIElement=true`) that owns the engine state and a rendered-text snapshot. On each keystroke it calls the engine, reads the new composed UTF-16, and diffs it against the snapshot to compute the minimal edit (common-prefix comparison). Replacement characters are emitted in a single multi-character `CGEvent` to reduce flicker. Synthetic events are tagged (`0x4C4558`) to avoid feedback loops. The shell resets engine state on app switches, mouse clicks, modifier keys (Cmd/Ctrl/Alt), navigation keys (arrows, Home/End, Tab, Escape, Return, forward delete), and tap-disabled events. A global hotkey (Ctrl+Opt+Space) toggles Vietnamese input on/off with audio feedback.
12: 
13: - **FFI bridge (`src/liblex.h`)** — C-compatible header declaring the engine API. Swift calls into the Zig static library through this bridging header. The engine is stateless from the caller's perspective — Swift allocates the opaque state buffer (`state_size()` bytes) and passes it to every call.
14: 
15: ## Prerequisites
16: 
17: - **Zig ≥ 0.16.0** (master recommended) — [download](https://ziglang.org/download/)
18: - **Xcode Command Line Tools** — `xcode-select --install`
19: - **macOS 26** (Tahoe)
20: 
21: ## Project Structure
22: 
23: ```
24: prototype-app/
25: ├── src/
26: │   ├── liblex.zig              # Span-based Telex engine (C library)
27: │   └── liblex.h                # C bridging header
28: ├── macos/
29: │   ├── Lex.app/
30: │   │   └── Contents/
31: │   │       └── Info.plist      # LSUIElement=true (menubar-only)
32: │   └── Lex.swift               # macOS app shell (diff-based rendering)
33: ├── build.zig                   # Zig build script (full pipeline)
34: ├── build.zig.zon               # Zig build manifest
35: └── .tool-versions              # Version management (zig master)
36: ```
37: 
38: ## Build
39: 
40: The `build.zig` script automates the entire pipeline — building the Zig static library, re-packing the archive (Zig master workaround for non-8-byte-aligned archive members), compiling Swift, and ad-hoc codesigning — in a single command:
41: 
42: ```sh
43: zig build
44: ```
45: 
46: To build and immediately launch the app:
47: 
48: ```sh
49: zig build run
50: ```
51: 
52: Or run the binary directly to see console output:
53:

55: ./macos/Lex.app/Contents/MacOS/Lex
56: ```
57: 
58: ### Manual steps (for reference)
59: 
60: <details>
61: <summary>Expand manual build steps</summary>
62: 
63: #### Step 1: Build the Zig static library
64: 
65: ```sh
66: zig build
67: ```
68: 
69: This produces `zig-out/lib/liblex.a`.
70: 
71: #### Step 2: Re-pack the archive (Zig master workaround)
72: 
73: Zig master produces archives with non-8-byte-aligned members that Apple's linker rejects. Re-pack with the system `ar`:
74: 
75: ```sh
76: cd zig-out/lib && \
77:   tmp=$(mktemp -d) && \
78:   (cd "$tmp" && ar x "$(cd - && pwd)/liblex.a" && chmod 644 *.o && /usr/bin/ar rcs "$(cd - && pwd)/liblex.a" *.o) && \
79:   rm -rf "$tmp" && \
80:   cd ../..
81: ```
82: 
83: #### Step 3: Compile Swift and link with the Zig library
84: 
85: ```sh
86: swiftc macos/Lex.swift \
87:     -import-objc-header src/liblex.h \
88:     -Lzig-out/lib -llex \
89:     -o macos/Lex.app/Contents/MacOS/Lex

91: 
92: #### Step 4: Sign the app (ad-hoc, for local development)
93: 
94: ```sh
95: codesign -f -s - macos/Lex.app
96: ```
97: 
98: </details>
99: 
100: ## Signing
101: 
102: ### Ad-hoc (local development)
103: 
104: Ad-hoc signing is sufficient for local testing and is performed automatically by `zig build`:
105: 
106: ```sh
107: codesign -f -s - macos/Lex.app
108: ```
109: 
110: ### Hardened Runtime (for notarization)
111: 
112: Requires a signing identity and entitlements:
113: 
114: ```sh
115: codesign -f -s "YOUR_IDENTITY" \
116:     --options runtime \

119: 
120: #### Finding your signing identity
121: 
122: List available identities:
123:

126: ```
127: 
128: ## Permissions
129: 
130: **Accessibility** is required for `CGEventTap` to intercept keyboard events. This is a TCC (Transparency, Consent, and Control) permission — not an entitlement.
131: 
132: On first launch, the app calls `AXIsProcessTrustedWithOptions()` which prompts the user. Grant access in:
133: 
134: > **System Settings → Privacy & Security → Accessibility**
135: 
136: Then relaunch the app.
137: 
138: ## Known Limitations
139: 
140: This is a **prototype-grade** application:
141: 
142: - **Synthetic event fragility** — the backspace+multi-char-insert approach is unreliable in terminal emulators, Electron-based apps, and secure input fields where `CGEventTap` may be blocked or events reordered. Some apps may not handle multi-character `keyboardSetUnicodeString` correctly.

145: - **Secure input fields block the tap** — password fields and other secure text inputs disable event taps by design.
146: - **Non-US layouts not handled** — only tested with standard US keyboard layout.
147: - **No Dock icon** — `LSUIElement=true` means the app only appears in the menubar.",
546:                    "result": "Based on the event handling implementation in `macos/Lex.swift` and the reference prototype, the following constraints and decisions inform a conceptual critique of the event handling order, reset behavior, and modifier chord strategy:

### 1. Event Handling Order
* **Current Order:** The callback processes events in the following sequence:
  1. **Tap Status/System Events:** Handles tap-disabled events (`.tapDisabledByTimeout`, `.tapDisabledByUserInput`) to re-enable the tap and reset the engine.
  2. **Mouse Events:** Intercepts mouse clicks (`.leftMouseDown`, `.rightMouseDown`) to immediately reset the engine (since a click implies the text caret has moved).
  3. **Modifier Flags:** Passes through `.flagsChanged` events without resetting the engine to allow plain modifier keys (like Shift or Caps Lock) to function normally.
  4. **Key Down Events (`.keyDown`):**
     * Filters out the engine's own synthetic events (using a unique user data tag) to prevent infinite feedback loops.
     * Bypasses processing entirely if the app is in literal mode.
     * Intercepts specific non-alphanumeric keycodes (like Backspace/Delete) to keep the engine's internal buffer synchronized with the editor, passing them through.
     * Filters out non-alphanumeric characters (e.g., punctuation, numbers, and Space) and resets the engine.
     * Feeds valid alphabetic characters to the engine, calculating synthetic backspaces and posting replacement characters.
* **Critique/Constraint:** The current order is highly fragile because it performs character extraction and validation *before* checking for modifier chords. This means modifier-key combinations (like Command + T) are evaluated as alphabetic characters first, which can block system hotkeys or corrupt the engine state.

### 2. Reset on Space and App Switches
* **App Switches:** App switching is handled out-of-band by registering a global observer on `NSWorkspace.didActivateApplicationNotification`. When triggered, it calls `resetEngine()`, which is clean and decoupled from the low-level event tap.
* **Space and Non-Alphanumerics:** Space (character code 32) is not explicitly handled as a special keycode. Instead, it falls through to the Unicode character extraction. Because Space is non-alphabetic, it fails the `is_alphabetic` validation check, which triggers `app_delegate.engine.reset()` and passes the Space event through. 
* **Critique/Constraint:** Relying on a generic "non-alphabetic" fallback to reset on Space is implicit. Explicitly handling Space (and other word-boundary keys like Return, Tab, or Escape) as early, dedicated reset triggers ensures predictable state clearing.

### 3. Modifier Chord Strategy
* **Current Strategy:** The prototype app handles modifier chords by checking if the event flags intersect with a modifier mask (`.maskCommand`, `.maskControl`, `.maskAlternate`). If a modifier is held, it resets the engine and passes the event through.
* **Critique/Constraint:** In the production `macos/Lex.swift`, this modifier check is missing or misplaced. Because the event tap intercepts `.keyDown` and immediately attempts to extract and validate Unicode characters, pressing a chord like `Cmd + T` or `Cmd + V` gets treated as an alphabetic input (`T` or `V`). This either blocks the hotkey or feeds unwanted characters into the engine. To prevent interference, the modifier chord check must be positioned at the very beginning of the `.keyDown` handling block, immediately resetting the engine and passing the event through before any character extraction occurs.",
553:                "message": "## 1) TL;DR

The minimal correct fix is to make `keyDown` classify “must pass through” cases before any Unicode/text composition: synthetic events first, then Command/Control/Option chords, then plain Space as an explicit reset boundary. Add an app-activation observer to reset state on app switches. Keep `flagsChanged` passive; do not reset on plain Shift or Caps Lock.

## 2) Recommended approach: simple path

1. **Keep current top-level event handling structure**
   - Tap-disabled events: reset, re-enable tap, pass through.
   - Mouse down: reset, pass through.
   - `flagsChanged`: pass through without resetting.
   - Only `keyDown` should participate in composition logic.

2. **Add app-switch reset out of band**
   - Observe `NSWorkspace.didActivateApplicationNotification`.
   - On activation change, reset the Telex engine state.
   - This is the right layer because app switches may happen without a relevant keyboard event reaching the tap.

3. **Reorder `keyDown` handling conceptually**
   - First: ignore Lex’s own synthetic events.
   - Then: check whether Command, Control, or Option is held.
     - If yes, reset state and pass the original event through.
     - This must happen before literal-mode handling, backspace handling, Unicode extraction, alphabetic checks, or synthetic replacement.
   - Then: explicitly treat plain Space as a word-boundary reset.
     - Reset state.
     - Pass Space through.
     - Do not rely only on the generic “non-alphabetic” fallback.
   - Then: apply literal-mode pass-through.
     - If literal mode is active, do not compose.
   - Then: handle plain Backspace.
     - Modified Backspace should already have been caught by the modifier-chord rule and should reset/pass through.
   - Then: do Unicode extraction and alphabetic Telex processing.

4. **Do not reset on plain Shift/Caps `flagsChanged`**
   - Shift and Caps Lock are casing mechanisms, not text-boundary or context-changing actions.
   - Resetting on them would make uppercase Telex input fragile.

## 3) Rationale and trade-offs

The current risky part is that modifier chords are not classified early enough. A `Command+T` or `Command+V` keyDown can still look like an alphabetic `T` or `V` when Unicode is extracted, so the Telex path may consume or transform a shortcut that should belong to the active app.

The safest minimal rule is:

> Any `keyDown` with Command, Control, or Option is not text input for Telex. Reset and pass it through.

That covers app shortcuts, paste, tab/window commands, browser shortcuts, terminal shortcuts, and modified deletes without needing to understand every shortcut individually.

Explicit Space handling is also worth doing even though the current non-alpha fallback may already reset on Space. Space is semantically important: it ends the current composition span/word. Making it a named reset case avoids future regressions if the fallback logic changes.

Effort: **S, likely <1h** conceptually and implementation-wise.

## 4) Risks and guardrails

- **Do not include Shift in the modifier-chord reset mask.**  
  Shifted letters should still compose normally.

- **Do not reset on `flagsChanged` for Shift/Caps.**  
  `flagsChanged` is not text input. Resetting there creates surprising behavior while typing uppercase syllables.

- **Check modifier chords before Backspace.**  
  Plain Backspace can update the engine buffer, but `Command+Delete`, `Option+Delete`, and similar editing shortcuts should reset/pass through because they may delete whole lines/words or otherwise invalidate the internal buffer.

- **Check modifier chords before Unicode extraction.**  
  Unicode extraction under Command/Control/Option can still produce a character-like value, which is exactly why shortcuts can be accidentally swallowed.

- **Synthetic event filtering should remain very early.**  
  Lex-generated replacement/backspace events must not re-enter the composition path. If the event mask expands later to include more keyboard event types, revisit synthetic filtering for those too.

- **App switch reset is necessary but not sufficient.**  
  It handles cross-app context changes. It does not cover all intra-app focus/caret moves, so mouse reset and shortcut reset are still needed.

- **Ctrl+Option+Space toggle should remain safe.**  
  The chord rule should reset and pass it through; the registered hotkey can toggle mode separately. A double reset is harmless.

## 5) When to consider expanding reset cases

After the minimal fix, consider broader reset coverage only if users observe stale composition after navigation or editing. Concrete triggers:

- Telex state survives after Return/Enter, Tab, Escape, or arrow navigation.
- State survives after Home/End/Page Up/Page Down.
- State becomes wrong after forward delete.
- State becomes wrong after intra-app focus changes, keyboard-driven field switching, or selection changes.
- Paste/undo/redo/menu commands leave the engine buffer inconsistent despite modifier-chord reset.
- Non-US layouts, dead keys, or Option-produced characters need first-class behavior.

## 6) Optional future expansion path

If needed later, add a small “reset-and-pass-through key” classification after the modifier-chord check and before composition. Candidate groups:

- Word/field boundaries: Return, Enter, Tab, Escape.
- Navigation: arrows, Home, End, Page Up, Page Down.
- Destructive edits: forward delete, possibly modified delete variants if not already covered by modifiers.
- Context changes: additional focus/window notifications if app-switch and mouse resets are not enough.

But do not add all of this immediately unless there is observed breakage. The minimal high-value fix is modifier chords plus explicit Space plus app-switch reset.",

The current callback in [`macos/Lex.swift`](file:///<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L394-L553) has a reasonable top-level structure:

1. tap-disabled events reset/re-enable/pass through
2. mouse clicks reset/pass through
3. `flagsChanged` passes through
4. `keyDown` does the real Telex work

The weak point is inside `keyDown`: after synthetic-event filtering, it goes directly to literal-mode check, backspace handling, Unicode extraction, alphabetic detection, engine mutation, and synthetic replacement. There is no early “this is a shortcut/modifier chord, not text input” classification.

That explains the `Command+T`, `Command+V`, etc. problem: a modified key event can still yield a single alphabetic Unicode character, so the callback treats it as Telex input and may swallow it.

## Minimal first approach

### 1. Keep top-level event order

Current top-level handling is acceptable:

- tap disabled → reset, re-enable, pass through
- mouse down → reset, pass through
- flags changed → pass through
- key down → inspect further

I would not expand `flagsChanged` yet. In particular, do not reset on plain Shift/Caps Lock, because those are part of normal uppercase text input.

### 2. Reorder `keyDown` handling conceptually

The minimal correct `keyDown` order should be:

```diagram
╭──────────────╮
│ keyDown only │
╰──────┬───────╯
       ▼
╭──────────────────────────╮
│ Lex synthetic event?      │──yes──▶ pass through
╰──────┬───────────────────╯
       ▼ no
╭──────────────────────────╮
│ Cmd/Ctrl/Option held?     │──yes──▶ reset + pass through
╰──────┬───────────────────╯
       ▼ no
╭──────────────────────────╮
│ Space key?                │──yes──▶ reset + pass through
╰──────┬───────────────────╯
       ▼ no
╭──────────────────────────╮
│ literal mode?             │──yes──▶ pass through
╰──────┬───────────────────╯
       ▼ no
╭──────────────────────────╮
│ plain Backspace?          │──yes──▶ engine backspace + pass through
╰──────┬───────────────────╯
       ▼ no
╭──────────────────────────╮
│ Unicode/text extraction   │
│ alphabetic Telex handling │
╰──────────────────────────╯
```

The important change is: modifier chords must be handled before Unicode extraction and before engine mutation.

### 3. SPACE reset

Current code already resets on Space indirectly, because Space is non-alphabetic and reaches the reset fallback at [`macos/Lex.swift`](file:///<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L451-L470).

But I would still make Space an explicit reset boundary in the conceptual order. Reason: Space is not just “some non-alpha key”; it is the normal word boundary for Telex composition. Treating it explicitly makes the behavior intentional and harder to break later.

### 4. App-switch reset

Current app does not observe app switches. The prototype does this with `NSWorkspace.didActivateApplicationNotification` in [`playground/prototype-app/macos/Lex.swift`](file:///<redacted>/lex/playground/prototype-app/macos/Lex.swift#L61-L68).

Minimal approach: add an app activation observer that resets the engine when the active app changes.

This belongs outside the event callback because app switches may happen in ways that are not cleanly represented as a normal key event to this tap.

### 5. Modifier handling

Minimal rule:

> Any `keyDown` with Command, Control, or Option held is not Telex text input. Reset engine state and pass the event through.

Do not include Shift or Caps Lock in this rule.

This should fix `Command+T`, `Command+V`, paste, browser/tab shortcuts, terminal shortcuts, app shortcuts, and modified delete/navigation commands without needing a special list of hotkeys.

The prototype has the same core idea at [`playground/prototype-app/macos/Lex.swift`](file:///<redacted>/lex/playground/prototype-app/macos/Lex.swift#L232-L239).

## Oracle perspective

Oracle agreed with the minimal approach:

- keep top-level event handling structure
- add app-switch reset via `NSWorkspace.didActivateApplicationNotification`
- filter synthetic events early
- handle Command/Control/Option chords before Unicode extraction
- make Space an explicit reset boundary
- keep `flagsChanged` passive for now
- do not reset on Shift/Caps Lock
- expand navigation/editing reset cases only after observed stale-state behavior

Oracle also called out one important ordering point: modified Backspace should be caught by the modifier-chord rule before plain Backspace handling, because `Command+Delete` / `Option+Delete` may delete larger text regions and invalidate the engine buffer.

## Expansion cases to discuss later

I would not add these in the first change unless you already see failures:

1. Return / Enter reset
2. Tab reset
3. Escape reset
4. Arrow keys reset
5. Home / End / PageUp / PageDown reset
6. Forward delete reset
7. focus change inside the same app
8. selection changes
9. paste/undo/redo/menu commands beyond the generic modifier-chord reset
10. Option-produced text on non-US layouts or dead-key input

The first minimal implementation target should be only:

- explicit Space reset
- app-switch reset
- Command/Control/Option `keyDown` reset + pass-through
- no Shift/Caps reset
- no broader navigation-key table yet unless current behavior proves stale state remains after those keys

737:          "text": "## Answers

### How to detect Cmd / Ctrl / Opt held?

In the `CGEventTap` callback, use `event.flags`.

Conceptually:

- Command: `CGEventFlags.maskCommand`
- Control: `CGEventFlags.maskControl`
- Option/Alt: `CGEventFlags.maskAlternate`

The rule should be:

> On `keyDown`, if `event.flags` intersects Command / Control / Option, reset engine and pass through.

Do not include Shift. Shifted letters should still be valid Telex input.

Also note: Carbon hotkey registration uses `controlKey | optionKey`, but the event tap uses `CGEventFlags.maskControl` / `.maskAlternate`. They are different APIs.

### What is the Space keycode name?

Use Carbon’s:

- `kVK_Space`

Its value is `49` / `0x31`, but use the named constant.

You are already using it for the global hotkey registration in [`register_toggle_input_mode_hot_key`](file:///<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L210-L217).

Backspace is currently using:

- `kVK_Delete`

That name is confusing, but in Carbon it means the normal Backspace/Delete key.

Forward Delete would be:

- `kVK_ForwardDelete`

## About adding modifiers + Space into the existing switch

Space belongs naturally in the existing `switch key_code` beside Backspace.

Modifier handling is different: it is not a keycode case for `Cmd+T`, `Cmd+V`, etc. The keycode is still `T` or `V`; the modifier state is in `event.flags`.

So I would structure it like this conceptually:

1. synthetic event check
2. modifier-chord check using `event.flags`
3. get `key_code`
4. `switch key_code`
   - `kVK_Space`: reset + pass through
   - `kVK_Delete`: engine backspace + pass through
   - default: continue to Unicode/alphabetic handling

So: yes, put Space with Backspace in the existing switch, but put modifier detection immediately before that switch, not as a switch case.

## Are you missing anything?

A few ordering details:

### 1. Modifier check should happen before Unicode extraction

This is the main bug source. `Command+V` can still look like the character `v` if you ask for Unicode, so the event must be classified as a shortcut first.

### 2. Modifier check should happen before Backspace handling

Plain Backspace can update the engine.

But `Option+Backspace`, `Command+Backspace`, etc. may delete a word/line or trigger app behavior. Those should reset + pass through, not call `engine.backspace()`.

### 3. Ctrl+Opt+Space hotkey should still work

If you handle modifiers first:

- Ctrl+Opt+Space reaches “modifier chord”
- engine resets
- event passes through
- Carbon hotkey handler can still toggle mode

A double reset is harmless because `toggle_input_mode()` already resets.

### 4. App switch reset is separate

You still need `NSWorkspace.didActivateApplicationNotification` for app switching. It should not be inside the event callback because app switches are not guaranteed to be represented as a useful keyboard event.

### 5. Literal mode order is not critical, but I prefer modifier reset before literal pass-through

If literal mode is active, you can pass everything through and probably be fine.

But for a consistent “shortcuts are context boundaries” rule, I would still check modifiers before literal mode and reset. It is harmless and makes behavior simpler:

- synthetic? pass
- modifier chord? reset + pass
- Space? reset + pass
- literal? pass
- Backspace/text handling

If you want the smallest possible behavioral change, keep literal mode before modifier handling. But then shortcuts in literal mode will not reset state. Since mode toggling already resets, this probably does not matter.",

957:          "text": "## Result: yes, it mostly achieves the intended minimal behavior

Your implementation in [`event_tap_callback`](file:///<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L414-L450) now does the important things:

- `Command+T`, `Command+V`, etc. should no longer be consumed by Telex.
- `Control`, `Option`, and `Command` chords reset the engine and pass through.
- `Space` explicitly resets and passes through.
- plain Backspace still updates engine state and passes through.
- Shift/Caps are not treated as reset modifiers.

That matches the minimal target.

## One ordering difference to be aware of

You currently check literal mode before synthetic-event filtering and before modifier/Space reset:

[`macos/Lex.swift#L417-L434`](file:///<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L417-L434)

That means:

- in Telex mode: behavior is correct
- in literal mode:
  - `Command+T`, `Command+V`, etc. pass through, but do not reset engine
  - `Space` passes through, but does not reset engine
  - synthetic events pass through, but are not identified first

This is probably okay because `toggle_input_mode()` already resets when entering literal mode, and literal mode does not mutate the engine. So practically, there should be no stale engine state to reset.

But if you want the stronger invariant:

> Space and modifier shortcuts are always composition boundaries regardless of input mode

then literal-mode pass-through should come after synthetic/modifier/Space handling.

I do not think that is required for the minimal fix, but it is the main semantic difference from the earlier order.

## Modifier handling is in the right place

This part is correctly before the keycode switch and before Unicode extraction:

[`macos/Lex.swift#L427-L434`](file:///<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L427-L434)

That is the important fix. `Command+V` can still look like `v` if you ask for Unicode, so checking `event.flags` before text extraction is correct.

Also good: this check comes before Backspace. So `Option+Backspace` / `Command+Backspace` will reset and pass through instead of calling `engine.backspace()` incorrectly.

## Space handling is correct

This is good:

[`macos/Lex.swift#L439-L443`](file:///<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L439-L443)

Using `kVK_Space` is correct. Handling it explicitly makes the word-boundary behavior intentional instead of relying on the later non-alphabetic fallback.

## Are you missing anything?

For the minimal target: no major missing piece, given that you intentionally ignore app-switch reset for now.

The only things I would keep in mind:

1. **Literal mode does not reset on Space/modifiers with current order.** Probably fine, but worth being intentional about.
2. **Navigation keys are still handled only indirectly.** Many will reach `character_count != 1` and reset/pass through. That is acceptable for now.
3. **Forward Delete is not explicitly handled.** It likely resets through the no-character path, but if you later expand special-key handling, add `kVK_ForwardDelete` explicitly.
4. **Tiny style issue:** there is trailing whitespace after the closing brace at [`macos/Lex.swift#L434`](file:///<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L427-L434). Not behavior-affecting.

My recommendation: keep this as the minimal behavior, unless you want the stricter invariant that Space/modifier reset should happen even while in literal mode.",

# Apple randomly closes bug reports unless you “verify” the bug remains unfixed
## March 25 2026
In March 2023, I filed <redacted:team-id> “Privacy: Network filter extension TCP connection and IP address leak.” I mentioned this bug report at the time in a blog post , which included the same steps to reproduce and example Xcode project that I provided to Apple. In the three years since I filed the bug report, I received no response whatsoever from Apple… until a couple of weeks ago, when Apple asked me to “verify” the issue with macOS 26.4 beta 4 and update my bug report.

...

Although I didn’t install the beta myself, I spoke to [the developers of Little Snitch](https://www.obdev.at/products/littlesnitch/) , who do run the macOS betas, and they kindly informed me that in their testing, they could still reproduce my issue with macOS 26.4 beta 4. It was no surprise, then, that when I updated to macOS 26.4, released to the public yesterday by Apple, I could still reproduce the bug with my instructions and example project. It appears that Apple knowingly sent me on a wild goose chase, demanding that I “verify” a bug they did nothing to fix, perhaps praying that the bug had magically disappeared on its own, with no effort from Apple.

# InputMethodKit

Develop input methods and manage communication with client applications, candidates windows, and input method modes.

macOS 10.5+

## Overview

The Input Method Kit, introduced in OS X v10.5, provides a streamlined programming interface that lets you develop input methods with far less code than older Mac programming interfaces. It is fully integrated with the Text Services Manager. The Input Method Kit allows 32-bit applications to work with 64-bit applications.

The Input Method Kit provides classes and protocols for managing communication with client applications, candidates windows, and input method modes. Input methods supply text from a conversion engine (written in any language, such as C, C++, Objective-C, Python, and so on), key bindings and optional event handling, and information about your input method in an extended `Info .plist` file. You also have the option to provide menu items that support input-method-specific commands or preferences settings.

## Topics

### Classes

`class IMKCandidates`

The `IMKCandidates` class presents candidates to users and notifies the appropriate `IMKInput Controller` object when the user selects a candidate. **Candidates** are alternate characters for a given input sequence. The `IMKCandidates` class supports using a candidates window in your input method; using `IMKCandidates` is optional. Not all input methods require them.

`class IMKInput Controller`

The `IMKInput Controller` class provides a base class for custom input controller classes. The `IMKServer` class, which is allocated in the main function of an input method, creates an input controller object for each input session created by a client application. For every input session there is a corresponding `IMKInput Controller` object.

`class IMKServer`

The `IMKServer` class manages client connections to your input method. When you write the main function for your input method, you create an `IMKServer` object. You should never need to override this class.

### Protocols

`protocol IMKMouse Handling`

The `IMKMouse Handling` protocol defines methods that your input method can implement to handle mouse events.

IMKServer Input

`IMKServer Input` is an informal protocol that defines methods for receiving text events. This is intentionally not a formal protocol because there are three ways to receive events. An input method chooses one of the following approaches and implements the appropriate methods:

`protocol IMKState Setting`

The `IMKState Setting` protocol defines methods for setting or accessing values that indicate the state of an input method.

Handling Keyboard Hotkeys and Shortcuts across Multiple Languages

We have a requirement to manage the shortcuts and hotkeys in our application, and have it to be intuitive and support multi-lingual fully. The understanding that we have currently is that most universal shortcuts and hotkeys on MacOS/iOS are expressed using English/Latin characters’ – and now, when a ‘pure foreign language physical or virtual keyboard’ is the ‘input device’ – we are unclear how the user would invoke such a hotkey.
Now, considering cases where other language keyboards have no Latin characters, in these environments, managing shortcuts and hotkeys becomes a rather difficult task. Taking a very simple example, the shortcut for Printing a page is Command/Control + 'P'. This can be an issue on Non English character keyboards like Arabic, where not only are there no letters for P, there is also no equivalent phonetic character as well, since the language itself does not have it.
Also – when we are wanting customizability of a hotkey by the user, how would the user express ‘which is the key combination for a given action they want to perform’.
So, based on these conditions, in order to provide the most comprehensive and optimal experience for the user in their own language, what is it that Apple recommend we do here, for Hotkeys/Shortcuts support in Pure Languages

NSLog("HelloWorldIME: Successfully cast client to NSObject.")
// 2. Now that we have an NSObject, we can safely check if it responds to the selector.
let selector = #selector(IMKTextInput.insertText(\_:replacementRange:))
if !clientObject.responds(to: selector) {
NSLog("HelloWorldIME: Error - client object does not respond to the insertText selector.")
return false
}
NSLog("HelloWorldIME: Client responds to insertText. Preparing to insert text.")
// 3. Since we've confirmed it responds, we can now safely treat it as an IMKTextInput
// and call the method.
let client = clientObject as! IMKTextInput
let stringToInsert = "A"
let replacementRange = NSRange(location: NSNotFound, length: 0)
client.insertText(stringToInsert, replacementRange: replacementRange)
NSLog("HelloWorldIME: Called insertText with string '\\(stringToInsert)'. Action complete.")
// ========================================================
return true
}
}

# Text fields

A text field is a rectangular area in which people enter or edit small, specific pieces of text.

## Best practices

**Use a text field to request a small amount of information, such as a name or an email address.** To let people input larger amounts of text, use a text view instead.

**Show a hint in a text field to help communicate its purpose.** A text field can contain placeholder text — such as “Email” or “Password” — when there’s no other text in the field. Because placeholder text disappears when people start typing, it can also be useful to include a separate label describing the field to remind people of its purpose.

**Use secure text fields to hide private data.** Always use a secure text field when your app asks for sensitive data, such as a password. For developer guidance, see `Secure Field` .

**To the extent possible, match the size of a text field to the quantity of anticipated text.** The size of a text field helps people visually gauge the amount of information to provide.

**Evenly space multiple text fields.** If your layout includes multiple text fields, leave enough space between them so people can easily see which input field belongs with each introductory label. Stack multiple text fields vertically when possible, and use consistent widths to create a more organized layout. For example, the first and last name fields on an address form might be one width, while the address and city fields might be a different width.

**Ensure that tabbing between multiple fields flows as people expect.** When tabbing between fields, move focus in a logical sequence. The system attempts to achieve this result automatically, so you won’t need to customize this too often.

**Validate fields when it makes sense.** For example, if the only legitimate value for a field is a string of digits, your app needs to alert people if they’ve entered characters other than digits. The appropriate time to check the data depends on the context: when entering an email address, it’s best to validate when people switch to another field; when creating a user name or password, validation needs to happen before people switch to another field.

**Use a number formatter to help with numeric data.** A number formatter automatically configures the text field to accept only numeric values. It can also display the value in a specific way, such as with a certain number of decimal places, as a percentage, or as currency. Don’t assume the actual presentation of data, however, as formatting can vary significantly based on people’s locale.

Formatted text

**Adjust line breaks according to the needs of the field.** By default, the system clips any text extending beyond the bounds of a text field. Alternatively, you can set up a text field to wrap text to a new line at the character or word level, or to truncate (indicated by an ellipsis) at the beginning, middle, or end.

Clipped text

Wrapped text

Truncated text

**Consider using an expansion tooltip to show the full version of clipped or truncated text.** An expansion tooltip behaves like a regular [tooltip](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/offering-help) and appears when someone places the pointer over the field.

**In iOS, iPadOS, tvOS, and visionOS apps, show the appropriate keyboard type.** Several different keyboard types are available, each designed to facilitate a different type of input, such as numbers or URLs. To streamline data entry, display the keyboard that’s appropriate for the type of content people are entering. For guidance, see Virtual keyboards .

**Minimize text entry in your tvOS and watchOS apps.** Entering long passages of text or filling out numerous text fields is time-consuming on Apple TV and Apple Watch. Minimize text input and consider gathering information more efficiently, such as with buttons.

## Platform considerations

_No additional considerations for tvOS or visionOS._

### iOS, iPadOS

**Display a Clear button in the trailing end of a text field to help people erase their input.** When this element is present, people can tap it to clear the text field’s contents, without having to keep tapping the Delete key.

**Use images and buttons to provide clarity and functionality in text fields.** You can display custom images in both ends of a text field, or you can add a system-provided button, such as the Bookmarks button. In general, use the leading end of a text field to indicate a field’s purpose and the trailing end to offer additional features, such as bookmarking.

### macOS

**Consider using a combo box if you need to pair text input with a list of choices.** For related guidance, see Combo boxes .

### watchOS

**Present a text field only when necessary.** Whenever possible, prefer displaying a list of options rather than requiring text entry.

playground/prototype-app/README.md:3:A playground prototype for a Vietnamese Telex input method on macOS. The core engine (`liblex`) is a Zig static library that models each rendered character as a **span** (base + modifier + tone), handling the full Telex input set: all vowels with diacritics (â, ă, ê, ô, ơ, ư), tones (sắc, huyền, hỏi, ngã, nặng), đ, cancellation logic, `gi`/`qu` onset reclassification, and `ươ` auto-fill. The shell (`Lex.swift`) is a macOS menubar app that intercepts keystrokes via `CGEventTap`, feeds them to the engine, and applies a **diff** against the currently rendered text — emitting only the minimal sequence of synthetic backspaces followed by a single multi-character insertion event to update the active application.
playground/prototype-app/README.md:11:- **Shell (`macos/Lex.swift`)** — A menubar-only macOS app (`LSUIElement=true`) that owns the engine state and a rendered-text snapshot. On each keystroke it calls the engine, reads the new composed UTF-16, and diffs it against the snapshot to compute the minimal edit (common-prefix comparison). Replacement characters are emitted in a single multi-character `CGEvent` to reduce flicker. Synthetic events are tagged (`0x4C4558`) to avoid feedback loops. The shell resets engine state on app switches, mouse clicks, modifier keys (Cmd/Ctrl/Alt), navigation keys (arrows, Home/End, Tab, Escape, Return, forward delete), and tap-disabled events. A global hotkey (Ctrl+Opt+Space) toggles Vietnamese input on/off with audio feedback.

trình chính được viết bởi ngôn ngữ phù hợp với từng nền tảng. Ý tưởng này bắt nguồn từ cách lập

người, đào tạo... Những khó khăn này không phải là vấn đề lớn khi tác giả là người duy nhất chịu
trách nhiệm cho toàn bộ chương trình.

## Chức năng

- [x] Nhập Tiếng Việt kiểu Telex với một số tùy chỉnh:

  - [x] Không bỏ dấu nếu từ bắt đầu bằng phụ âm không phải Tiếng Việt: _f_, _j_, _w_, _z_.

- [x] Chỉ hiện biểu tượng trên thanh Menu của macOS.
- [x] Khởi động khi đăng nhập.
- [x] Khóa bàn phím bằng lựa chọn trên thanh Menu hoặc tổ hợp phím: `Ctrl + Opt + Cmd + L`.

Lưu ý: chương trình được thiết lập mặc định theo những chức năng trên và không thể tùy chỉnh. Người
dùng có thể tắt chức năng _Khởi động khi đăng nhập_ trong menu (macOS 26): System Settings \>
General \> Login Items & Extensions \> Open at Login.

## Hướng dẫn cấp quyền _Accessibility_ cho Lex

Vì bộ gõ Tiếng Việt cần truy cập vào tín hiệu gõ phím của người dùng để bỏ dấu, Lex cần được cung
cấp quyền _Accessibility_ trước khi khởi động. Truy cập vào menu: System Settings \> Privacy &
Security \> Accessibility: thêm _Lex.app_ vào danh sách được cấp quyền.

Khởi động Lex sau khi đã cấp quyền.

## Lộ trình

- [x] 0.1.x
  - [x] Chỉ hiện biểu tượng trên thanh Menu của macOS.
  - [x] Nhập Tiếng Việt kiểu Telex với một số tùy chỉnh:
    - [x] Bỏ dấu kiểu cũ: _òa_, _úy_. Ví dụ: _hòa_, _thúy_.
    - [x] Không bỏ dấu nếu từ bắt đầu bằng phụ âm không phải Tiếng Việt: _f_, _j_, _w_, _z_.

## Tự biên dịch chương trình

Yêu cầu:

- macOS 26 hoặc mới hơn.
- Zig 0.16.0.
- Xcode 26 hoặc mới hơn.

Biên dịch liblex.a:

```
zig build-obj -target aarch64-macos.26.0 -O ReleaseFast src/lex.zig -femit-bin=liblex.o \
    && xcrun libtool -static -o liblex.a liblex.o
```

Bên dịch Lex:

```
mkdir -p macos/Lex.app/Contents/MacOS/
swiftc -parse-as-library -import-objc-header src/lex.h ./liblex.a macos/Lex.swift -o macos/Lex.app/Contents/MacOS/Lex
```

Ký chữ ký điện tử để macOS đồng ý cấp quyền _Accessibility_:

```
codesign -f -s - macos/Lex.app
```

Ngoài ra, người dùng có thể chạy `zig build` để tự động chạy các bước trên.
