run.result:
## Conclusion

**No WebKit path found allows an earlier Backspace’s DOM/default editing action to finish after a later Unicode insertion merely because IPC replies complete later.** Keyboard events are queued and sent one at a time; the Web-process reply is produced only after synchronous handling of that event. Therefore, with an ordinary editable element and no page script scheduling extra work, a burst that reaches WebKit as:

```text
Backspace down, Backspace up, …, Unicode down, Unicode up
```

executes in that order.

The symptoms are more plausibly caused **before or alongside WebKit’s ordered editing path**:

- asynchronous `NSTextInputContext` interpretation of these nonstandard synthetic events;
- key code `0` falsely identifying every Unicode event as the physical **A** key;
- one key event carrying multiple characters (`"ãn"`), which is valid as text but inconsistent with its hardware identity;
- unmatched physical `x`/`e` keyups being paired, semantically, with synthetic keydowns having a different key code/text;
- page JavaScript reacting to `keydown`/`keyup`, especially by physical `code` or by maintaining key state;
- AppKit input-method/modeless-input state.

## Processing path

### 1. `WKWebView` and asynchronous AppKit interpretation

`-[WKWebView keyDown:]` directly calls `WebViewImpl::keyDown` ([WKWebViewMac.mm:639–647](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/API/mac/WKWebViewMac.mm#L639-L647)).

For editable content, `WebViewImpl` obtains the superclass `NSTextInputContext`; it returns `nil` outside editable content ([WebViewImpl.mm:6301–6318](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L6301-L6318)). `interpretKeyEvent` then invokes AppKit’s asynchronous:

```objective-c
-[NSTextInputContext handleEventByInputMethod:completionHandler:]
```

([WebViewImpl.mm:5867–5873](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5867-L5873), [5917–5924](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5917-L5924)).

If input-method handling does not consume the event, WebKit performs a keyboard-layout interpretation using `handleEventByKeyboardLayout:` or `interpretKeyEvents:` and collects callbacks such as `deleteBackward:` and `insertText:` into `KeypressCommand`s ([WebViewImpl.mm:5840–5864](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5840-L5864)).

`doCommandBySelector:` stores commands while interpretation is active ([WebViewImpl.mm:6010–6023](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L6010-L6023)). `insertText:` likewise stores the **entire NSString**, including its replacement range, as one command ([WebViewImpl.mm:6034–6079](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L6034-L6079)). Thus `"ãn"` is not inherently split into independent physical keys; it can become one `insertText:` command containing both characters.

### 2. Current input-method ordering logic

On the “correct key-event order” path, every in-flight keydown gets its own command queue. Keydowns may be submitted concurrently to the input method, but input-method callbacks are assumed to arrive in dispatch order. Keyups are held until a keydown’s input-method completion has dispatched its keyboard-event IPC ([WebViewImpl.mm:5875–5913](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5875-L5913)).

The completion takes the commands belonging to that keydown, decides whether the input method handled it, optionally performs keyboard-layout interpretation, and only then forwards the resulting `NativeWebKeyboardEvent` ([WebViewImpl.mm:5926–6007](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5926-L6007)).

This machinery was added specifically to preserve:

```text
keydown → its composition/editing commands → keyup
```

The May 2026 change explicitly states that keyups stay in a holding tank and each keydown completion releases one, preserving strict keydown/keyup IPC order ([commit 313336](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/commit/2b952923a66cd56a0acd48875418f742e995b4fc)).

There is a relevant exception: current WebKit can disable this “correct order” mode for Apple Vietnamese Simple Telex and Korean 2-set under a composition-events quirk ([WebViewImpl.mm:3793–3810](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L3793-L3810); [commit 315032](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/commit/98e37dad7f63446307c87e1f17269307d27b64d0)). That is evidence that AppKit/modeless-input interaction is subtle, but it does not establish reversal of Web-process default actions.

### 3. UI-process keyboard queue and IPC

The keyboard message is an async IPC with a `handled` reply:

```text
KeyEvent(frameID, event) -> (bool handled)
```

([WebPage.messages.in:67–69](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/WebProcess/WebPage/WebPage.messages.in#L67-L69)).

Current `WebPageProxy::sendKeyEvent` uses an async reply, and its queue is advanced only in the reply handler. This was made explicit in [commit 317427](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/commit/55f1bf713ee4e46f83429240e0e6b6bc8ce3572b). Consequently, later queued keyboard IPC is not sent to the Web process while the earlier event remains outstanding.

The reply is not the operation that performs deletion. The Web process handles the event first and invokes its completion afterward. `WebPage::keyEvent` calls `WebFrame::handleKeyEvent`, obtains the handled result, and then completes the IPC; the same commit shows this transition from a separate acknowledgement message to an async reply. Therefore, late UI-process callbacks cannot retroactively execute an earlier Backspace after a later insertion.

### 4. Web-process default handling

On macOS, WebCore asks `WebEditorClientMac::handleKeyboardEvent`, which delegates synchronously to `WebPage::handleEditingKeyboardEvent` and marks the DOM event’s default as handled if the editor command succeeds ([WebEditorClientMac.mm](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/WebProcess/WebCoreSupport/mac/WebEditorClientMac.mm)).

The commands captured in the UI process travel in `WebKeyboardEvent`; text, virtual key codes, input-method status, and command vector are distinct fields ([WebKeyboardEvent.cpp:35–49](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/Shared/WebKeyboardEvent.cpp#L35-L49)). Thus a Backspace keydown carries its delete command with that event, while the later Unicode event carries its insertion command. These are not independent asynchronous edit requests that can overtake each other.

## Key code `0` with `"ãn"`

This combination is internally contradictory:

- macOS hardware key code `0` is mapped by WebKit’s table to Windows virtual key **A** ([KeyEventMac.mm:50–58](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebCore/platform/mac/KeyEventMac.mm#L50-L58)).
- WebKit preserves the full `NSEvent.characters` string as event text ([PlatformEventFactoryMac.mm:241–256](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebCore/platform/mac/PlatformEventFactoryMac.mm#L241-L256)).
- For `KeyboardEvent.key`, when the character string has more than one UTF-16 unit, WebKit returns that string rather than deriving a named key from only its first unit ([PlatformEventFactoryMac.mm:284–299](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebCore/platform/mac/PlatformEventFactoryMac.mm#L284-L299)).

Accordingly, a synthetic event may expose approximately:

```text
code: "KeyA"
keyCode / which: 65
key: "ãn"
text / characters: "ãn"
```

Exact legacy DOM fields depend on the event phase and current WebCore logic, but the supported fact is that **hardware identity and textual payload are derived separately**.

Consequences:

1. Normal editable default handling can insert the entire `"ãn"` string.
2. JavaScript that assumes one printable character per keydown can behave unexpectedly.
3. JavaScript using `code`, `keyCode`, or `which` sees **A**, not the physical `x` or `e`.
4. Keyboard-layout/input-method interpretation may treat the event as an A-key event carrying foreign text.
5. Every synthetic insertion using virtual key `0` is reported as the same hardware key, creating impossible down/up sequences when mixed with surviving physical keyups.

Using key code `0` as “no key” is therefore incorrect on macOS; it is the ANSI **A** position.

## Unmatched physical `x`/`e` keyup

Because the tap excludes keyup, WebKit receives:

```text
synthetic keydown(s) and keyup(s)
...
physical KeyX/KeyE keyup
```

without the corresponding physical keydown. WebKit does forward keyups through the same input-method interpretation route, and current ordering code explicitly manages them ([WebViewImpl.mm:5885–5912](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5885-L5912)). A keyup itself normally has no text insertion or deletion default action, so **WebKit source does not support the claim that this keyup directly re-inserts `e` or removes `n`**.

It can nevertheless matter outside default editing:

- DOM receives an unmatched `keyup`.
- `keyup.code` describes the real `KeyX`/`KeyE`, whereas the preceding synthetic Unicode down/up used `KeyA`.
- Site code may maintain pressed-key state, implement transliteration, normalize controlled inputs, or rewrite the value on keyup.
- AppKit/input-method state may observe a physically impossible sequence.

Those are plausible mechanisms, not demonstrated WebKit default-action behavior.

## Classification of the reported symptoms

### Code-supported

- Multiple-character Unicode text can be preserved and inserted as one command.
- Key code `0` is treated as **A**, not as neutral.
- Input-method interpretation is asynchronous.
- Current WebKit explicitly queues commands per keydown and holds keyups to preserve event ordering.
- UI-process keyboard IPC is serialized by its outstanding-event queue.
- The IPC reply follows Web-process handling; it does not defer the edit itself.
- A surviving physical keyup reaches Safari with no matching physical keydown.

### Not supported by the traced code

- A Backspace DOM/default action remaining pending and executing after the later `"ãn"` insertion solely because its IPC acknowledgement arrived later.
- An unmatched keyup directly performing the missing deletion or inserting its character through WebKit’s ordinary default editor path.

### Plausible but requiring instrumentation

- `NSTextInputContext` interpreting key code `0` plus multi-character text inconsistently.
- A modeless input method responding to stale or synthetic state.
- Page JavaScript reacting to the impossible `KeyA` down / `KeyX` or `KeyE` up pairing.
- A site-controlled editor asynchronously restoring an earlier model value.
- Event-tap recursion or incomplete filtering causing some synthetic/physical event to be processed twice.

The most probative capture would log, for every event, `type`, `keyCode`, `characters`, `charactersIgnoringModifiers`, `CGEventSource` state/source PID, and DOM `keydown`/`beforeinput`/`input`/`keyup` fields. That would distinguish WebKit-ordered editing from AppKit interpretation or page-script rewriting.

# CGEvent

Defines an opaque type that represents a low-level hardware event.

Mac Catalyst macOS

```
class CGEvent
```

## Overview

Low-level hardware events of this type are referred to as Quartz events. A typical event in macOS originates when the user manipulates an input device such as a mouse or a keyboard. The device driver associated with that device, through the I/O Kit, creates a low-level event, puts it in the window server’s event queue, and notifies the window server. The window server creates a Quartz event, annotates the event, and dispatches the event to the appropriate run-loop port of the target process. There the event is picked up by the Carbon Event Manager and forwarded to the event-handling mechanism appropriate to the application environment. You can use event taps to gain access to Quartz events at several different steps in this process.

This opaque type is derived from CFType and inherits the properties that all Core Foundation types have in common. For more information, see `CFType Ref` .

# macOS 27 Golden Gate Preview

## Introducing Siri AI.  
Truly helpful. Truly yours.

macOS 27 Golden Gate coming this fall.  
Siri AI coming in English later this year.

## Explore what’s new for macOS 27.

macOS 27 Golden Gate coming this fall.

* New Siri AI
* Siri conversations
* Next-generation Apple Intelligence
* Visual Intelligence
* Design enhancements
* Performance improvements

* New Siri AI. An even more capable AI assistant with expanded intelligence to be more helpful every day. ¹
* Type or talk naturally with Siri AI to find what you need and get more done.
* Next-generation Apple Intelligence enhances the apps you use most — like Photos, Messages, and Safari. ²
* Visual Intelligence on Mac lets you learn more and take action about virtually anything onscreen. ³
* More refined design with enhanced Liquid Glass, ensuring exceptional readability and greater consistency across apps.
* An expansive set of improvements across key areas that makes your Mac even more responsive and delightful.

## Siri AI on Mac

Your AI assistant.  
More personal. More powerful.

Siri AI is powered by Apple Intelligence and more helpful than ever. ¹ Get more done every day with richer answers, natural conversations, and a new, dedicated app.

Siri AI coming in English later this year.

* ### Just ask Siri AI.
  
  Powered by Apple Intelligence, Siri AI is your conversational AI assistant with entirely new capabilities on your Mac. Ask open-ended questions, brainstorm ideas for work or creative projects, and engage in natural, back-and-forth conversations. And when you search in Spotlight, you can choose “Ask Siri” as the top hit.
* ### Siri understands your personal context.
  
  Siri AI can find relevant answers to what you’re looking for just by asking. Search for a photo from years ago, easily locate an email buried in your inbox, or pull up a note you saved on your Mac.
* ### Take action in more apps.
  
  Siri AI can take actions in apps like Messages, Music, Reminders, and more based on what you’re doing in the moment. Quickly edit a message you just sent or add a song from a show you’re watching to your workout playlist.
* ### Tap into broad world knowledge.
  
  Ask about virtually any topic, do research for a project, or prepare for an interview. Siri AI can reference information online to give you detailed, up-to-date insights.
* ### Introducing the Siri app.
  
  A dedicated app brings together all your conversations in one place, so you can ask a question on your Mac and pick up where you left off on your iPhone. You can also pin conversations for easy access or start a new one.
* ### Visual Intelligence with Siri on Mac.
  
  Ask Siri AI about virtually anything on your screen. Just take a screenshot of what’s on your display, like an image or a PDF, to get answers, search, or take action. ³
* ### Write with Siri virtually anywhere you type.
  
  Siri AI can now generate a draft from scratch or provide feedback on what you’ve written. Just describe what you need in your own words. And in Messages and Mail, Siri AI can match your writing style, punctuation, and tone — so you sound like you.
* ### Customize how Siri sounds.
  
  Pick a voice, then customize expressivity and pace until it clicks for you. ⁴

*

## Apple Intelligence in apps

Helpful in all the right places.

Express yourself through photos and images, save time with Safari, and get more done with Apple Intelligence seamlessly integrated into your everyday apps and experiences. ²

* ### Safari works smarter for you.
  
  Now your tabs can be automatically grouped into topics, so related pages are easier to find on your Mac. And Safari Notify Me monitors pages for changes — for example, a price change or restock — and alerts you when it’s time to act.
* ### Fix passwords with a click.
  
  The Passwords app alerts you to weak or compromised passwords and can update them on your behalf without the hassle.
* ### Next-level intelligent photo editing.
  
  Reframe a photo after it’s been taken with Spatial Reframing. Expand your shots with the Extend tool. And remove even larger objects with the enhanced Clean Up tool.
* ### Express more with Image Playground.
  
  Create unique, high-quality images for any project in just about any style, including photorealistic. Modify and transform your images with just a description for endless possibilities.
* ### Describe a shortcut.
  
  Automate daily tasks with a simple description. Just describe what you need and Shortcuts connects actions across multiple apps to get it done.

*

## Child Safety

Committed to building a safe and trusted platform for kids.

New and expanded child safety features help make it easier for parents and guardians to keep kids safe online.

Learn more

* ### Approve new websites.
  
  With the new Ask to Browse, ⁵ kids must request permission to access new websites. Parents can take a closer look at the request in Messages before approving. ⁶
* ### Help them communicate safely.
  
  Communication Safety helps protect children from viewing or sharing nudity in Messages, FaceTime, and more. It now also intervenes before children see gore or violence in shared images and videos.
* ### Time Allowances and Schedules.
  
  Parents can set Time Allowances across categories like Entertainment, Games, and Social Media. We provide parents with guidance for setting Time Allowances that is based on a child’s age and developed with clinical and child development experts. Parents can always adjust these allowances based on what’s best for their child. And Schedules lets parents choose which apps are available to their child at different times or days of the week.
* ### Intuitive, easy-to-use controls.
  
  An all-new design makes parental controls in System Settings even easier to use. At a glance, parents can check how their kids have been using their Mac. And parents can quickly adjust access in the moment with just a click.

*

## OS improvements

Every little detail makes it all delightful.

Discover tons of refinements that make your Mac even more responsive, reliable, and delightful to use.

* ### Design refinements.
  
  Updates to Liquid Glass ensure exceptional readability with more uniform refraction and improved contrast. Uniform toolbars, edge-to-edge sidebars, and updated window shapes and menu bar icons deliver a more refined design. And a new slider lets you easily customize how Liquid Glass looks, from ultraclear to fully tinted.
* ### Faster performance.
  
  With quicker AirDrop transfers, faster network file browsing, and speedier start page content loading in Safari, your Mac feels more responsive than ever.
* ### More relevant search in Mail.
  
  A new ranking system brings the most relevant results to the top to help you find what you need right away — even if it’s buried deep in your inbox.
* ### And so many more.
  
  With improvements at the very core of the system and enhancements to apps and experiences you rely on every day, macOS feels better than ever.

*

## macOS 27 Golden Gate features And so much more.

### Accessibility.

VoiceOver gets new capabilities for understanding onscreen content, including richer image descriptions. A new captioning feature automatically generates synced subtitles for any video you watch, and it can even translate existing captions into other languages.

### Describe an event, add to Calendar.

Add and edit events on your calendar with just a description. Easily edit the description to change a lunch meeting to a coffee chat and the Calendar app adjusts the details.

### Ultrawide display support.

Now you can get higher resolutions on ultrawide displays, such as 5K at 120Hz. And your display arrangements stay exactly as you left them, for a seamless experience every time you plug in.

### Improved iCloud Shared Albums.

It’s easier for friends and family on Android or Windows to join and contribute their own photos on iCloud.com. Shared Albums also adds support for full-resolution sharing and new ways to filter and react to photos and invite others to share an album.

### Get things done with Suggestions.

Messages and Mail offer suggestions to help you take quick actions based on context from your conversation — add a calendar event or search for a photo with just a click. Coming in English.

### Get relevant information while on a call.

Call Context can proactively surface relevant information from across your apps when calling a business — like a confirmation code from Mail when you call an airline. Coming in English.

### Enhanced Flyover in Maps.

Flyover now uses aerial imagery combined with Visual Intelligence models to render everything from architectural fixtures to the shapes of individual trees in stunning, sharp detail.

### Swipe down to refresh.

Swipe down in apps like Safari, Mail, News, Podcasts, and Calendar to get up-to-date information in your apps.

### Updated video podcasts experience on Mac.

Switch seamlessly between watching and listening to shows, making the experience of discovering and viewing video podcasts as simple and enjoyable as listening to audio podcasts has always been.

## macOS 27 is compatible with these devices.

Explore Mac

* MacBook Neo (2026)
* MacBook Air with Apple silicon (2020 and later)
* MacBook Pro with Apple silicon (2020 and later)
* iMac with Apple silicon (2021 and later)
* Mac mini with Apple silicon (2020 and later)
* Mac Studio (2022 and later)
* Mac Pro with Apple silicon (2023)

## Developers will  
love macOS 27, too.

[Learn more about developing for macOS](https://developer.apple.com/macos/)

## Apple Footer

1. Siri AI will be available In beta later this year and requires an Apple Intelligence–enabled device set to a supported language. Available in English to start. Siri AI will not initially be available in the EU on iOS, iPadOS and watchOS.

# Event taps: Varying results with CGEventPost, kCGSessionEventTap, kCGAnnotatedSessionEventTap, CGEventTapPostEvent

Ask Question

Asked 17 years, 4 months ago

Modified [7 years, 1 month ago](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/553284/event-taps-varying-results-with-cgeventpost-kcgsessioneventtap-kcgannotatedse?lastactivity "2019-05-27 23:50:35Z")

Viewed 3k times

5

I'm running into a thorny problem with posting an event from an event tap. I'm tapping for NSSystemDefined at kCGHIDEventTap, then replacing the event with a new one. The problem I'm running in to is that depending on how I post the event, it's being seen only by some applications. My test applications are Opera, Firefox, Quicksilver, and Xcode. Here are the different techniques I've tried within my event tap callback, with results. I'm expecting an action (the "correct response") from each app; "system beep" means the nothing-is-bound-to-that-key system sound.

1. Create a new event, and return it from the callback.
   Opera: no response/system beep, Firefox: no response/system beep, Quicksilver: correct response, Xcode: no response/system beep
2. Create a new event, post to kCGSessionEventTap with CGEventPost, return null.
   Opera: no response/system beep, Firefox: no response/system beep, Quicksilver: correct response, Xcode: no response/system beep
3. Create a new event, post to kCGAnnotatedSessionEventTap with CGEventPost, return null.
   Opera: correct response, Firefox: correct response, Quicksilver: no response/system beep, Xcode: no response/system beep
4. Create a new event, post with CGEventTapPostEvent, return null.
   Opera: no response/system beep, Firefox: no response/system beep, Quicksilver: correct response, Xcode: no response/system beep
5. Create a new event, post to kCGSessionEventTap with CGEventPost, and return new event.
   Opera: no response/system beep, Firefox: no response/system beep, Quicksilver: correct response, Xcode: no response/system beep
6. Create a new event, post to kCGAnnotatedSessionEventTap with CGEventPost, and return new event.
   Opera: correct response and system beep, Firefox: correct response and system beep, Quicksilver: correct response and system beep, Xcode: no response/double system beep
7. Create a new event, post with CGEventTapPostEvent, and return new event.
   Opera: no response/system beep, Firefox: no response/system beep, Quicksilver: correct response, Xcode: no response/system beep

(6) is the best, but users are complaining about the extra system beep on correct responses, which I'm guessing is coming from the double-posting of the event. I'm not sure of other combinations to try, or where else to look. Can anyone offer any guidance? Is there any way to get the results of both returning the event from my callback and posting to the annotated tap without doing both?

Sorry for the lengthy question; I've been doing a lot of experimenting.

Thanks in advance

* * *

Update: this is the code I use to create the event tap:

```
CFMachPortRef eventTap;
eventTap = CGEventTapCreate(kCGHIDEventTap, kCGHeadInsertEventTap, 0,CGEventMaskBit(NX_SYSDEFINED) | (1 << kCGEventKeyDown) | (1 << kCGEventKeyUp), myCGEventCallback, (void *)hidEventQueue);
```

I think I fixed this. I had been using `+[NSEvent keyEventWithType:location:modifierFlags:timestamp:windowNumber:context:characters:charactersIgnoringModifiers:isARepeat:keyCode:]` to create an NSEvent, then returning that event's `-CGEvent` . excerpts:
# Atomic Update Ordering
Specifies the memory ordering semantics of an atomic read-modify-write operation.
iOS 18.0+ iPadOS 18.0+ Mac Catalyst 18.0+ macOS 15.0+ tvOS 18.0+ visionOS 2.0+ watchOS 11.0+
```
@frozen struct AtomicUpdateOrdering
```

## Topics
### Type Properties
`static var acquiring : Atomic Update Ordering`
An acquiring update synchronizes with a releasing operation whose value its reads. It ensures that the releasing and acquiring threads agree that all subsequent variable accesses on the acquiring thread happen after the atomic operation itself.
`static var acquiring And Releasing : Atomic Update Ordering`
An acquiring-and-releasing operation is a combination of `.acquiring` and `.releasing` operation on the same variable.
`static var relaxed : Atomic Update Ordering`
Guarantees the atomicity of the specific operation on which it is applied, but imposes no ordering constraints on any other variable accesses.
`static var releasing : Atomic Update Ordering`
A releasing update synchronizes with acquiring operations that read the value it stores. It ensures that the releasing and acquiring threads agree that all preceding variable accesses on the releasing thread happen before the atomic operation itself.
`static var sequentially Consistent : Atomic Update Ordering`
A sequentially consistent update performs an acquiring-and-releasing update and also guarantees that it and all other sequentially consistent atomic operations (loads, stores, updates) appear to be executed in a single, total sequential ordering.

## See Also
### Memory Ordering Semantics
`struct Atomic Load Ordering`
Specifies the memory ordering semantics of an atomic load operation.
`struct Atomic Store Ordering`
Specifies the memory ordering semantics of an atomic store operation.

Establishes a memory ordering without associating it with a particular atomic operation.

## Conclusion

**No: the historical evidence does not support synthetic Backspace and Unicode-insertion `keyDown`s overtaking one another before the May fix.** Under the April 2026 algorithm enabled by bug 311717, WebKit deliberately serialized `interpretKeyEvent` calls: while one `handleEventByInputMethod:` operation was outstanding, every later keyboard event was appended to a FIFO holding tank. Completion drained that tank in insertion order.

The defect fixed in April was primarily **ordering within each key**—DOM `keydown` had previously occurred after the key’s composition/input effects—plus duplicate dead-key insertion. The May change removed WebKit-side serialization of **keydown delivery to the input method**, but relied explicitly on `NSTextInputContext`/the input method to process concurrent keydowns serially in dispatch order.

Therefore, for a tap emitting:

```text
Backspace keyDown × N, then Unicode-insertion keyDown
```

the relevant algorithms preserve that relative keydown order. The old path could **delay and later burst** the sequence, and the affected IM could stall or mishandle commands, but there is no demonstrated WebKit mechanism here by which the final insertion keydown jumps ahead of an earlier Backspace keydown.

## April 2026: bug 311717 / `310826@main`

[Bug 311717](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=311717) landed as commit [`6031db379af6aec30c03b076077c57e1c4b3c93d`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/commit/6031db379af6aec30c03b076077c57e1c4b3c93d), **April 8, 2026 at 23:19:21 PDT**. It made `InputMethodUsesCorrectKeyEventOrder` stable and enabled it by default in [`UnifiedWebPreferences.yaml`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/6031db379af6aec30c03b076077c57e1c4b3c93d/Source/WTF/Scripts/Preferences/UnifiedWebPreferences.yaml).

This built on the July 2025 algorithm from [`297270@main`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/commit/1322eea39d8f8bcaa4d562c9edca2f5016c7b6bc):

1. Start processing key N through asynchronous `handleEventByInputMethod:completionHandler:`.
2. While that operation is active, `m_collectedKeypressCommands` is nonempty.
3. Any later event N+1 is appended to `m_interpretKeyEventHoldingTank` and not sent to the input method yet.
4. The IM’s `setMarkedText:`, `insertText:`, and command callbacks are collected rather than immediately mutating the document.
5. On completion, key N and its collected commands are forwarded so that the web process first dispatches DOM `keydown`, then executes that key’s composition/editing commands.
6. The holding tank is moved out and invoked from beginning to end. Because invoking N+1 synchronously marks another key operation active, later entries re-tank behind it. The result is effective FIFO serialization, not parallel completion.

The purpose is stated in the original change: defer `setMarkedText:` until after the corresponding `keydown`, and defer later `interpretKeyEvent` calls “to maintain the correct ordering of input method processing of key events.” The test added shortly afterward verifies **`keydown` before `compositionstart`**, i.e. ordering internal to a key, rather than cross-key overtaking.

Bug 311717 itself fixed a separate duplication inside that algorithm: if the IM had already supplied final `insertText:`, WebKit must not append the keyboard-layout interpretation of the same key and insert the character twice. The one-line behavior change is visible in [`WebViewImpl.mm`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/6031db379af6aec30c03b076077c57e1c4b3c93d/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm): layout commands are appended only when the IM did not already produce `insertText:`. Its new test was `KeyDownInsertAccentedCharacterOnce`.

Notably, the April test mock also had been consuming actions in reverse order; bug 311717 changed it from `lastObject/removeLastObject` to `firstObject/removeObjectAtIndex:0`. That is a **test-harness correction**, not evidence that production WebKit reversed key events.

## May 2026: `2b952923…` / bug 314888

Commit [`2b952923a66cd56a0acd48875418f742e995b4fc`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/commit/2b952923a66cd56a0acd48875418f742e995b4fc), canonical `313336@main`, landed **May 15, 2026 at 15:21:06 PDT**. The associated report is [bug 314888](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=314888), reported earlier that day for rapid Zhuyin input stalls.

The old FIFO serialization had an unintended liveness effect:

- While keydown N was outstanding, keydown N+1 remained inside WebKit.
- N+1 therefore did not enter the input method’s XPC queue.
- Traditional Chinese Zhuyin apparently needed incoming queue activity to wake/nudge its main thread.
- It could stall for 1–20 seconds and eventually return without commands.
- WebKit would then release delayed events in a burst, sometimes producing visible garbage.

The commit explicitly says narrowing experiments showed that **holding later keydowns**, not per-command queueing, triggered the stall.

### New algorithm

The fix changes the single optional command vector to a deque of per-key vectors in [`WebViewImpl.h`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/2b952923a66cd56a0acd48875418f742e995b4fc/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.h), then:

- Every keydown immediately gets its own queue at the deque’s back.
- Every keydown is immediately passed to `handleEventByInputMethod:`.
- Keyups alone remain held while keydowns are outstanding.
- On completion, the command queue is removed from the deque’s front.
- One queued keyup is released after each keydown, preserving keydown/keyup IPC sequencing.

The source comments state the ordering assumption directly: the IM serializes `handleEventByInputMethod:` work on its main thread, so callbacks arrive in dispatch order; therefore the deque front always belongs to the currently processed keydown ([`WebViewImpl.mm` lines 5875–5893](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5875-L5893)). Completion correspondingly consumes the first queue ([lines 5926–5932](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5926-L5932)).

The regression test sends `a` and `b` back-to-back with delayed responses and expects:

```text
received_a,received_ab,fired_a,fired_ab
```

See [`ConcurrentInputMethodKeyDownsScopeQueueingPerKey`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/2b952923a66cd56a0acd48875418f742e995b4fc/Tools/TestWebKitAPI/Tests/WebKit/WKWebView/mac/WKWebViewMacEditingTests.mm). This establishes that both keydowns reach the IM before either response fires, while response/command association remains FIFO.

Thus the May fix is not “allow arbitrary asynchronous completion order.” It changes:

```text
WebKit serializes keydown admission to the IM
```

into:

```text
WebKit admits keydowns concurrently;
the NSTextInputContext/IM queue serializes their processing in dispatch order;
WebKit keeps one command queue per key.
```

## Implication for the event-tap corruption

These commits support several plausible Safari-specific effects:

- substantial delay before edits appear;
- a burst of queued Backspaces and insertion afterward;
- wrong DOM `keydown` versus composition/input ordering on older builds;
- duplicate Unicode insertion in the dead-key case fixed by bug 311717;
- lost or malformed IM commands during the Zhuyin stall described by bug 314888.

They do **not** provide evidence that rapidly posted keydowns were completed or forwarded in arbitrary order. In particular:

- **Before April/default enablement:** the older legacy path had the known within-key DOM ordering problem, but these changes do not identify cross-key overtaking.
- **April 8–May 15 algorithm:** explicit WebKit FIFO holding-tank serialization prevents overtaking.
- **After May 15:** multiple keydowns are in flight from WebKit’s perspective, but the implementation explicitly depends on NSTextInputContext/IM main-thread FIFO ordering, with per-key FIFO command queues.

A Backspace/insertion reversal would therefore require some mechanism outside the behavior established here—such as the event tap posting events in an unexpected order, Unicode insertion using a different API/path than ordinary `keyDown`, event coalescing or filtering elsewhere, or an input-method bug that violates WebKit’s stated serialization assumption.

## Safari availability

Bug 311717 was cherry-picked to `safari-7624-branch` on **April 30, 2026**, and Safari 26.5 shipped **May 11, 2026**, so Safari 26.5 likely contains the April default-enable/duplicate-insertion fix.

The May 15 commit landed **four days after Safari 26.5 shipped**, so Safari 26.5 cannot contain it absent an undocumented later servicing backport. As of August 2, 2026, Safari 26.6 had shipped on July 27 and Safari 27 was in beta. A release after May 15—particularly Safari 26.6 or Safari 27 beta—**may** include the fix, but main-branch landing alone does not prove it was merged into Apple’s release branch. No public cherry-pick analogous to bug 311717’s `safari-7624-branch` landing is shown on bug 314888. The safe classification is:

| Safari build | Likely state |
|---|---|
| 26.4 and earlier | April fix probably absent |
| 26.5 | April bug-311717 fix likely present; May fix absent |

530:                      "content": "1: # Prototype — Span-based Vietnamese Telex IME
2: 
3: A playground prototype for a Vietnamese Telex input method on macOS. The core engine (`liblex`) is a Zig static library that models each rendered character as a **span** (base + modifier + tone), handling the full Telex input set: all vowels with diacritics (â, ă, ê, ô, ơ, ư), tones (sắc, huyền, hỏi, ngã, nặng), đ, cancellation logic, `gi`/`qu` onset reclassification, and `ươ` auto-fill. The shell (`Lex.swift`) is a macOS menubar app that intercepts keystrokes via `CGEventTap`, feeds them to the engine, and applies a **diff** against the currently rendered text — emitting only the minimal sequence of synthetic backspaces followed by a single multi-character insertion event to update the active application.
4: 
5: ## Architecture
6: 
7: The system is split into two layers communicating through a C ABI:
8: 
9: - **Core (`src/liblex.zig`)** — A span-based composition engine. Each keystroke mutates an array of `Span` structs (base letter, modifier, tone, flags). The engine handles modifier application (doubled vowels `aa`→`â`, `w`→`ơ`/`ư`/`ă`, `dd`→`đ`), tone placement following Vietnamese linguistic rules (region analysis: onset → nucleus → coda, with semi-vowel coda detection), cancellation (repeating a filled modifier/tone strips it and enters literal mode), `gi`/`qu` onset binding, and `ươ` auto-fill. Unicode output is produced via lookup tables covering all 12 vowel bases × 6 tone variants in both cases. The engine exposes `add`, `backspace`, `reset`, `get_composed_utf16`, `init_state`, and `state_size`.
10: 
11: - **Shell (`macos/Lex.swift`)** — A menubar-only macOS app (`LSUIElement=true`) that owns the engine state and a rendered-text snapshot. On each keystroke it calls the engine, reads the new composed UTF-16, and diffs it against the snapshot to compute the minimal edit (common-prefix comparison). Replacement characters are emitted in a single multi-character `CGEvent` to reduce flicker. Synthetic events are tagged (`0x4C4558`) to avoid feedback loops. The shell resets engine state on app switches, mouse clicks, modifier keys (Cmd/Ctrl/Alt), navigation keys (arrows, Home/End, Tab, Escape, Return, forward delete), and tap-disabled events. A global hotkey (Ctrl+Opt+Space) toggles Vietnamese input on/off with audio feedback.
12: 
13: - **FFI bridge (`src/liblex.h`)** — C-compatible header declaring the engine API. Swift calls into the Zig static library through this bridging header. The engine is stateless from the caller's perspective — Swift allocates the opaque state buffer (`state_size()` bytes) and passes it to every call.
14: 
15: ## Prerequisites
16: 
17: - **Zig ≥ 0.16.0** (master recommended) — [download](https://ziglang.org/download/)
18: - **Xcode Command Line Tools** — `xcode-select --install`
19: - **macOS 26** (Tahoe)
20: 
21: ## Project Structure
22: 
23: ```
24: prototype-app/
25: ├── src/
26: │   ├── liblex.zig              # Span-based Telex engine (C library)
27: │   └── liblex.h                # C bridging header
28: ├── macos/
29: │   ├── Lex.app/
30: │   │   └── Contents/
31: │   │       └── Info.plist      # LSUIElement=true (menubar-only)
32: │   └── Lex.swift               # macOS app shell (diff-based rendering)
33: ├── build.zig                   # Zig build script (full pipeline)
34: ├── build.zig.zon               # Zig build manifest
35: └── .tool-versions              # Version management (zig master)
36: ```
37: 
38: ## Build
39: 
40: The `build.zig` script automates the entire pipeline — building the Zig static library, re-packing the archive (Zig master workaround for non-8-byte-aligned archive members), compiling Swift, and ad-hoc codesigning — in a single command:
41: 
42: ```sh
43: zig build
44: ```
45: 
46: To build and immediately launch the app:
47: 
48: ```sh
49: zig build run
50: ```
51: 
52: Or run the binary directly to see console output:
53: 
54: ```sh
55: ./macos/Lex.app/Contents/MacOS/Lex
56: ```
57: 
58: ### Manual steps (for reference)
59: 
60: <details>
61: <summary>Expand manual build steps</summary>
62: 
63: #### Step 1: Build the Zig static library
64: 
65: ```sh
66: zig build
67: ```
68: 
69: This produces `zig-out/lib/liblex.a`.
70: 
71: #### Step 2: Re-pack the archive (Zig master workaround)
72: 
73: Zig master produces archives with non-8-byte-aligned members that Apple's linker rejects. Re-pack with the system `ar`:
74: 
75: ```sh
76: cd zig-out/lib && \
77:   tmp=$(mktemp -d) && \
78:   (cd "$tmp" && ar x "$(cd - && pwd)/liblex.a" && chmod 644 *.o && /usr/bin/ar rcs "$(cd - && pwd)/liblex.a" *.o) && \
79:   rm -rf "$tmp" && \
80:   cd ../..
81: ```
82: 
83: #### Step 3: Compile Swift and link with the Zig library
84: 
85: ```sh
86: swiftc macos/Lex.swift \
87:     -import-objc-header src/liblex.h \
88:     -Lzig-out/lib -llex \
89:     -o macos/Lex.app/Contents/MacOS/Lex
90: ```
91: 
92: #### Step 4: Sign the app (ad-hoc, for local development)
93: 
94: ```sh
95: codesign -f -s - macos/Lex.app
96: ```
97: 
98: </details>
99: 
100: ## Signing
101: 
102: ### Ad-hoc (local development)
103: 
104: Ad-hoc signing is sufficient for local testing and is performed automatically by `zig build`:
105: 
106: ```sh
107: codesign -f -s - macos/Lex.app
108: ```
109: 
110: ### Hardened Runtime (for notarization)
111: 
112: Requires a signing identity and entitlements:
113: 
114: ```sh
115: codesign -f -s "YOUR_IDENTITY" \
116:     --options runtime \
117:     macos/Lex.app
118: ```
119: 
120: #### Finding your signing identity
121: 
122: List available identities:
123: 
124: ```sh
125: security find-identity -v -p codesigning
126: ```
127: 
128: ## Permissions
129: 
130: **Accessibility** is required for `CGEventTap` to intercept keyboard events. This is a TCC (Transparency, Consent, and Control) permission — not an entitlement.
131: 
132: On first launch, the app calls `AXIsProcessTrustedWithOptions()` which prompts the user. Grant access in:
133: 
134: > **System Settings → Privacy & Security → Accessibility**
135: 
136: Then relaunch the app.
137: 
138: ## Known Limitations
139: 
140: This is a **prototype-grade** application:
141: 
142: - **Synthetic event fragility** — the backspace+multi-char-insert approach is unreliable in terminal emulators, Electron-based apps, and secure input fields where `CGEventTap` may be blocked or events reordered. Some apps may not handle multi-character `keyboardSetUnicodeString` correctly.
143: - **Single-char assumption** — the engine expects one text-producing `UniChar` per `keyDown` event, which may fail for complex dead-key layouts or surrogate pairs.
144: - **`ươ` auto-fill edge cases** — the auto-fill heuristic for `ươ` only triggers when a coda consonant is present and may not cover all valid Vietnamese syllable patterns.
145: - **Secure input fields block the tap** — password fields and other secure text inputs disable event taps by design.
146: - **Non-US layouts not handled** — only tested with standard US keyboard layout.
147: - **No Dock icon** — `LSUIElement=true` means the app only appears in the menubar.",

546:                    "result": "Based on the event handling implementation in `macos/Lex.swift` and the reference prototype, the following constraints and decisions inform a conceptual critique of the event handling order, reset behavior, and modifier chord strategy:

### 1. Event Handling Order
* **Current Order:** The callback processes events in the following sequence:
  1. **Tap Status/System Events:** Handles tap-disabled events (`.tapDisabledByTimeout`, `.tapDisabledByUserInput`) to re-enable the tap and reset the engine.
  2. **Mouse Events:** Intercepts mouse clicks (`.leftMouseDown`, `.rightMouseDown`) to immediately reset the engine (since a click implies the text caret has moved).
  3. **Modifier Flags:** Passes through `.flagsChanged` events without resetting the engine to allow plain modifier keys (like Shift or Caps Lock) to function normally.
  4. **Key Down Events (`.keyDown`):**
     * Filters out the engine's own synthetic events (using a unique user data tag) to prevent infinite feedback loops.
     * Bypasses processing entirely if the app is in literal mode.
     * Intercepts specific non-alphanumeric keycodes (like Backspace/Delete) to keep the engine's internal buffer synchronized with the editor, passing them through.
     * Filters out non-alphanumeric characters (e.g., punctuation, numbers, and Space) and resets the engine.
     * Feeds valid alphabetic characters to the engine, calculating synthetic backspaces and posting replacement characters.
* **Critique/Constraint:** The current order is highly fragile because it performs character extraction and validation *before* checking for modifier chords. This means modifier-key combinations (like Command + T) are evaluated as alphabetic characters first, which can block system hotkeys or corrupt the engine state.

### 2. Reset on Space and App Switches
* **App Switches:** App switching is handled out-of-band by registering a global observer on `NSWorkspace.didActivateApplicationNotification`. When triggered, it calls `resetEngine()`, which is clean and decoupled from the low-level event tap.
* **Space and Non-Alphanumerics:** Space (character code 32) is not explicitly handled as a special keycode. Instead, it falls through to the Unicode character extraction. Because Space is non-alphabetic, it fails the `is_alphabetic` validation check, which triggers `app_delegate.engine.reset()` and passes the Space event through. 
* **Critique/Constraint:** Relying on a generic "non-alphabetic" fallback to reset on Space is implicit. Explicitly handling Space (and other word-boundary keys like Return, Tab, or Escape) as early, dedicated reset triggers ensures predictable state clearing.

### 3. Modifier Chord Strategy
* **Current Strategy:** The prototype app handles modifier chords by checking if the event flags intersect with a modifier mask (`.maskCommand`, `.maskControl`, `.maskAlternate`). If a modifier is held, it resets the engine and passes the event through.
* **Critique/Constraint:** In the production `macos/Lex.swift`, this modifier check is missing or misplaced. Because the event tap intercepts `.keyDown` and immediately attempts to extract and validate Unicode characters, pressing a chord like `Cmd + T` or `Cmd + V` gets treated as an alphabetic input (`T` or `V`). This either blocks the hotkey or feeds unwanted characters into the engine. To prevent interference, the modifier chord check must be positioned at the very beginning of the `.keyDown` handling block, immediately resetting the engine and passing the event through before any character extraction occurs.",
553:                "message": "## 1) TL;DR

The minimal correct fix is to make `keyDown` classify “must pass through” cases before any Unicode/text composition: synthetic events first, then Command/Control/Option chords, then plain Space as an explicit reset boundary. Add an app-activation observer to reset state on app switches. Keep `flagsChanged` passive; do not reset on plain Shift or Caps Lock.

## 2) Recommended approach: simple path

1. **Keep current top-level event handling structure**
   - Tap-disabled events: reset, re-enable tap, pass through.
   - Mouse down: reset, pass through.
   - `flagsChanged`: pass through without resetting.
   - Only `keyDown` should participate in composition logic.

2. **Add app-switch reset out of band**
   - Observe `NSWorkspace.didActivateApplicationNotification`.
   - On activation change, reset the Telex engine state.
   - This is the right layer because app switches may happen without a relevant keyboard event reaching the tap.

3. **Reorder `keyDown` handling conceptually**
   - First: ignore Lex’s own synthetic events.
   - Then: check whether Command, Control, or Option is held.
     - If yes, reset state and pass the original event through.
     - This must happen before literal-mode handling, backspace handling, Unicode extraction, alphabetic checks, or synthetic replacement.
   - Then: explicitly treat plain Space as a word-boundary reset.
     - Reset state.
     - Pass Space through.
     - Do not rely only on the generic “non-alphabetic” fallback.
   - Then: apply literal-mode pass-through.
     - If literal mode is active, do not compose.
   - Then: handle plain Backspace.
     - Modified Backspace should already have been caught by the modifier-chord rule and should reset/pass through.
   - Then: do Unicode extraction and alphabetic Telex processing.

4. **Do not reset on plain Shift/Caps `flagsChanged`**
   - Shift and Caps Lock are casing mechanisms, not text-boundary or context-changing actions.
   - Resetting on them would make uppercase Telex input fragile.

## 3) Rationale and trade-offs

The current risky part is that modifier chords are not classified early enough. A `Command+T` or `Command+V` keyDown can still look like an alphabetic `T` or `V` when Unicode is extracted, so the Telex path may consume or transform a shortcut that should belong to the active app.

The safest minimal rule is:

> Any `keyDown` with Command, Control, or Option is not text input for Telex. Reset and pass it through.

That covers app shortcuts, paste, tab/window commands, browser shortcuts, terminal shortcuts, and modified deletes without needing to understand every shortcut individually.

Explicit Space handling is also worth doing even though the current non-alpha fallback may already reset on Space. Space is semantically important: it ends the current composition span/word. Making it a named reset case avoids future regressions if the fallback logic changes.

Effort: **S, likely <1h** conceptually and implementation-wise.

## 4) Risks and guardrails

- **Do not include Shift in the modifier-chord reset mask.**  
  Shifted letters should still compose normally.

- **Do not reset on `flagsChanged` for Shift/Caps.**  
  `flagsChanged` is not text input. Resetting there creates surprising behavior while typing uppercase syllables.

- **Check modifier chords before Backspace.**  
  Plain Backspace can update the engine buffer, but `Command+Delete`, `Option+Delete`, and similar editing shortcuts should reset/pass through because they may delete whole lines/words or otherwise invalidate the internal buffer.

- **Check modifier chords before Unicode extraction.**  
  Unicode extraction under Command/Control/Option can still produce a character-like value, which is exactly why shortcuts can be accidentally swallowed.

- **Synthetic event filtering should remain very early.**  
  Lex-generated replacement/backspace events must not re-enter the composition path. If the event mask expands later to include more keyboard event types, revisit synthetic filtering for those too.

- **App switch reset is necessary but not sufficient.**  
  It handles cross-app context changes. It does not cover all intra-app focus/caret moves, so mouse reset and shortcut reset are still needed.

- **Ctrl+Option+Space toggle should remain safe.**  
  The chord rule should reset and pass it through; the registered hotkey can toggle mode separately. A double reset is harmless.

## 5) When to consider expanding reset cases

After the minimal fix, consider broader reset coverage only if users observe stale composition after navigation or editing. Concrete triggers:

- Telex state survives after Return/Enter, Tab, Escape, or arrow navigation.
- State survives after Home/End/Page Up/Page Down.
- State becomes wrong after forward delete.
- State becomes wrong after intra-app focus changes, keyboard-driven field switching, or selection changes.
- Paste/undo/redo/menu commands leave the engine buffer inconsistent despite modifier-chord reset.
- Non-US layouts, dead keys, or Option-produced characters need first-class behavior.

## 6) Optional future expansion path

If needed later, add a small “reset-and-pass-through key” classification after the modifier-chord check and before composition. Candidate groups:

- Word/field boundaries: Return, Enter, Tab, Escape.
- Navigation: arrows, Home, End, Page Up, Page Down.
- Destructive edits: forward delete, possibly modified delete variants if not already covered by modifiers.
- Context changes: additional focus/window notifications if app-switch and mouse resets are not enough.

But do not add all of this immediately unless there is observed breakage. The minimal high-value fix is modifier chords plus explicit Space plus app-switch reset.",

651:          "text": "## Current order: mostly sound, but incomplete for text-vs-shortcut classification

The current callback in [`macos/Lex.swift`](file:///<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L394-L553) has a reasonable top-level structure:

1. tap-disabled events reset/re-enable/pass through
2. mouse clicks reset/pass through
3. `flagsChanged` passes through
4. `keyDown` does the real Telex work

The weak point is inside `keyDown`: after synthetic-event filtering, it goes directly to literal-mode check, backspace handling, Unicode extraction, alphabetic detection, engine mutation, and synthetic replacement. There is no early “this is a shortcut/modifier chord, not text input” classification.

That explains the `Command+T`, `Command+V`, etc. problem: a modified key event can still yield a single alphabetic Unicode character, so the callback treats it as Telex input and may swallow it.

## Minimal first approach

### 1. Keep top-level event order

Current top-level handling is acceptable:

- tap disabled → reset, re-enable, pass through
- mouse down → reset, pass through
- flags changed → pass through
- key down → inspect further

I would not expand `flagsChanged` yet. In particular, do not reset on plain Shift/Caps Lock, because those are part of normal uppercase text input.

### 2. Reorder `keyDown` handling conceptually

The minimal correct `keyDown` order should be:

```diagram
╭──────────────╮
│ keyDown only │
╰──────┬───────╯
       ▼
╭──────────────────────────╮
│ Lex synthetic event?      │──yes──▶ pass through
╰──────┬───────────────────╯
       ▼ no
╭──────────────────────────╮
│ Cmd/Ctrl/Option held?     │──yes──▶ reset + pass through
╰──────┬───────────────────╯
       ▼ no
╭──────────────────────────╮
│ Space key?                │──yes──▶ reset + pass through
╰──────┬───────────────────╯
       ▼ no
╭──────────────────────────╮
│ literal mode?             │──yes──▶ pass through
╰──────┬───────────────────╯
       ▼ no
╭──────────────────────────╮
│ plain Backspace?          │──yes──▶ engine backspace + pass through
╰──────┬───────────────────╯
       ▼ no
╭──────────────────────────╮
│ Unicode/text extraction   │
│ alphabetic Telex handling │
╰──────────────────────────╯
```

The important change is: modifier chords must be handled before Unicode extraction and before engine mutation.

### 3. SPACE reset

Current code already resets on Space indirectly, because Space is non-alphabetic and reaches the reset fallback at [`macos/Lex.swift`](file:///<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L451-L470).

But I would still make Space an explicit reset boundary in the conceptual order. Reason: Space is not just “some non-alpha key”; it is the normal word boundary for Telex composition. Treating it explicitly makes the behavior intentional and harder to break later.

### 4. App-switch reset

Current app does not observe app switches. The prototype does this with `NSWorkspace.didActivateApplicationNotification` in [`playground/prototype-app/macos/Lex.swift`](file:///<redacted>/lex/playground/prototype-app/macos/Lex.swift#L61-L68).

Minimal approach: add an app activation observer that resets the engine when the active app changes.

This belongs outside the event callback because app switches may happen in ways that are not cleanly represented as a normal key event to this tap.

### 5. Modifier handling

Minimal rule:

> Any `keyDown` with Command, Control, or Option held is not Telex text input. Reset engine state and pass the event through.

Do not include Shift or Caps Lock in this rule.

This should fix `Command+T`, `Command+V`, paste, browser/tab shortcuts, terminal shortcuts, app shortcuts, and modified delete/navigation commands without needing a special list of hotkeys.

- explicit Space reset
- app-switch reset
- Command/Control/Option `keyDown` reset + pass-through

737:          "text": "## Answers

### How to detect Cmd / Ctrl / Opt held?

In the `CGEventTap` callback, use `event.flags`.

Conceptually:

- Command: `CGEventFlags.maskCommand`
- Control: `CGEventFlags.maskControl`
- Option/Alt: `CGEventFlags.maskAlternate`

The rule should be:

> On `keyDown`, if `event.flags` intersects Command / Control / Option, reset engine and pass through.

Do not include Shift. Shifted letters should still be valid Telex input.

Also note: Carbon hotkey registration uses `controlKey | optionKey`, but the event tap uses `CGEventFlags.maskControl` / `.maskAlternate`. They are different APIs.

### What is the Space keycode name?

Use Carbon’s:

- `kVK_Space`

Its value is `49` / `0x31`, but use the named constant.

You are already using it for the global hotkey registration in [`register_toggle_input_mode_hot_key`](file:///<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L210-L217).

Backspace is currently using:

- `kVK_Delete`

That name is confusing, but in Carbon it means the normal Backspace/Delete key.

Forward Delete would be:

- `kVK_ForwardDelete`

## About adding modifiers + Space into the existing switch

Space belongs naturally in the existing `switch key_code` beside Backspace.

Modifier handling is different: it is not a keycode case for `Cmd+T`, `Cmd+V`, etc. The keycode is still `T` or `V`; the modifier state is in `event.flags`.

So I would structure it like this conceptually:

1. synthetic event check
2. modifier-chord check using `event.flags`
3. get `key_code`
4. `switch key_code`
   - `kVK_Space`: reset + pass through
   - `kVK_Delete`: engine backspace + pass through
   - default: continue to Unicode/alphabetic handling

So: yes, put Space with Backspace in the existing switch, but put modifier detection immediately before that switch, not as a switch case.

## Are you missing anything?

A few ordering details:

### 1. Modifier check should happen before Unicode extraction

This is the main bug source. `Command+V` can still look like the character `v` if you ask for Unicode, so the event must be classified as a shortcut first.

### 2. Modifier check should happen before Backspace handling

Plain Backspace can update the engine.

But `Option+Backspace`, `Command+Backspace`, etc. may delete a word/line or trigger app behavior. Those should reset + pass through, not call `engine.backspace()`.

### 3. Ctrl+Opt+Space hotkey should still work

If you handle modifiers first:

- Ctrl+Opt+Space reaches “modifier chord”
- engine resets
- event passes through
- Carbon hotkey handler can still toggle mode

A double reset is harmless because `toggle_input_mode()` already resets.

### 4. App switch reset is separate

You still need `NSWorkspace.didActivateApplicationNotification` for app switching. It should not be inside the event callback because app switches are not guaranteed to be represented as a useful keyboard event.

### 5. Literal mode order is not critical, but I prefer modifier reset before literal pass-through

If literal mode is active, you can pass everything through and probably be fine.

But for a consistent “shortcuts are context boundaries” rule, I would still check modifiers before literal mode and reset. It is harmless and makes behavior simpler:

- synthetic? pass
- modifier chord? reset + pass
- Space? reset + pass
- literal? pass
- Backspace/text handling

If you want the smallest possible behavioral change, keep literal mode before modifier handling. But then shortcuts in literal mode will not reset state. Since mode toggling already resets, this probably does not matter.",

Your implementation in [`event_tap_callback`](file:///<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L414-L450) now does the important things:

- `Command+T`, `Command+V`, etc. should no longer be consumed by Telex.
- `Control`, `Option`, and `Command` chords reset the engine and pass through.
- `Space` explicitly resets and passes through.
- plain Backspace still updates engine state and passes through.
- Shift/Caps are not treated as reset modifiers.

That matches the minimal target.

## One ordering difference to be aware of

You currently check literal mode before synthetic-event filtering and before modifier/Space reset:

[`macos/Lex.swift#L417-L434`](file:///<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L417-L434)

That means:

- in Telex mode: behavior is correct
- in literal mode:
  - `Command+T`, `Command+V`, etc. pass through, but do not reset engine
  - `Space` passes through, but does not reset engine
  - synthetic events pass through, but are not identified first

This is probably okay because `toggle_input_mode()` already resets when entering literal mode, and literal mode does not mutate the engine. So practically, there should be no stale engine state to reset.

But if you want the stronger invariant:

> Space and modifier shortcuts are always composition boundaries regardless of input mode

then literal-mode pass-through should come after synthetic/modifier/Space handling.

I do not think that is required for the minimal fix, but it is the main semantic difference from the earlier order.

## Modifier handling is in the right place

This part is correctly before the keycode switch and before Unicode extraction:

[`macos/Lex.swift#L427-L434`](file:///<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L427-L434)

That is the important fix. `Command+V` can still look like `v` if you ask for Unicode, so checking `event.flags` before text extraction is correct.

Also good: this check comes before Backspace. So `Option+Backspace` / `Command+Backspace` will reset and pass through instead of calling `engine.backspace()` incorrectly.

## Space handling is correct

This is good:

[`macos/Lex.swift#L439-L443`](file:///<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L439-L443)

Using `kVK_Space` is correct. Handling it explicitly makes the word-boundary behavior intentional instead of relying on the later non-alphabetic fallback.

## Are you missing anything?

For the minimal target: no major missing piece, given that you intentionally ignore app-switch reset for now.

The only things I would keep in mind:

1. **Literal mode does not reset on Space/modifiers with current order.** Probably fine, but worth being intentional about.
2. **Navigation keys are still handled only indirectly.** Many will reach `character_count != 1` and reset/pass through. That is acceptable for now.
3. **Forward Delete is not explicitly handled.** It likely resets through the no-character path, but if you later expand special-key handling, add `kVK_ForwardDelete` explicitly.
4. **Tiny style issue:** there is trailing whitespace after the closing brace at [`macos/Lex.swift#L434`](file:///<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L427-L434). Not behavior-affecting.

My recommendation: keep this as the minimal behavior, unless you want the stricter invariant that Space/modifier reset should happen even while in literal mode.",

The reason for “only consume on nonzero synthetic backspaces” is practical: ordinary letters should remain native key events. Synthetic Unicode events are less faithful across apps than the original physical key event. The engine’s replacement path should be reserved for retrospective Telex edits.

This slightly changes your “engine can handle → consume” idea:

- If the engine merely appends a literal letter, prefer passthrough.
- If the engine modifies previous visible text, consume and synthesize.

That maps better to the current ABI.

## 4. Mirror length update rule

The mirror cannot be just “number of alpha keys typed”, because some Telex actions modify existing spans without appending a new span.

Use the visible-edit result to update the mirror:

- If passthrough literal alpha after `lex_add`: mirror length increases by 1.
- If consumed rewrite:
  - new mirror length = previous mirror length − synthetic backspaces + replacement count.
- If full-before-add passthrough: mirror length increases by 1.
- If backspace passthrough and mirror length > 0: mirror length decreases by 1.
- If reset: mirror length becomes 0.

This matches the engine’s own model: `buffer_modification_index` tells how far back to erase, and replacement count tells how many UTF-16 code units are emitted.

## 5. Backspace should synchronize, not synthesize

With the current ABI, backspace is not a composition operation. It only decrements engine state and clears modification bookkeeping. See [the backspace implementation](file:///<redacted>/lex/src/lex.zig#L1748-L1758).

So for Backspace:

- If mirror length > 0:
  - call `lex_backspace`
  - decrement mirror
  - pass native Backspace through
- If mirror length == 0:
  - pass through without calling Zig

Do not call `lex_compose_utf16_string_replacement` after backspace. The replacement API is designed for the previous `lex_add` action, not arbitrary deletion.

## 6. Full buffer behavior

Your buffer-full idea is mostly right.

`buffer_effective_length` is 16. Once `lex_buffer_effective_full` is true, the engine has switched into literal-tail behavior: it can keep tracking total length, but Telex processing is no longer useful for new characters.

So:

- If full before an alpha add:
  - feed `lex_add` to keep state synchronized
  - pass through original event
  - avoid composition
- Backspaces later can bring the engine below the full threshold.
- If the `u8` length limit would be exceeded, reset with `lex_init`.

Important nuance: call `lex_buffer_effective_full` before `lex_add`. If you call `lex_add` while already full, `buffer_length` may become greater than the effective buffer length. At that point replacement composition would violate its internal precondition.

# Reset triggers

I would reset on:

- SPACE
- app switch
- input mode toggle
- mouse down
- tap disabled/re-enabled
- Return / Enter / Tab / Escape
- arrows / Home / End / PageUp / PageDown
- forward Delete
- Command / Control / Option shortcuts
- non-ASCII or multi-code-unit text input
- dead-key/composition uncertainty
- engine mirror length reaching the `u8` safety boundary

For `.literal` mode, simplest behavior is:

- reset engine when entering literal mode
- pass all events through

From `playground/prototype-app`, keep these techniques:

- tag synthetic events with a private `CGEventSource.userData`
- ignore tagged synthetic events early in the tap callback
- reset on app switch
- reset on caret/navigation/mouse boundary events
- re-enable event tap on tap-disabled events
- keep event tap work lightweight

Do **not** keep its structural model:

- no Swift-side rendered-buffer diff

- no dependency on add/backspace disposition returns
- no prototype ABI assumptions

Oracle agreed with the overall direction, with these corrections:

1. Treat the current ABI as a **retrospective-edit engine**, not a full input-method state machine.
2. Keep a Swift-side mirror because the ABI does not expose length or empty-state queries.
3. Filter aggressively before calling Zig.
4. Prefer native passthrough for ordinary literal alpha input.
5. Consume only when `lex_calculate_synthetic_backspaces` is nonzero.
6. Use `lex_backspace` only for state synchronization; do not synthesize replacements on backspace.
7. Use `lex_init` as reset because no separate reset ABI exists.
8. If this becomes fragile, the smallest future ABI improvement would be explicit reset/length/status exports or an `add` result.

# My recommendation

Implement the first integration with the current ABI unchanged:

- Swift owns event classification and reset policy.
- Zig owns Telex state and replacement calculation.
- Consume only retrospective rewrites.
- Pass through literal input and synchronize state.
- Reset aggressively at text-boundary uncertainty.

Only change the ABI later if Swift-side mirroring proves fragile. The likely useful additions would be a reset export, current length/empty query, and possibly an `add` status result, but they are not required for the first working app integration.",

1318:          "text": "# Revised approach with the new ABI

Your added functions remove the main reason for Swift-side mirroring. With:

- `lex_buffer_full`
- `lex_buffer_empty`
- existing `lex_buffer_effective_full`
- existing replacement APIs

Swift can treat the engine as the source of truth and avoid duplicating internal state.

The host should still not infer too much. It should ask the ABI:

- “Is the engine empty?” before `lex_backspace`.
- “Is the total buffer at its hard limit?” before `lex_add`.
- “Is the effective Telex buffer full?” before deciding whether replacement synthesis is valid/useful.

# Important distinction: `buffer_full` vs `buffer_effective_full`

I would keep both concepts separate:

## `lex_buffer_effective_full`

Meaning: the Telex-processing window is full.

In the current engine this corresponds to the 16-span `buffer_effective` limit. After this point the engine may still track total length, but new input is effectively literal-tail synchronization.

Use this to decide:

- if `false`: the engine may produce retrospective Telex replacement.
- if `true`: feed alpha input for synchronization, but pass through and avoid replacement composition.

## `lex_buffer_full`

Meaning: the total engine buffer length reached the hard representable limit, probably `u8` max.

Use this as a safety boundary:

- If true before an add, call `lex_init`.
- Then handle the current event as the first event of a new session.

That gives the behavior you want: once the old long session is exhausted, the next valid alpha key starts fresh Vietnamese input again.

# Revised event flow

## On mode switch

When app mode changes:

1. call `lex_init`
2. update app mode
3. play sound/update UI
4. do not feed the toggle key event to the engine

This applies both directions:

- Telex → Literal: reset because engine should no longer track literal-mode typing.
- Literal → Telex: reset because the previous literal text is outside the engine session.

This is cleaner than keeping engine state alive across modes.

## In Literal mode

If app mode is `.literal`:

- never call `lex_add`
- never call `lex_backspace`
- pass events through
- ignore synthetic events as usual

The engine always being Telex-mode is a good simplification. “Literal mode” becomes purely an app-level bypass state.

## In Telex mode: alpha keyDown

For a real user keyDown that produces exactly one ASCII alphabetic character:

1. Ignore if synthetic.
2. If `lex_buffer_full(state)`:
   - call `lex_init(state)`
   - continue handling this same key as a fresh session.
3. Check `lex_buffer_effective_full(state)` before `lex_add`.
4. Call `lex_add(state, ascii_byte)`.
5. If effective buffer was already full before the add:
   - pass original event through
   - do not call replacement composition
6. Otherwise call `lex_calculate_synthetic_backspaces(state)`.
7. If synthetic backspaces is `0`:
   - pass original event through
8. If synthetic backspaces is nonzero:
   - call `lex_compose_utf16_string_replacement`
   - post synthetic backspaces
   - post synthetic replacement text
   - consume original event

This keeps native key events for plain letters and uses synthetic events only for retrospective corrections.

# Why consume only on retrospective edits?

Because a normal alpha key already does exactly what we want in the target app. If the engine only appended a literal span, synthesizing the same letter is unnecessary and less compatible.

Example behavior:

```text
User types: n
Engine state: n
Synthetic backspaces: 0
Action: pass through native "n"

User types: u
Engine state: nu
Synthetic backspaces: 0
Action: pass through native "u"

User types: o
Engine state: nuo
Synthetic backspaces: maybe 0
Action: pass through if no rewrite

User types: w
Engine changes prior vowels to produce Vietnamese form
Synthetic backspaces: nonzero
Action: consume "w", synthesize erase+replacement
```

That matches the current ABI design: Zig tells Swift when visible text must be rewritten.

# Backspace flow

With `lex_buffer_empty`, backspace becomes clean.

On Backspace keyDown in Telex mode:

1. If synthetic, ignore.
2. If `lex_buffer_empty(state)`:
   - pass native Backspace through
3. Else:
   - call `lex_backspace(state)`
   - pass native Backspace through

Do not synthesize replacement on backspace with the current ABI. Current `lex_backspace` is state synchronization, not a Telex rewrite operation.

If you later want Telex-aware backspace behavior—such as decomposing `ư` back to `u` or removing only tone/diacritic—that needs explicit engine support and probably a different backspace ABI.

# Reset triggers remain important

Even without Swift-side mirroring, reset boundaries are still required because the global event tap cannot know target-app text state perfectly.

Reset via `lex_init` on:

- SPACE
- app switch
- mode switch
- mouse down
- Return / Enter
- Tab
- Escape
- arrow keys
- Home / End / PageUp / PageDown
- Forward Delete
- Command / Control / Option shortcuts
- non-ASCII or multi-code-unit input
- tap disabled/re-enabled
- secure/special uncertainty if detectable

For `flagsChanged`, I would not reset on plain Shift/Caps Lock. But if the following keyDown has Command/Control/Option, reset and pass through.

# Suggested C ABI shape

Conceptually, the useful ABI becomes:

```text
state allocation:
- lex_state_size
- lex_state_alignment
- lex_init

input mutation:
- lex_add
- lex_backspace

state queries:
- lex_buffer_empty
- lex_buffer_effective_full
- lex_buffer_full

replacement:
- lex_calculate_synthetic_backspaces
- lex_replacement_buffer_length
- lex_compose_utf16_string_replacement
```

That is enough for a first robust app integration without Swift mirroring.

# One naming concern

`lex_buffer_full` and `lex_buffer_effective_full` must be documented very clearly.

Otherwise it will be easy to confuse:

- “effective full” = Telex window full; still safe to feed for synchronization.
- “buffer full” = hard total length full; must reset before feeding more input.

I would document `lex_buffer_full` as something like:

> Returns true when the next `lex_add` would exceed the engine’s total buffer length limit. The caller must reset with `lex_init` before feeding another character.

And `lex_buffer_effective_full` as:

> Returns true when the Telex-effective buffer is full. The caller may still feed alphabetic input for synchronization, but should pass the original event through and should not request replacement composition for that input.

# Final proposed responsibility split

```diagram
╭──────────────────╮
│ macOS event tap  │
╰────────┬─────────╯
         │ classify event
         ▼
╭─────────────────────────────╮
│ Swift app policy             │
│ - mode bypass                │
│ - reset boundaries           │
│ - shortcut/navigation filter │
│ - synthetic event tagging    │
╰────────┬────────────────────╯
         │ safe ASCII alpha / backspace only
         ▼
╭─────────────────────────────╮
│ Lex C ABI                    │
│ - owns Telex state           │
│ - reports empty/full         │
│ - reports replacement edit   │
╰────────┬────────────────────╯
         │ replacement only if needed
         ▼
╭─────────────────────────────╮
│ Synthetic events             │
│ - backspaces                 │
│ - UTF-16 replacement         │
╰─────────────────────────────╯
```

# Main remaining risk

Removing Swift mirroring is correct, but it does not solve global event-tap drift completely.

If the app passes through an alpha key but the target app treats that alpha as a command rather than text insertion, the engine will still believe text was inserted. Later retrospective synthetic backspaces may affect unexpected content.

This is inherent to global event taps. The mitigation is conservative reset policy plus only running in contexts where normal text input is expected. For the first version, the proposed ABI is enough; deeper correctness would require integration with macOS text input APIs rather than only a session event tap.",

# Revised alpha flow

For user alpha keyDown in Telex mode:

1. Ignore synthetic events first.
2. If `lex_buffer_full(state)`:
   - `lex_init(state)`
   - continue with current key as first input of new session.
3. Check `lex_buffer_effective_full(state)` before add.
4. If effective buffer is full:
   - call `lex_add(state, c)` only for synchronization
   - pass original event through
   - do not compose replacement
5. If effective buffer is not full:
   - call `lex_add(state, c)`
   - call `lex_calculate_synthetic_backspaces(state)`
   - call `lex_compose_utf16_string_replacement(state, ...)`
   - post synthetic backspaces if count > 0
   - post synthetic replacement text
   - consume original event

This is coherent.

# Why this is simpler

The previous branch:

```text
synthetic_backspaces == 0 → pass through
synthetic_backspaces > 0  → consume and synthesize
```

mixed two rendering authorities:

- native app inserts ordinary letters
- Lex inserts retrospective edits

Your version has one authority inside the effective window:

- Lex renders every ASCII alpha input while Telex mode is active.

That eliminates ambiguity around whether native insertion happened.

# The only trade-off

The cost is compatibility.

When Telex mode is on and the effective buffer is not full, Lex will consume all ASCII alpha keyDown events. So in an app where plain letters are commands rather than text insertion, Lex will interfere more aggressively than the passthrough-literal approach.

But for an input method app, this is acceptable if the design intent is:

> Telex mode means Lex owns alphabetic text input until a reset boundary or buffer limit.

That is a clearer model.

# Effective-full behavior still needs passthrough

The key boundary remains `lex_buffer_effective_full`.

If effective buffer is full before `lex_add`, Swift should not consume and synthesize, because after `lex_add` the engine’s total `buffer_length` may exceed the effective buffer length, and replacement composition is not valid for that state.

So:

```text
effective not full → consume + synthesize replacement
effective full     → feed for sync + passthrough
buffer full        → reset before feeding
```

# Backspace remains passthrough sync

Even under the “engine owns alpha insertion” model, Backspace should still be:

- if `lex_buffer_empty`: pass through
- else `lex_backspace`, then pass through

Current ABI does not expose a composed replacement for backspace, so Backspace remains native deletion plus engine synchronization.
