If consuming keyDown events, consider whether the tap should also include keyUp events for alphabetic keys. Otherwise the target app may see keyUp without the original keyDown. For ordinary text fields this usually does not matter, but some apps with custom key handling may care.

# 1. Event mask shape in `start_event_tap`

Current mask includes:

- `keyDown`
- `flagsChanged`
- `leftMouseDown`
- `rightMouseDown`

But your callback already checks tap-disabled events, so include these too:

- `tapDisabledByTimeout`
- `tapDisabledByUserInput`

Conceptually:

```swift
let event_mask =
    (CGEventMask(1) << CGEventType.keyDown.rawValue)
    | (CGEventMask(1) << CGEventType.flagsChanged.rawValue)
    | (CGEventMask(1) << CGEventType.leftMouseDown.rawValue)
    | (CGEventMask(1) << CGEventType.rightMouseDown.rawValue)
    | (CGEventMask(1) << CGEventType.tapDisabledByTimeout.rawValue)
    | (CGEventMask(1) << CGEventType.tapDisabledByUserInput.rawValue)
```

# 2. Top-level callback pattern

Use `switch event_type` first. Keep every branch shallow.

```swift
private func event_tap_callback(
    proxy: CGEventTapProxy,
    type event_type: CGEventType,
    event: CGEvent,
    userInfo: UnsafeMutableRawPointer?
) -> Unmanaged<CGEvent>? {
    guard let userInfo else {
        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
    }

    let app_delegate = Unmanaged<AppDelegate>
        .fromOpaque(userInfo)
        .takeUnretainedValue()

    switch event_type {
    case .tapDisabledByTimeout, .tapDisabledByUserInput:
        // Re-enable tap.
        // Reset engine.
        // Pass through event.
        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)

    case .leftMouseDown, .rightMouseDown:
        // Reset engine.
        // Pass through event.
        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)

    case .flagsChanged:
        // Usually pass through.
        // Do not reset for plain Shift/Caps Lock here.
        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)

    case .keyDown:
        // Delegate to keyDown branch.
        return handle_key_down(
            app_delegate: app_delegate,
            proxy: proxy,
            event: event
        )

    default:
        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
    }
}
```

Because `event_tap_callback` is currently a free function, `handle_key_down` can also start as a free private function.

# 3. KeyDown branch pattern

This is where most policy lives. Keep it as a sequence of early returns.

```swift
private func handle_key_down(
    app_delegate: AppDelegate,
    proxy: CGEventTapProxy,
    event: CGEvent
) -> Unmanaged<CGEvent>? {
    // 1. Ignore Lex synthetic events.
    if event.getIntegerValueField(.eventSourceUserData) == synthetic_event_source_user_data {
        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
    }

    // 2. Literal app mode: engine is bypassed.
    if app_delegate.app_state.mode == .literal {
        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
    }

    // 3. Shortcut/modifier combinations.
    // Command / Control / Option should reset and pass through.
    // Shift alone should not reset.
    if has_command_control_or_option(event) {
        // Reset engine.
        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
    }

    let key_code = event.getIntegerValueField(.keyboardEventKeycode)

    // 4. Key-code based boundaries.
    switch key_code {
    case Int64(kVK_Delete):
        // Backspace sync branch.
        // If engine empty: pass through.
        // Else lex_backspace + pass through.
        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)

    case Int64(kVK_Return), Int64(kVK_ANSI_KeypadEnter):
        // Reset engine.
        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)

    case Int64(kVK_Tab):
        // Reset engine.
        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)

    case Int64(kVK_Escape):
        // Reset engine.
        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)

    case Int64(kVK_LeftArrow),
         Int64(kVK_RightArrow),
         Int64(kVK_DownArrow),
         Int64(kVK_UpArrow):
        // Reset engine.
        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)

    case Int64(kVK_Home),
         Int64(kVK_End),
         Int64(kVK_PageUp),
         Int64(kVK_PageDown):
        // Reset engine.
        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)

    case Int64(kVK_ForwardDelete):
        // Reset engine.
        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)

    default:
        break
    }

    // 5. Character extraction.
    // If not exactly one UTF-16 code unit: reset and pass through.

    // 6. ASCII alpha check.
    // If not A-Z or a-z: reset and pass through.

    // 7. Telex alpha branch.
    // If lex_buffer_full: reset first.
    // If lex_buffer_effective_full before add:
    //     lex_add for sync, pass through.
    // Else:
    //     lex_add.
    //     calculate synthetic backspaces.
    //     compose replacement.
    //     post synthetic edit.
    //     consume original event by returning nil.

    return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
}
```

# 4. Small helper patterns

For readability, define tiny helpers later. For now, names are enough.

```swift
private func has_command_control_or_option(_ event: CGEvent) -> Bool {
    let flags = event.flags
    let mask: CGEventFlags = [
        .maskCommand,
        .maskControl,
        .maskAlternate,
    ]
    return !flags.intersection(mask).isEmpty
}
```

For ASCII alpha, eventually:

```swift
private func is_ascii_alpha(_ c: UniChar) -> Bool {
    return (c >= 65 && c <= 90) || (c >= 97 && c <= 122)
}
```

# 5. Recommended branch order

Use this exact order because it avoids accidental engine mutation:

```text
keyDown
 ├─ synthetic event?                → pass through, do nothing
 ├─ app literal mode?               → pass through, do nothing
 ├─ command/control/option?         → reset, pass through
 ├─ backspace?                      → sync backspace, pass through
 ├─ navigation/boundary key?        → reset, pass through
 ├─ not exactly one UTF-16 unit?    → reset, pass through
 ├─ not ASCII alpha?                → reset, pass through
 ├─ buffer full?                    → reset, then continue
 ├─ effective buffer full?          → lex_add, pass through
 └─ effective buffer not full?      → lex_add, synthesize replacement, consume
```

# 6. AppDelegate methods worth stubbing

Before filling logic, add method names on `AppDelegate` mentally or as TODOs:

```swift

private func handle_alpha_key(...)
private func post_synthetic_backspaces(...)
private func post_synthetic_replacement(...)
```

But for the first pass, do not implement them. Just make the callback structure readable.

`app_state` is marked `@MainActor`. Accessing `app_delegate.app_state.mode` from the event tap callback may trigger actor-isolation issues depending on compiler settings.

# Post synthetic Backspace events

Backspace is virtual key `kVK_Delete` in Carbon. Despite the name, `kVK_Delete` is the normal Backspace key. Forward Delete is `kVK_ForwardDelete`.

Pattern:

```swift
private func post_synthetic_backspaces(
    proxy: CGEventTapProxy,
    count: Int
) {
    guard let synthetic_event_source else {
        return
    }

    guard count > 0 else {
        return
    }

    for _ in 0..<count {
        if let down = CGEvent(
            keyboardEventSource: synthetic_event_source,
            virtualKey: CGKeyCode(kVK_Delete),
            keyDown: true
        ) {
            down.tapPostEvent(proxy)
        }

        if let up = CGEvent(
            keyboardEventSource: synthetic_event_source,
            virtualKey: CGKeyCode(kVK_Delete),
            keyDown: false
        ) {
            up.tapPostEvent(proxy)
        }
    }
}
```

# Post synthetic replacement text

Replacement should be posted as Unicode text, not as physical key codes.

Pattern:

```swift
private func post_synthetic_replacement(
    proxy: CGEventTapProxy,
    characters: [UInt16]
) {
    guard let synthetic_event_source else {
        return
    }

    guard !characters.isEmpty else {
        return
    }

    var characters = characters

    if let down = CGEvent(
        keyboardEventSource: synthetic_event_source,
        virtualKey: 0,
        keyDown: true
    ) {
        down.keyboardSetUnicodeString(
            stringLength: characters.count,
            unicodeString: &characters
        )
        down.tapPostEvent(proxy)
    }

    if let up = CGEvent(
        keyboardEventSource: synthetic_event_source,
        virtualKey: 0,
        keyDown: false
    ) {
        up.keyboardSetUnicodeString(
            stringLength: characters.count,
            unicodeString: &characters
        )
        up.tapPostEvent(proxy)
    }
}
```

This is the same technique the prototype used: create a keyboard event with virtual key `0`, attach Unicode code units, then post it through the tap proxy.

The overall direction is right: keep the event tap as an `AppDelegate`-owned, process-wide concern and hook it into `applicationDidFinishLaunching` / `applicationWillTerminate`. For this first step, I’d make it strictly passive, keep the event mask as small as possible, and avoid copying the prototype’s broader permission and reset logic until you actually need it.  
**Scope:** S (<1h) conceptually.

2) **Recommended approach (simple path)**

1. **Let `AppDelegate` own the tap lifecycle**
   - That matches the current architecture well: the delegate already owns other global OS integrations like signal handling, engine lifetime, and the Carbon hot key.
   - This is a better fit than pushing event-tap concerns into SwiftUI views or `AppState`.

2. **Start on launch, stop on terminate**
   - The comments in `applicationDidFinishLaunching` and `applicationWillTerminate` are the right integration points.
   - On startup, try to create/start the tap once.
   - On shutdown, explicitly invalidate/tear down the tap and clear references so you don’t leave callback plumbing half-alive during termination.

3. **Use a passive tap for the first step**
   - Since you only want to observe and print characters, the prototype’s fully modifiable tap is more power than you need right now.
   - A passive/listen-only setup better matches intent and reduces the chance of accidentally suppressing or altering user input.
   - You can switch to a modifiable tap later when you actually need swallowing or event rewriting.

4. **Keep the event mask minimal**
   - For the current goal, only keyboard-down events are really needed.
   - The prototype’s extra monitoring of flags changes, mouse clicks, and reset-related events is tied to composition logic that you explicitly are not doing yet.
   - Fewer observed event types means less callback traffic, less noise, and less risk.

5. **Keep the callback extremely lightweight**
   - Treat it as a diagnostic observer only.
   - Read the text representation from the key event and print only when it meaningfully maps to a character.
   - Avoid touching engine state, `AppState`, sound playback, or any SwiftUI-facing state from the callback for now.

6. **Handle failure and disabled-state recovery deliberately**
   - If tap creation fails, the app should still launch and the hot key should still work.
   - For a first step, it’s enough to log a clear message that keyboard monitoring is unavailable.
   - If you keep a regular tap instead of a passive one, then handling timeout/user-disable re-enable events becomes more important.

3) **Rationale and trade-offs**

- **Why this is the right simple path**
  - Your current `AppDelegate` is already the “global integration layer,” so putting the event tap there is architecturally consistent.
  - A passive tap keeps this first step low-risk and aligned with the stated goal: just verify that you can see characters.
  - Reusing the prototype wholesale would pull in a lot of behavior that only makes sense once the engine is participating.

- **Why the prototype should not be copied too literally yet**
  - The prototype mixes several concerns: permission prompting, event filtering, engine resets, synthetic event detection, composition diffing, and event swallowing.
  - For the current checkpoint, most of that is unnecessary complexity and makes failures harder to reason about.

- **Most important permission critique**
  - The prototype’s Accessibility trust check is not the cleanest fit for this first stage.
  - For global keyboard observation via event taps, the practical gate is usually **Input Monitoring**, not just Accessibility.
  - So I would not anchor the first-step design around an Accessibility prompt flow unless you already know you’ll need Accessibility immediately for later behavior.
  - In other words: don’t let a mismatched permission story become the first source of confusion.

4) **Risks and guardrails**

- **Permission mismatch risk**
  - The biggest risk is assuming Accessibility permission is the whole story.
  - In practice, event tap creation may still fail unless the app has the right keyboard-monitoring permission.
  - Guardrail: treat tap-creation failure as a normal runtime state and explain clearly that the app needs keyboard monitoring access.

- **Callback performance risk**
  - Event tap callbacks are latency-sensitive.
  - Even something as simple as frequent printing can become noisy or, in worst cases, contribute to timeout behavior.
  - Guardrail: keep logging minimal and temporary; don’t do any heavy work there.

- **Character extraction is not always one-to-one**
  - Not every key-down produces a single printable character.
  - Dead keys, non-printing keys, layout-dependent behavior, and composed input can all produce surprising results.
  - Guardrail: treat the first pass as “best-effort character visibility,” not a full text-input model.

- **Global capture / privacy risk**
  - This tap will observe user keystrokes system-wide.
  - Guardrail: keep logging temporary, avoid persistent storage, and be aware that test logs may include sensitive input.

- **Secure input / special-app behavior**
  - Some apps or fields may prevent normal event observation.
  - Guardrail: if the tap seems to “miss” input in specific places, that does not automatically mean your architecture is wrong.

- **Thread / actor boundary risk**
  - Your `AppState` is main-actor-bound.
  - Even if the callback happens to run on the main run loop today, don’t build on that assumption yet.
  - Guardrail: keep the callback decoupled from UI state until you intentionally design that interaction.

5) **When to consider the advanced path**

Move beyond this simple setup when one of these becomes true:

- You need to **swallow** original keystrokes or emit replacement text.
- You need composition-aware behavior tied to the Zig engine.
- You need to reset state on mouse clicks, modifiers, app switches, or navigation keys.
- You need reliable behavior across more edge cases than “print what looks like a typed character.”
- The callback starts doing enough work that timeout/re-enable behavior becomes common or performance-sensitive.

6) **Optional advanced path**

When you reach that point, the next clean step is to split the tap into a dedicated input-monitor component owned by `AppDelegate`, then port over only the prototype behaviors you actually need: disabled-tap recovery, synthetic event tagging, reset conditions, and engine-driven consume/replace logic. 898:          "text": "I inspected both files and consulted Oracle with an explicit “no example code” constraint. Recommended first integration: add a minimal, passive CGEventTap owned by `AppDelegate`, started/stopped at the existing lifecycle placeholders in [`macos/Lex.swift`](file://<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L44-L58), and only print observed input characters for now.

## Proposed approach

- Keep the event tap in `AppDelegate`.
  - Current `AppDelegate` already owns global OS resources: signal handlers, engine state, and the Carbon hot key.
  - The event tap fits the same ownership model.

- Add only the minimal tap state needed:
  - Store the tap port so it stays alive and can be disabled/invalidated later.
  - If needed, store the run-loop source as well, depending on cleanup strategy.
  - Do not introduce a separate input manager yet; this checkpoint is small.

- Start the tap during launch, where the current file already has `// Start event tap.`.
  - Reference: prototype starts the tap from launch at [`playground/prototype-app/macos/Lex.swift`](file://<redacted>/lex/playground/prototype-app/macos/Lex.swift#L23-L40).
  - Current target already has the right hook at [`macos/Lex.swift`](file://<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L44-L51).

- Stop/cleanup the tap during termination, where the current file already has `// Stop event tap.`.
  - This should happen before or alongside other OS resource cleanup.
  - Current hook: [`macos/Lex.swift`](file://<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L53-L58).

- Use a passive/listen-only tap for this first step.
  - Because the first milestone is “passthrough callback with print,” the app should not be able to swallow or rewrite events yet.
  - This reduces risk versus copying the prototype’s default/modifying tap immediately.

- Keep the event mask narrow.
  - For this checkpoint, observe key-down events only.
  - Do not copy the prototype’s mouse, flags, disabled-tap, reset, synthetic-event, or engine-related logic yet.
  - The prototype’s broader mask at [`playground/prototype-app/macos/Lex.swift`](file://<redacted>/lex/playground/prototype-app/macos/Lex.swift#L76-L83) belongs to the later composition phase.

- Callback behavior:
  - Always return the original event.
  - Try to read the Unicode string from key-down events.
  - Print only diagnostic information: character if available, otherwise optionally key code / non-printable marker.
  - Do not touch `app_state`, `engine_state`, or SwiftUI state from the callback yet.

## Permission handling

Oracle’s strongest caution: do not overfit to the prototype’s Accessibility permission flow.

The prototype checks Accessibility permission at [`playground/prototype-app/macos/Lex.swift`](file://<redacted>/lex/playground/prototype-app/macos/Lex.swift#L52-L59), but for global keyboard observation the practical blocker is often Input Monitoring. For the first step, I would treat tap creation failure as expected and print a clear message that keyboard monitoring permission may be required.

I would not add a full permission UI or complex prompting flow yet.

## What not to copy from the prototype yet

Do not bring over these parts in the first pass:

- synthetic event tagging
- engine reset logic
- mouse-click reset behavior
- modifier filtering
- app-switch observation
- backspace handling
- diff/composition output
- event swallowing
- replacement text emission

Those are relevant only once the tap starts driving the Zig engine. The only prototype pieces worth reusing now are the lifecycle shape, event tap creation pattern, callback registration, run-loop source registration, and Unicode extraction concept.

## Oracle perspective

Oracle agreed with the general plan and recommended:

- keep event tap ownership inside `AppDelegate`
- use a passive tap for this checkpoint
- keep the mask minimal
- keep the callback lightweight
- make failure non-fatal so the menu bar app and hot key still work
- avoid assuming Accessibility permission is the complete permission story
- avoid touching main-actor UI state from the callback until that interaction is intentionally designed

My recommended implementation plan, if applied later, would be:

1. Add tap storage to `AppDelegate`.
2. Replace the launch/terminate comments with start/stop calls.
3. Add a minimal start function that creates a passive session tap for key-down events.
4. Add a tiny callback that extracts and prints characters, then passes events through.
5. Log clear failure if the tap cannot be created due to permissions.",

Let me preview your plan.",
958:          "text": "Agreed. Revised plan: use a modifiable event tap now, but keep the callback behavior passthrough until the engine integration step.

## Plan preview

1. **Add event-tap ownership to `AppDelegate`**
   - Add stored state for:
     - the `CFMachPort` event tap
     - the `CGEventSource` for future synthetic events
   - Keep this inside `AppDelegate`, next to current global OS resources like `engine_state`, signal sources, and hot key refs in [`macos/Lex.swift`](file://<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L35-L43).

2. **Create the synthetic event source at launch**
   - Match the prototype’s direction: create a private `CGEventSource` and assign a recognizable `userData` tag.
   - Even if the first callback only prints and passes through, this prepares the structure for later:
     - identifying Lex-generated events
     - avoiding re-processing synthetic events
     - posting replacement text/backspaces through the tap proxy

3. **Start a modifiable session event tap**
   - Use `.cgSessionEventTap`.
   - Use `.headInsertEventTap`.
   - Use a non-passive/default tap option so returning `nil` later can consume events.
   - This follows the prototype’s technical model at [`playground/prototype-app/macos/Lex.swift`](file://<redacted>/lex/playground/prototype-app/macos/Lex.swift#L76-L102).

4. **Use a deliberately small event mask for the first implementation**
   - Include:
     - `keyDown`
     - `tapDisabledByTimeout`
     - `tapDisabledByUserInput`
   - I would still avoid mouse, flags, navigation reset logic, and app-switch observation for this checkpoint.
   - Reason: because we are using a modifiable tap, disabled-tap recovery is worth including immediately; the rest belongs to engine behavior.

5. **Callback behavior for this checkpoint**
   - Always pass through normal key events for now.
   - For `keyDown`:
     - ignore Lex synthetic events using the event-source user-data tag
     - read the Unicode string if available
     - print the observed input character / characters
     - return the original event
   - For tap-disabled events:
     - re-enable the tap
     - return the original event
   - No engine calls yet.
   - No event swallowing yet.
   - No synthetic event posting yet, except the source is initialized and ready.

6. **Permission/failure behavior**
   - Attempt to start the tap during `applicationDidFinishLaunching`, replacing the current placeholder at [`macos/Lex.swift`](file://<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L44-L51).
   - If creation fails, print a clear message that Input Monitoring / Accessibility-related permission may be required.
   - Do not prevent the app from launching; menu bar and hot key should still work.

7. **Shutdown cleanup**
   - Stop/invalidate the event tap during `applicationWillTerminate`, replacing the current placeholder at [`macos/Lex.swift`](file://<redacted>/lex/macos/Lex.swift#L53-L58).
   - Clear the stored tap/source references.
   - Then continue existing hot-key and engine cleanup.

## Deliberate exclusions for this pass

I would not yet port:

- composition buffer
- `currentRendered`
- engine add/backspace calls
- diff emission
- navigation/mouse/app-switch reset rules
- mode-dependent consuming
- menu UI changes

Those should come after we verify the modifiable tap sees input and can safely pass everything through.

## Resulting shape

```diagram
╭─────────────╮
│ App launch  │
╰──────┬──────╯
       ▼
╭────────────────────────────╮
│ AppDelegate creates source │
│ and modifiable event tap   │
╰──────┬─────────────────────╯
       ▼
╭────────────────────────────╮
│ Callback receives keyDown  │
╰──────┬─────────────────────╯
       ▼
╭────────────────────────────╮
│ Print observed character   │
│ Return original event      │
╰────────────────────────────╯
```

This keeps the first code change small while aligning with the future consuming/synthetic-event architecture from the prototype.",
1018:          "text": "Below are snippets you can paste into `macos/Lex.swift`. They follow the revised plan: **modifiable event tap**, **passthrough callback**, **print observed characters**, and **prepare synthetic event source/tag for later consuming/replacement logic**.

### 1. Add import if needed

Near the top:

```swift
import CoreGraphics
```

Current file already imports `Carbon` and `SwiftUI`. If `CGEvent`, `CFMachPort`, or `CGEventSource` already resolve without this, you can omit it.

### 2. Add synthetic-event tag constant

Near the existing hot-key constant:

```swift
private let synthetic_event_source_user_data: Int64 = 0x4C4558
```

This matches the prototype’s idea of tagging Lex-generated events so the tap can ignore them later.

### 3. Add stored properties to `AppDelegate`

Inside `AppDelegate`, near the other private state:

```swift
private var event_tap: CFMachPort?
private var event_tap_run_loop_source: CFRunLoopSource?
private var synthetic_event_source: CGEventSource?
```

### 4. Wire launch / shutdown lifecycle

In `applicationDidFinishLaunching`, replace the placeholder comment:

```swift
initialize_synthetic_event_source()
start_event_tap()
```

So the launch body becomes conceptually:

```swift
func applicationDidFinishLaunching(_ notification: Notification) {
    print("Activated.")
    install_signal_handler(SIGINT)
    install_signal_handler(SIGTERM)
    initialize_engine_state()
    register_toggle_input_mode_hot_key()
    initialize_synthetic_event_source()
    start_event_tap()
}
```

In `applicationWillTerminate`, replace the stop placeholder:

```swift
stop_event_tap()
destroy_synthetic_event_source()
```

Conceptually:

```swift
func applicationWillTerminate(_ notification: Notification) {
    print("Shutting down...")
    stop_event_tap()
    destroy_synthetic_event_source()
    unregister_toggle_input_mode_hot_key()
    destroy_engine_state()
    signal_sources.removeAll()
}
```

### 5. Add synthetic source lifecycle helpers

Inside `AppDelegate`:

```swift
private func initialize_synthetic_event_source() {
    precondition(synthetic_event_source == nil)

    let source = CGEventSource(stateID: .privateState)
    source?.userData = synthetic_event_source_user_data
    synthetic_event_source = source
}

private func destroy_synthetic_event_source() {
    synthetic_event_source = nil
}
```

For this checkpoint, the source is not posting anything yet. It is just ready for the next phase.

### 6. Add event tap start / stop helpers

Inside `AppDelegate`:

```swift
private func start_event_tap() {
    precondition(event_tap == nil)
    precondition(event_tap_run_loop_source == nil)

    let event_mask =
        (1 << CGEventType.keyDown.rawValue) |
        (1 << CGEventType.tapDisabledByTimeout.rawValue) |
        (1 << CGEventType.tapDisabledByUserInput.rawValue)

    let self_pointer = Unmanaged.passUnretained(self).toOpaque()

    guard let tap = CGEvent.tapCreate(
        tap: .cgSessionEventTap,
        place: .headInsertEventTap,
        options: .defaultTap,
        eventsOfInterest: CGEventMask(event_mask),
        callback: lex_event_tap_callback,
        userInfo: self_pointer
    ) else {
        print("Failed to create event tap. Input Monitoring or Accessibility permission may be required.")
        return
    }

    let run_loop_source = CFMachPortCreateRunLoopSource(kCFAllocatorDefault, tap, 0)

    event_tap = tap
    event_tap_run_loop_source = run_loop_source

    CFRunLoopAddSource(CFRunLoopGetCurrent(), run_loop_source, .commonModes)
    CGEvent.tapEnable(tap: tap, enable: true)

    print("Event tap started.")
}

private func stop_event_tap() {
    guard let tap = event_tap else {
        return
    }

    CGEvent.tapEnable(tap: tap, enable: false)

    if let run_loop_source = event_tap_run_loop_source {
        CFRunLoopRemoveSource(CFRunLoopGetCurrent(), run_loop_source, .commonModes)
    }

    CFMachPortInvalidate(tap)

    event_tap_run_loop_source = nil
    event_tap = nil

    print("Event tap stopped.")
}
```

### 7. Add small helper for disabled-tap recovery

Inside `AppDelegate`:

```swift
func enable_event_tap() {
    guard let event_tap else {
        return
    }

    CGEvent.tapEnable(tap: event_tap, enable: true)
}
```

This lets the C callback re-enable the tap without exposing the stored property directly.

### 8. Add the callback function

Place this outside `AppDelegate`, for example after the class definition and before `enum InputMode`.

```swift
private func lex_event_tap_callback(
    proxy: CGEventTapProxy,
    type event_type: CGEventType,
    event: CGEvent,
    userInfo: UnsafeMutableRawPointer?
) -> Unmanaged<CGEvent>? {
    guard let userInfo else {
        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
    }

    let app_delegate = Unmanaged<AppDelegate>
        .fromOpaque(userInfo)
        .takeUnretainedValue()

    if event_type == .tapDisabledByTimeout || event_type == .tapDisabledByUserInput {
        app_delegate.enable_event_tap()
        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
    }

    guard event_type == .keyDown else {
        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
    }

    if event.getIntegerValueField(.eventSourceUserData) == synthetic_event_source_user_data {
        return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
    }

    var character_count = 0
    event.keyboardGetUnicodeString(
        maxStringLength: 0,
        actualStringLength: &character_count,
        unicodeString: nil
    )

    if character_count > 0 {
        var characters = [UniChar](repeating: 0, count: character_count)
        event.keyboardGetUnicodeString(
            maxStringLength: character_count,
            actualStringLength: &character_count,
            unicodeString: &characters
        )

        let string = String(
            utf16CodeUnits: characters,
            count: character_count
        )

        print("Input character: \(string)")
    } else {
        let key_code = event.getIntegerValueField(.keyboardEventKeycode)
        print("Input key code: \(key_code)")
    }

    return Unmanaged.passUnretained(event)
}
```

Notes:

- This is a **modifiable** tap because it uses `.defaultTap`, not listen-only.
- It still **passes every event through**.
- Later, consuming is done by returning `nil`.
- Later, synthetic text/backspace events can be posted using `synthetic_event_source`.
- The callback ignores Lex-generated synthetic events by checking `.eventSourceUserData`.",
1065:          "text": "`0x4C4558` is a hexadecimal integer used as a recognizable tag for Lex-generated synthetic events.

Hex bytes:

```text
0x4C 0x45 0x58
```

Interpreted as ASCII:

```text
0x4C = L
0x45 = E
0x58 = X
```

So:

```text
0x4C4558 == "LEX"
```

In the prototype, it is used here:

```swift
private let syntheticTag: Int64 = 0x4C4558
```

The purpose is not numeric meaning; it is a human-readable magic value. When Lex later creates synthetic keyboard events, it can set the event source’s `userData` to this tag. Then the event tap callback can detect those events and avoid processing its own generated keystrokes.

Conceptually:

```text
real user key event      -> no Lex tag -> process/observe
Lex synthetic key event  -> "LEX" tag  -> ignore/pass through
```

This prevents feedback loops once Lex starts consuming input and posting replacement events.",
1125:          "text": "Yes, but I would do the opposite: keep the hot key signature as `0x4C455821` and change the synthetic event tag to match it.

Current values:

```text
0x4C4558   = "LEX"
0x4C455821 = "LEX!"
```

`toggle_input_mode_hot_key_id` currently uses:

```swift
EventHotKeyID(signature: OSType(0x4C455821), id: 1)
```

That is a proper 4-byte Carbon-style signature: `"LEX!"`.

The synthetic event tag is just an `Int64`, so it can also use `0x4C455821` without issue:

```swift
private let synthetic_event_source_user_data: Int64 = 0x4C455821
```

I would not change `toggle_input_mode_hot_key_id` to `0x4C4558`, because `EventHotKeyID.signature` is an `OSType`, which conventionally represents 4-byte codes. `0x4C4558` is only 3 visible bytes and would effectively be:

```text
0x004C4558
```

That is less clear than `"LEX!"`.

Recommended naming:

```swift
// Namespace: LEX!
private let lex_event_signature: OSType = 0x4C455821
private let synthetic_event_source_user_data: Int64 = Int64(lex_event_signature)
private let toggle_input_mode_hot_key_id = EventHotKeyID(signature: lex_event_signature, id: 1)
```

Conceptually, this gives both systems the same Lex namespace while still keeping separate meanings:

```text
Carbon hot key signature     -> "LEX!" namespace + id: 1
CGEventSource userData tag   -> "LEX!" marker for synthetic events
```",
1172:          "text": "Yes. `callback: lex_event_tap_callback` is still a Swift callback function. It is only named with a `lex_` prefix in the snippet, which makes it look like a C ABI function. If you want to reserve `lex_` for Zig/C ABI symbols, rename the Swift callback.

Better Swift-side naming:

```swift
callback: event_tap_callback,
```

And the function:

    proxy: CGEventTapProxy,
    type event_type: CGEventType,
    event: CGEvent,
    userInfo: UnsafeMutableRawPointer?
) -> Unmanaged<CGEvent>? {
    ...
}
```

That keeps the boundary clear:

```text

    ↓ later
lex_* C ABI functions from Zig engine

  - `start_event_tap`

  - `initialize_synthetic_event_source`
- Zig/C ABI imported functions:

  - `lex_state_add`
  - `lex_state_backspace`
  - etc.

This avoids making a Swift function look like an imported engine symbol.",

## 1. Exact symptom reconstruction

Engine output is verifiable from [lex.zig](src/lex.zig#L1780-L1815) and its tests:

- `nguyee`, 2nd `e`: buffer `nguye`, `buffer_modification_index=4`, backspaces=1, replacement=`ê`. Bridge posts: `BS↓ BS↑ ê↓ ê↑`.
- `hoanx`, `x`: buffer `hoan`, tone on `a` (index 2), `buffer_modification_index=2`, backspaces=2, replacement=`ãn`. Bridge posts: `BS↓ BS↑ BS↓ BS↑ ãn↓ ãn↑`.

Now solve for the edit order that yields the observed strings:

| Case | Correct order | Observed final | Only order that produces it |
|---|---|---|---|
| `nguyee` | `nguye`→BS→`nguy`→ins→`nguyê` | `nguye` (ê flashes) | ins→`nguyeê`, BS→`nguye` |
| `hoanx` | `hoan`→BS→`hoa`→BS→`ho`→ins→`hoãn` | `hoaã` | BS→`hoa`, ins→`hoaãn`, BS→`hoaã` |

Both observations are explained by exactly one mechanism: **the last synthetic Backspace's deletion is applied after the replacement insertion**. I checked the alternatives you asked me to be critical about, and they produce *different* strings:

- Dropped BS event: `hoan`→BS→`hoa`→ins→`hoaãn` (not `hoaã`); `nguye`→ins→`nguyeê` persisting (not `nguye`).
- Stale/reset engine state: produces missing diacritics (`nguyee` literal, `hoanx` literal), never a reordered delete.
- Engine arithmetic: ruled out — the `bans` test (bmi=1, BS=2, `án`) is the exact analog of `hoanx`, and the `aa`→`â` test the analog of `nguyee`; both pass, and manual trace above matches.
- Autocorrect revert: could fake case 1 (`nguyê`→`nguye`), but cannot produce `hoaã` from `hoãn`.
- Page JS restoring a stale value snapshot: mimics case 1 (`nguye` was the pre-replacement value) but requires a contrived two-snapshot sequence for case 2.

So "delayed Backspace" is not a guess here — it is the unique single-cause reconstruction of both final strings, *assuming the reported strings are accurate*. The question is which layer delays it, since your own posting code ([Lex.swift 856–906](macos/Lex.swift#L856-L906)) posts strictly in order via `tapPostEvent`, and the tap cannot double-feed the engine (the synthetic-source check at line 762 precedes the `kVK_Delete` case at 784).

## 2. Ranked root causes

**#1 (most likely, ~60%): Safari's asynchronous NSTextInputContext key interpretation in the UI process reorders the dispatched edits under load.** I had the Librarian read current WebKit source rather than assume. Findings: `WebPageProxy`'s `keyEventQueue` is *not* a one-at-a-time dispatch gate; `interpretKeyEvent` is **asynchronous** when an input context is present; multiple keydowns can be in flight with the input method concurrently, with keyups held and callback sets re-associated to their keydown queues (`Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm` ~L5875–6007). The `deleteBackward:`/`insertText:` commands ride inside each `NativeWebKeyboardEvent`, and WebProcess executes them in IPC order — so ordering holds *if* the UI-process async IM completions dispatch in order. That async completion/association machinery is precisely where an intermittent inversion can occur, and your event stream stresses it unusually: **every** keystroke becomes a `vk=0` (KeyA) keydown/up pair, multi-char strings ride on keydowns, and every physical keyUp arrives unmatched (your mask omits keyUp, [Lex.swift 455–461](macos/Lex.swift#L455-L461)) — feeding Safari's keyup-holding logic keyups it never saw downs for. Native apps (`NSTextView`) interpret keys synchronously, which explains "Safari-only." This is consistent with WebKit source but the inversion itself is unproven — hence the instrumentation below.

**#2 (~20%): Safari autocomplete/autocorrect interference** (smart search field, or autocorrection in web forms). Prior art is strong: OpenKey ships a dedicated "fix autocomplete" workaround for Safari/Chrome/Firefox/Excel — it inserts an invisible character (U+202F) and adds one extra backspace before every replacement, exactly to defeat this (`OpenKey.mm:741–754, 339–356`). Fits case 1 loosely, case 2 poorly; matters mainly if your repro was the URL bar or a form with autofill.

**#3 (~15%): target-page controlled-input JS** (React-style value sync, search-box rewriting on keydown/keyup). Site-specific and intermittent by nature; aggravated by your events reporting `keyCode 65`/"KeyA" for every letter and stray keyups. Cannot be assessed from Linux; trivially distinguished by a JS-free probe page.

**#4 (~5%): event-source local-event suppression** (`.privateState` default suppression interval eating subsequent *hardware* events). Produces dropped keystrokes, not reordered deletes — does not match these two outputs. Worth zeroing anyway.

**#5 (<5% combined): tap timeout / stale engine state / engine arithmetic / window-server reorder.** Timeout resets the engine and would produce missing-diacritic output, not post-insert deletes. Engine ruled out above. Window-server delivery is FIFO and all six posted events traverse the same path; OpenKey posts the identical pattern (`vk=51` BS pairs, `vk=0` unicode pairs, same private source, no delays) with no reorder complaints at this layer. One unverifiable variant: a *third-party* event tap (Karabiner, clipboard managers) between you and Safari.

## 3. Proven vs. inferred (from Linux)

Proven from code/tests: engine emits BS=1/`ê` and BS=2/`ãn` for the two cases; bridge posts events strictly in order; every keystroke (not just retro-edits) is swallowed and re-synthesized as `vk=0`; keyUp is absent from the tap mask so physical keyups pass unmatched; synthetic events cannot double-feed the engine; WebKit's UI process interprets keys asynchronously with concurrent in-flight keydowns (source reading, version unverified against your Safari).

Inferred only: that the observed final strings are exact (whole diagnosis rests on this); that window-server delivery preserved posting order; that no third-party tap sits in the chain; which Safari surface (URL bar vs. web page vs. plain input) the repro occurred in; anything about page JS.

## 4. Smallest macOS instrumentation to distinguish the top causes

1. **JS probe page (decisive, ~15 min).** Local static HTML, one plain `<input>`, zero framework JS, logging `beforeinput`/`input` (`inputType`, `data`, `target.value`) plus `keydown`/`keyup` (`key`, `keyCode`, `timeStamp`). Type `hoanx` repeatedly.
   - `deleteContentBackward` logged *after* `insertText` → cause #1 proven (WebKit/AppKit applied edits out of order).
   - Correct `beforeinput` order but corruption only on real sites → cause #3.
   - Corruption only in the URL bar / autofill fields, never in the probe input → cause #2.
2. **Listen-only annotated tap (~30 min).** Second `CGEventTap` with `.listenOnly` at `.annotatedSessionEventTap`, logging type/vk/characters/source-userdata/timestamp. Confirms the order Safari-bound events actually left the window server; a mismatch here implicates the window server or a third-party tap instead of Safari.
3. **Two one-line toggles as differential experiments (S each):** (a) when `backspace_count == 0` and the replacement equals the literal input, pass the original event through instead of synthesizing — if incidents vanish, the per-keystroke synthesis surface is the trigger; (b) `synthetic_event_source.localEventsSuppressionInterval = 0` — rules #4 out; (c) a 1–3 ms spacing between the last BS pair and the insert pair — if that eliminates it, the async-race diagnosis (#1) is confirmed.

## Follow-up direction (not part of diagnosis, for planning)

If #1 confirms, prior art offers non-timing fixes: OpenKey's Shift+Left-Arrow selection replacement (select N characters, then insert — the insert atomically replaces the selection, eliminating the BS-vs-insert ordering hazard entirely; it uses this for Spotlight and Chromium), per-app step-by-step sending, and the invisible-character autocomplete fix. Independently, passing plain keystrokes through untouched and adding keyUp to the mask (swallowing the matching keyUp of swallowed keyDowns) shrinks the synthetic-event surface by roughly an order of magnitude and restores sane `keyCode`s to page JS. Confirm before implementing.

content.text:
# Finding: the macOS event bridge is the likely cause

The Zig Telex engine appears correct. The likely failure is that Lex represents one logical text replacement as several independent synthetic keyboard events, which Safari and website JavaScript do not necessarily treat as an atomic text edit.

```diagram
┌──────────────────┐
│ Physical keyDown │
└────────┬─────────┘
         ▼
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│ Lex swallows physical event  │
│ and advances Zig state       │
└────────┬─────────────────────┘
         ▼
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│ Backspace down/up × N        │
│ Unicode keyDown/keyUp        │
└────────┬─────────────────────┘
         ▼
┌───────────┐   ┌────────────┐   ┌───────────────┐
│ AppKit IM │──▶│ Safari UI  │──▶│ WebContent/JS │
└───────────┘   └────────────┘   └───────────────┘

Physical keyUp bypasses Lex and reaches Safari separately.
```

The synthetic batch is emitted in [`Lex.swift`](macos/Lex.swift#L849-L907). Apple documents where `tapPostEvent` inserts an event, but does not guarantee that several calls become one atomic text transaction.

## The reported results reconstruct the failure precisely

### `nguyee`

Before the last `e`, the field contains `nguye`.

The engine correctly requests:

```text
Backspace
insert "ê"
```

Intended result:

```text
nguye → nguy → nguyê
```

The reported result behaves as though the target applied:

```text
insert "ê"
Backspace
```

That gives:

```text
nguye → nguyeê → nguye
```

This matches the observation that `ê` appears briefly and then disappears.

The relevant Zig rule correctly turns the second `e` into `ê` at [`lex.zig`](src/lex.zig#L763-L776).

### `hoanx`

Before `x`, the field contains `hoan`. The engine correctly moves the ngã tone to `a`, requiring:

```text
Backspace × 2
insert "ãn"
```

Intended:

```text
hoan → hoa → ho → hoãn
```

The observed `hoaã` is produced if the effective target-side order is:

```text
hoan
→ hoa       first Backspace
→ hoaãn     insert "ãn"
→ hoaã      delayed deletion of trailing "n"
```

This is particularly strong evidence: merely dropping one Backspace would leave `hoaãn`, not `hoaã`.

The engine’s suffix replacement calculation is at [`lex.zig`](src/lex.zig#L1778-L1815), with equivalent two-Backspace/two-character cases covered at [`lex.zig`](src/lex.zig#L3853-L3907) and [`lex.zig`](src/lex.zig#L3971-L4001).

## Two concrete event-stream defects amplify it

### 1. Lex swallows `keyDown` but passes the physical `keyUp`

The event mask includes `keyDown`, but not `keyUp`, at [`Lex.swift`](macos/Lex.swift#L454-L468).

Consequently, Safari can receive an impossible sequence such as:

```text
synthetic KeyA down, characters="ê"
synthetic KeyA up, characters="ê"
physical KeyE up               ← no physical KeyE down
```

For `hoanx`, the final unmatched event is `KeyX up`.

A normal text field may ignore this. A website listening to `keydown`, `keyup`, `beforeinput`, and `input`, or maintaining a controlled input value, may not.

### 2. `virtualKey: 0` is not a neutral Unicode key

Synthetic insertion uses `virtualKey: 0` at [`Lex.swift`](macos/Lex.swift#L882-L905). On macOS, key code zero is the physical ANSI **A** key.

For the `ãn` replacement, Safari/page JavaScript can therefore see approximately:

```text
code: "KeyA"
keyCode: 65
key: "ãn"
text: "ãn"
```

That is one key event containing two characters and claiming to be the physical A key. It is legal for Core Graphics to carry the Unicode string, but it violates assumptions commonly made by web editors and keyboard handlers.

Safari also passes key events through asynchronous `NSTextInputContext` interpretation and then to the WebContent process. WebKit has had a long-standing [macOS key/composition ordering defect](https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=165004), fixed only recently in upstream WebKit. That bug is related evidence, not proof that the exact Backspaces here are reordered by WebKit itself.

## Confidence assessment

**High confidence:**

- The Zig engine’s edit arithmetic is correct.
- `nguyee` produces one Backspace plus `ê`.
- `hoanx` produces two Backspaces plus `ãn`.
- The Swift bridge exposes each replacement as separate observable commands.
- Physical keyups reach Safari without their physical keydowns.
- Unicode insertion events use the identity of the A key.
- Once Safari applies one batch incorrectly, Lex’s state diverges because it never verifies what the target committed.

**Strong inference:**

- Safari’s AppKit/WebKit input handling or the website’s controlled-input logic applies a deletion or stale-value rollback after the insertion.
- The malformed key lifecycle and multi-character KeyA event make that race substantially more likely.

**Not determinable from Linux:**

- Whether the late operation originates in AppKit, Safari’s UI process, WebContent, website JavaScript, autocomplete, or another downstream event tap.
- Whether the low-level CGEvents themselves arrive out of order. Current WebKit code generally attempts to preserve keyboard-event order, so raw WebKit IPC reordering should not be asserted without a macOS trace.

## Minimal macOS confirmation

1. Use a plain local page with one `<input>` and log `keydown`, `beforeinput`, `input`, and `keyup`, including the value after every event.
2. Compare it with the affected JavaScript-heavy website.
3. Add a second listen-only tap downstream and log event type, key code, Unicode string, timestamp, and Lex’s source tag.

Interpretation:

- Downstream CGEvents ordered correctly, but DOM deletion occurs after insertion: Safari/AppKit/WebKit.
- DOM events ordered correctly, then value reverts: website JavaScript/autocomplete.
- Downstream tap already sees the wrong order: WindowServer, another event tap, or event posting.
- Plain input always works but the real website fails: controlled-input JavaScript reacting to the impossible event sequence.

`zig build test` passes, and the working tree remains unchanged. A robust long-term solution is to perform an actual text replacement through the macOS text-input/InputMethodKit protocol rather than emulating it with Backspaces and synthetic keystrokes.

My comments:

- The bug happen in all input, including normal <input>.
- The bug doesn't happen on URL input of the browser, only on the input of the website.
- If I close the Safari window and open a new window, the bug may disappear.

run.result:
## Conclusion

**On current trunk, unmatched physical `keyUp`s are a credible direct cause of an accumulating, per-`WKWebView` ordering defect.** The holding logic does **not** match by hardware key identity, event number, virtual key code, or down/up pairing. It merely counts queued keyups against outstanding keydown completions.

For the malformed stream

```text
synthetic KeyA down
synthetic KeyA up
physical-letter up
```

WebKit can hold both ups while one down is in flight, but that down completion releases only one. The second remains at the front of the per-view holding tank. A later keydown completion releases that stale up, and the newly generated ups remain behind it. The backlog therefore grows by approximately one keyup per physical letter.

Backspace down/up pairs are balanced and normally do not create the net surplus. They increase concurrency and make the ordering problem easier to expose, but **the extra original physical keyup is the distinctive accumulating input**.

This mechanism exists only in the “correct input-method event order” path introduced in 2025 and substantially changed in May 2026. It does not explain Safari’s URL field, because that field is native Safari UI rather than the affected `WKWebView`’s `WebViewImpl`.

## Current-trunk operations

The relevant state is owned directly by each `WebViewImpl`:

- [`m_collectedKeypressCommands`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.h#L1153-L1160) is a deque with one command vector for each in-flight keydown.
- [`m_interpretKeyEventHoldingTank`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.h#L1158-L1160) is a deque of callbacks, each capturing an `NSEvent`, currently used principally for held keyups.

The public event entry points perform no down/up validation:

- [`keyUp`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L6708-L6719) sends every received up through `interpretKeyEvent`, then constructs and forwards a `NativeWebKeyboardEvent`.
- [`keyDown`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L6722-L6742) does the same for every down, except for WebKit’s own re-sent event case.
- Neither path records a pressed-key set or compares key codes.

In current `interpretKeyEvent`:

1. Each keydown appends one empty command queue at the back: [`WebViewImpl.mm` lines 5875–5893](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5875-L5893).
2. Any non-keydown arriving while **any** command queue exists is appended to the holding tank: [`lines 5891–5913`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5891-L5913).
3. The held callback captures the exact event, but there is no identity comparison. When invoked, it calls the input method directly and dispatches that event’s keyboard IPC with no commands: [`lines 5894–5910`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5894-L5910).
4. A keydown completion removes exactly the **front command queue** with `takeFirst()`: [`lines 5917–5932`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5917-L5932).
5. Whether the key was handled or not, that completion releases at most **one** held event using `m_interpretKeyEventHoldingTank.takeFirst()()`:
   - handled path: [`lines 5982–5989`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5982-L5989)
   - unhandled/layout path: [`lines 5992–6006`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5992-L6006)

The implementation comment explicitly describes this as “each keydown completion releases one keyup,” not “the matching keyup” ([`lines 5885–5890`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5885-L5890)).

## Applying the malformed stream

Assume the synthetic down’s IM callback has not completed when its ups arrive.

### First physical letter

```text
D1 = synthetic KeyA down
U1 = synthetic KeyA up
P1 = original physical-key up
```

Operations:

```text
D1: command queues = [Q1]
U1: holding tank   = [U1]
P1: holding tank   = [U1, P1]

completion(D1):
    takeFirst(command queues) -> Q1
    takeFirst(holding tank)() -> U1

remaining:
    command queues = []
    holding tank   = [P1]
```

`P1` is not discarded merely because no down matches it. It remains captured in a callback.

### Second physical letter

If the stale `P1` already exists before the next down:

```text
D2: command queues = [Q2]
U2: holding tank   = [P1, U2]
P2: holding tank   = [P1, U2, P2]

completion(D2):
    releases P1
```

Remaining tank:

```text
[U2, P2]
```

Thus a later keydown completion can release a keyup from a previous physical key. After `k` malformed letters, the queue can have roughly `k` surplus ups, subject to timing.

This is strict FIFO counting—not hardware matching. The synthetic virtual key value `0` (`KeyA`) and multi-character Unicode payload do not provide protection against this. The queue does not inspect them.

### Retroactive Backspaces

Each Backspace pair contributes:

```text
Backspace down -> +1 outstanding command queue
Backspace up   -> +1 held up
completion     -> -1 queue and -1 held up
```

So, absent timing failure, each Backspace pair has net zero backlog. With `N` Backspaces followed by the synthetic Unicode pair and then the unmatched physical up, the whole edit has:

```text
downs: N + 1
ups:   N + 2
net:   +1 unmatched up
```

Therefore generic “non-atomic backspacing” is not the primary accounting error. It can increase the number of simultaneous queues and alter which event is released, but the surplus physical keyup supplies the persistent positive imbalance.

## Persistence and reset behavior

There is no normal empty-queue drain:

- A keyup is held whenever command queues are nonempty.
- Only a **keydown completion** removes one holding-tank entry.
- If the command deque becomes empty while stale holding callbacks remain, those callbacks are not automatically flushed.
- A later keydown completion can consume one of those stale entries.
- New unmatched ups continue accumulating faster than completions remove them.

The state is **per `WebViewImpl`**, not per DOM `<input>`. Consequently:

- moving focus among ordinary HTML inputs in the same `WKWebView` retains it;
- the Safari URL field is unaffected because it is outside that content `WKWebView`;
- destroying the `WKWebView` destroys these member deques and their retained events;
- opening another window/WebView begins with fresh empty members.

The queued callbacks use a weak pointer before re-entering the implementation, so destruction prevents use-after-free and completes the callback as unhandled ([`lines 5894–5905`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5894-L5905)). That lifetime design makes “closing the window clears it” consistent with this state.

I found no explicit clearing of either keyboard deque on focus changes, navigation, window resign-key, or ordinary process-swap handling. Destruction is the definitive reset supplied by member lifetime. A process swap by itself should therefore not be assumed to clear the UI-process `WebViewImpl` queues.

## Important qualification

This proves that trunk can retain and mis-release unmatched keyups. It does **not by source inspection alone prove** exactly how a particular macOS input method reacts after receiving the resulting stale/mismatched ups. A persistent “all HTML inputs fail” symptom could be:

1. continued WebKit queue skew;
2. input-method state corrupted by the skewed event sequence;
3. both.

The per-WebView scope, absence in the URL field, growth under surplus keyups, and reset after WebView/window destruction all fit the first mechanism closely.

## Version timeline

### Before July 2025

This holding-tank mechanism did not exist. The malformed stream could still upset AppKit or an input method, but not through these WebKit members.

### July 11, 2025: initial implementation

[297270@main, bug 295763](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/commit/1322eea39d8f8bcaa4d562c9edca2f5016c7b6bc) introduced:

- an optional single command vector;
- a holding tank;
- serialization of **all subsequent** `interpretKeyEvent` calls while one IM event was in flight.

It was initially off by default and enabled as a Google Docs quirk. The commit’s stated purpose was to make `keydown` precede composition/input events.

In that version a completion moved the **entire** holding tank out and ran every deferred event. Extra ups could be deferred, but it did not have trunk’s explicit “one keydown completion releases one keyup” counter behavior.

### April 8, 2026: enabled globally

[310826@main, bug 311717](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/commit/6031db379af6aec30c03b076077c57e1c4b3c93d) made `InputMethodUsesCorrectKeyEventOrder` stable and enabled it by default. It also changed stored callbacks from `CompletionHandler` to `Function`, specifically because the input method may never complete while a view is being destroyed.

This is the key boundary for affected Safari builds: before this change, ordinary sites generally did not use the special ordering path; after it, they did.

Current trunk has since returned the preference to unstable/default-false in source ([`UnifiedWebPreferences.yaml` lines 4285–4298](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WTF/Scripts/Preferences/UnifiedWebPreferences.yaml#L4285-L4298)), while `inputMethodUsesCorrectKeyEventOrder()` also consults editor state and excludes specific modeless IMEs in some circumstances ([`WebViewImpl.mm` lines 3793–3807](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L3793-L3807)). Shipping Safari configuration may differ from the open-source default.

### May 13–15, 2026: regressions and the current queue model

Related fixes demonstrate that this area caused persistent input-mode and event-order failures:

- [313212@main, bug 314752](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/commit/300105f8996dbbd074b3ca9b2d3a3aaaa9d00c40): composition confirmation produced a beep and triggered Google search because handled-state and key code ordering were wrong.
- [313286@main, bug 314823](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/commit/4951276cc765d82514a1a3d7d6ef10e363ea7d18): Vietnamese and Korean modeless IMEs abandoned modeless mode “for the rest of the session” after seeing stale cursor/content while commands were queued.
- [313336@main, bug 314888](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/commit/2b952923a66cd56a0acd48875418f742e995b4fc): replaced the single optional command vector with a deque, stopped holding keydowns, continued holding keyups, and introduced the exact **one held keyup per keydown completion** behavior now relevant here. Its commit message says delayed events could drain as a burst and produce visible garbage.
- [313779@main, bug 315381](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/commit/92da80f85aff418abc9af18eaaac43613e5dc502): repaired partial multi-character Indic commits and stale staged text/range observations, confirming that multi-character event strings and deferred command execution require special handling.

### Distinction from Safari versions before May 2026

For Safari builds predating the May 15 `313336@main` change:

- there was no deque of concurrent keydown command queues;
- all event types were serialized behind one in-flight event;
- completion drained the moved holding tank in bulk;
- the precise permanent surplus-up accounting described above did **not** yet exist.

For Safari versions containing `313336@main` or equivalent:

- keydowns are admitted concurrently;
- keyups are held;
- one completion releases one FIFO keyup without identity matching;
- surplus ups can accumulate and be consumed by later, unrelated keydowns.

That makes the unmatched physical keyups a substantially stronger primary-cause candidate specifically for **post-May-15-2026 code** than for earlier Safari versions.

result.title: WebKit Features for Safari 26.4 | WebKit
excerpts: # [WebKit Features for Safari 26.4](https://webkit.org/blog/17862/webkit-features-for-safari-26-4/ "Permanent Link: WebKit Features for Safari 26.4") Beyond the headliners, the heart of this release is focused on what web developers ask for most. We hear you loud and clear. Results from 2025 developer surveys made it clear you want time to catch up with new features, not be swamped with more. You want existing features to work consistently across every browser. You asked for browser engineers working on WebKit to help you by squashing bugs and closing gaps in spec coverage. That’s what this release aims to do. Most of the features listed in the [Safari 26.4 release notes](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/safari-release-notes/safari-26_4-release-notes) are not entirely new. Many update features where the behavior didn’t quite match the latest web standard. Others make specific combinations of existing features work better together. Here’s one example — we shipped support for the CSS `min()` and `max()` functions in 2018, almost two years before any other browser. And we shipped the HTML `sizes` attribute for responsive images even longer ago, back in 2014. But until now, you couldn’t use `min()` , `max()` , or `clamp()` inside of the `sizes` attribute in WebKit. In Safari 26.4, you can. ... As we continue this work, we greatly value your input. If something has been bothering you, it’s worth testing in Safari 26.4 to see if it’s been fixed. If the bug is still there, please file it at [bugs.webkit.org](https://bugs.webkit.org/) . Or if it’s already filed, add additional comments to the existing issue describing your experience and why fixing it matters for you. When multiple websites signal that something needs fixing, that helps. The more concrete you can be — a brief story about why this hurts your users, a link to a real website affected, a snippet of code or reduced test case — the better equipped we are to prioritize and fix what matters most. We are paying attention, even if our response shows up as a shipped fix rather than a reply in the issue. We care deeply about the experience people have when using Safari. And we care about the experience people have when using any of the millions of iOS, iPadOS, macOS, visionOS, and watchOS apps that are built using WebKit and JavaScriptCore. When our customers open a news app, a shopping app, a travel app, a banking app — there’s a good chance the interface they’re interacting with is powered by the same HTML, CSS, and JavaScript you write every day when making web apps and websites that live at a URL. Every rendering fix, every improved feature, every performance gain we ship benefits everything touched by the web platform. ... ## Web API ### Keyboard Lock API Safari 26.4 adds support for the Fullscreen Keyboard Lock API, which allows web applications to capture keyboard input that would normally be handled by the browser. If you’ve ever built a game, a remote desktop client, or a creative tool, you’ve probably encountered this frustration: certain keyboard shortcuts are off-limits. Press the Escape key and you are thrown out of fullscreen mode. There’s been no way to prevent this — until now. The Keyboard Lock API lets you request access to specific keys when your application needs it. A game can now use the Escape key for its own menu system. To exit fullscreen mode then the user would need to hold down the escape key for 1.5 seconds. A remote desktop client can pass through all keyboard shortcuts to the remote machine. ``` element . requestFullscreen ({ keyboardLock : "browser" }); ``` ... ### Auxiliary Mouse Button Support Safari 26.4 adds support for auxiliary mouse button values in `MouseEvent.button` , so you can now detect additional mouse buttons beyond the standard left, middle, and right clicks. If you’re building applications that take advantage of gaming mice or other input devices with extra buttons, you can now respond to those inputs. ``` element . addEventListener ( 'mousedown' , ( e ) = > { if ( e . button = = = 3 ) { /* back button */ } if ( e . button = = = 4 ) { /* forward button */ } }); ``` The `button` property will correctly report values for buttons 3, 4, and beyond, matching the behavior in other browsers. ... ### Resolved issues * Fixed an issue where `IntersectionObserver` computed the root rectangle incorrectly when overflow clipping was present. (117143395) * Fixed Trusted Types to correctly send CSP violation reports when a default policy returns an invalid `javascript:` URL or throws an exception. (160960418) * Fixed `Element.requestFullscreen` on iOS to correctly reflect hardware keyboard attachment state during fullscreen sessions and exit automatically when the keyboard is detached. (161429040) * Fixed event ordering and committed promise timing for intercepted `Navigation API` traverse navigations. (161445256) * Fixed the processing order of Trusted Types for DOM attribute setting. (162143148) * Fixed `NavigateEvent` to correctly fire an `AbortSignal` when a navigation is aborted. (163957784) * Fixed `NavigateEvent.sourceElement` to correctly reference elements from different browsing contexts. (163962362) ... ## HTML ### Resolved issues * Fixed an issue where nested `about:blank` frames were incorrectly treated as self-referencing, preventing them from loading. (148373033) * Fixed `HTMLImageElement.currentSrc` to return an empty string for `` instead of resolving to the document base URL. (167229274) * Fixed image uploading to not transcode images when `accept="image/*"` is specified. (166124206) * Fixed an issue where input fields did not display user input while typing. (163613957) * Fixed an issue where `input[type="search"]` fields with `appearance: none` incorrectly reserved space for the datalist dropdown button. (166754216) * Fixed an incorrect fallback for the menu style for empty lists, improving readability and correctness. (167662316) ... ## Web Inspector ### Resolved issues * Fixed incorrect breakpoint and search result positions in the Web Inspector after pretty-printing inline scripts containing multi-line template literals. (29417859) * Fixed the Styles sidebar filter in Web Inspector to be case-insensitive. (36086981) * Fixed an issue where a large number of search results in the Search tab would freeze Web Inspector. (49234522) * Fixed an issue where the Console tab search bar in Web Inspector would disappear when the window was too narrow. (50922509) * Fixed an issue where CSS properties added to new rules were not applied and were marked as invalid. (103548968) * Fixed context menu items to rename `Copy HTTP Request` and `Copy HTTP Response` to `Copy HTTP Request Headers` and `Copy HTTP Response Headers` for clarity. (117708766) * Fixed incorrect grid track sizing display in the Web Inspector when using CSS custom properties. (141709306) * Fixed an issue in the Console where the count of identical consecutive messages could be wrong. (162612099) * Fixed an issue where breakpoints and search results in Web Inspector could point to the wrong location after a previously formatted source file was reopened in an unformatted state. (165059693) * Fixed an issue where the Sources navigation sidebar could be empty when reloading the page. (166141968) * Fixed timestamp formatting in the Web Inspector to remove unnecessary trailing `.0` values for readability. (166500013) * Fixed item order labels in the Web Inspector grid and flex overlays to remove the `#` symbol, changing from `Item #N` to `Item N` . (166767949) * Fixed an issue where the text filter in the Sources tab did not apply to the Local Overrides and Console Snippets sections. (169804196) ... ## WebRTC Safari 26.4 adds two significant WebRTC enhancements for audio and networking. On macOS, `getUserMedia` now supports capturing audio from multiple microphones simultaneously while intelligently managing echo cancellation. The system dynamically migrates existing audio captures to appropriate processing units, making it easier to build applications like podcasting tools, multi-participant recording, or music collaboration apps that need multiple audio inputs. On iOS, Safari 26.4 adds network slicing support for WebRTC. Network slicing allows different types of traffic to be prioritized differently on cellular networks, which can improve quality and reliability for real-time communication applications in challenging network conditions. ... ## Additional resolved issues ### Editing * Fixed incorrect text selection when dragging across pseudo elements. (142905243) * Fixed an issue on iOS 26 where the edit menu would not appear when tapping inside an already-focused text field that had a looping `content` animation. (164290305) * Fixed an issue where focusing a hidden editable element would incorrectly display the text cursor and selection at full opacity. (165489471) * Fixed a regression where dragging to select text would stop scrolling when the cursor left the window. (169983104) ### Events * Fixed an issue where `mouseleave` and `mouseout` events were not dispatched when a window moved out from under a stationary cursor. (161493924) ... ### Rendering * Fixed over-aggressive clipping of child layers in multicolumn layouts to prevent visual overflow issues with `position: relative` elements and `transform:scale()` text. (126413036) * Fixed unreadable Scroll-to-Text-Fragment highlights on dark pages. (126539910) * Fixed an issue where auto-positioned absolutely positioned descendants were not always marked for layout when their parent’s border box moved. (131806062) * Fixed an issue where positioned, transformed, or opacity-altered `` elements with HDR JPEG gainmaps would incorrectly render in SDR. (156858374) * Fixed an issue on iPadOS where closing the sidebar or resizing the window could cause the page to remain zoomed in by recalculating the target scale to automatically match the new minimum scale. (157676989) * Fixed an issue where fixed positioned elements were not rendered correctly in right-to-left pages using the `vertical-rl` writing mode. (161712734) ... ### Web Extensions * Fixed an issue where `window.open()` calls from web extensions would incorrectly open “about:blank” instead of the intended URL by ensuring each extension URL loads in a fresh tab configuration. (143901129) ... ## Feedback We love hearing from you. To share your thoughts, find us online: Jen Simmons on [Bluesky](https://bsky.app/profile/jensimmons.bsky.social) / [Mastodon](https://front-end.social/@jensimmons) , Saron Yitbarek on [BlueSky](https://bsky.app/profile/saron.bsky.social) / [Mastodon](https://front-end.social/@saron) , and Jon Davis on [Bluesky](https://bsky.app/profile/jondavis.bsky.social) / [Mastodon](https://mastodon.social/@jondavis) . You can follow WebKit [on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/apple-webkit/) . If you run into any issues, we welcome your [bug report](https://bugs.webkit.org/) . Filing issues really does make a difference. You can also find this information in the [Safari release notes](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/safari-release-notes/) . [Next Release Notes for Safari Technology Preview 240 Learn more](https://webkit.org/blog/17896/release-notes-for-safari-technology-preview-240/)

# Text fields in Safari browser not working
Text fields in my internet browser (I'm using Safari 11.0.1) have not been working about 50% of the time. I will go to type something in a text field on a website, and nothing will happen; It's as if the keyboard (I'm not using an external keyboard, I am using my MacBook Pro keyboard) has magically stopped working, until I go to use it in literally any other program, and it actually works fine. The only way I have found to get it working, is to repeatedly refresh, click the URL bar, type something in the URL bar, then reselect the text field on the website, until the text field starts working again.
Occasionally instead of a text field on a website not working, it will be the URL bar that doesn't work. In this case, I need to do the same thing to get it working, but instead of clicking the URL bar and typing something then reselecting the text field on the website, I have to repeatedly refresh, click any text field on the website, type something in the text field, then reselect the URL bar, until the URL bar starts working again.
