## Ownership and lifetime

| State | Actual owner / scope | Reset behavior |
|---|---|---|
| `NSTextInputContext` used by HTML editing | AppKit supplies it for the particular `WKWebView` text-input client. `WKWebView` implements `NSTextInputClient`; `WebViewImpl::inputContext()` returns `[WKWebView _web_superInputContext]`, ultimately `[super inputContext]`. It is not a WebKit process-global object. | Replacing/destroying the `WKWebView`, or AppKit tearing down that responder/input-context association, gives a fresh context. A navigation alone ordinarily retains the same view/context. |
| IM interpretation/command state | Per `WebViewImpl`, hence per `WKWebView`: `m_keyDownEventBeingResent`, `m_stagedMarkedRange`, `m_collectedKeypressCommands`, and `m_interpretKeyEventHoldingTank`. | Destroying the `WebViewImpl` destroys these deques and retained events. A normal page navigation does not. Web-process replacement also does not recreate the `WebViewImpl`. |
| WebKit IPC keyboard queue | Per `WebPageProxy`: `WebPageProxy::Internals::keyEventQueue`. One `WebViewImpl` owns one `WebPageProxy`. | Cleared on Web-process exit/reset; destroyed when the `WebPageProxy` closes. A normal navigation need not recreate it. |
| First-responder routing | `NSWindow` owns the current first-responder chain and decides whether the web view or Safari chrome receives an event. | Closing the window destroys that responder topology. Merely changing focus changes the route, not the WebView/WebPageProxy state. |
| Input-source/InputMethodKit service state, `NSApp`, static caches | Process-wide or external IM-service state. WebKit does have isolated statics such as the immutable marked-text attribute array, but its mutable keyboard queues are not process-global. | A new Safari window would normally share this state, so “new window fixes it” argues against a purely process-global fault. |

### `NSTextInputContext`

`WKWebView` declares conformance to `NSTextInputClient` in [`WKWebViewMac.mm` lines 110–120](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/API/mac/WKWebViewMac.mm#L110-L120). Its editing callbacks, including `insertText:replacementRange:`, forward into that view’s `WebViewImpl` ([lines 1574–1582](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/API/mac/WKWebViewMac.mm#L1574-L1582)).

`WebViewImpl::inputContext()` does not maintain a WebKit singleton:

```objective-c
if (!m_page->editorState().isContentEditable)
    return nil;
return [protect(m_view) _web_superInputContext];
```

See [`WebViewImpl.mm` lines 6301–6308](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L6301-L6308). `_web_superInputContext` calls AppKit’s `[super inputContext]`. Thus the relevant context is associated with the individual `WKWebView`/text-input client and its responder environment, not with `WebPageProxy` or the Safari process as a whole.

The context is used twice for each editable key:

1. Input-method interpretation through `handleEventByInputMethod:completionHandler:` ([`WebViewImpl.mm` lines 5917–5932](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5917-L5932)).
2. If needed, keyboard-layout interpretation through `handleEventByKeyboardLayout:` or `interpretKeyEvents:` ([lines 5840–5855](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5840-L5855)).

This distinction matters for malformed Telex streams: the synthetic Unicode down/up and the unmatched physical up can perturb an AppKit input context or leave WebKit’s per-view interpretation bookkeeping inconsistent even though the CGEvent stream itself has finished.

## Per-`WebViewImpl` interpretation state

The mutable macOS interpretation state is explicitly stored on the `WebViewImpl` instance:

- `m_keyDownEventBeingResent`
- `m_stagedMarkedRange`
- `m_collectedKeypressCommands`
- `m_interpretKeyEventHoldingTank`

See [`WebViewImpl.h` lines 1153–1167](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.h#L1153-L1167).

For the modern asynchronous IM path:

- Every keyDown appends its own command vector.
- A keyUp arriving while keyDown interpretation is pending is retained in `m_interpretKeyEventHoldingTank`.
- Each keyDown completion releases one held keyUp.

That ordering protocol is documented and implemented in [`WebViewImpl::interpretKeyEvent`, lines 5867–5913](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5867-L5913). IM callbacks such as `setMarkedText:` and `insertText:` append commands to the front command vector ([`setMarkedText`, lines 6509–6517](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L6509-L6517); [`insertText`, lines 6063–6079](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L6063-L6079)).

Consequently, swallowing physical down, injecting unrelated Unicode down/up, and later admitting the physical up violates the pairing assumptions at precisely this layer. Possible manifestations include:

- a keyUp held behind the wrong interpreted keyDown;
- commands attributed to the wrong in-flight command vector;
- stale marked/composition staging;
- an event being classified as IM-handled when it did not correspond to the physical key that eventually released.

This state is shared by all editable elements rendered by that `WKWebView`; it is **not per DOM input element**.

## Per-`WebPageProxy` keyboard queue

`WebViewImpl` creates and retains exactly one `WebPageProxy`:

- constructor: `m_page(processPool.createWebPage(...))` in [`WebViewImpl.mm` lines 1331–1337](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L1331-L1337);
- members: `m_view`, `m_pageClient`, `m_page` in [`WebViewImpl.h` lines 1029–1034](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.h#L1029-L1034).

The IPC queue is a member of `WebPageProxy::Internals`, not a global:

```cpp
Deque<NativeWebKeyboardEvent> keyEventQueue;
```

See [`WebPageProxyInternals.h`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/WebPageProxyInternals.h).

`WebPageProxy::handleKeyboardEvent` appends every event to that queue and sends only the first event. The asynchronous reply calls `keyEventHandlingCompleted`, which removes the front event, sends the next, and reports completion through `PageClient::doneWithKeyEvent`. On macOS that ultimately reaches `WebViewImpl::doneWithKeyEvent`.

For an unhandled keyDown, `doneWithKeyEvent` temporarily records the exact event in `m_keyDownEventBeingResent` and resends it through `NSApp`:

[`WebViewImpl.mm` lines 5792–5812](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5792-L5812).

That resend guard is also per view. A malformed down/up sequence can therefore disturb both adjacent layers:

1. per-view AppKit/IME interpretation;
2. per-page asynchronous WebKit dispatch and completion ordering.

On process termination/reset, WebKit explicitly clears `internals().keyEventQueue`. A process relaunch therefore resets the `WebPageProxy` IPC backlog even though the same `WebViewImpl` may survive. By contrast, the `WebViewImpl` command deque and AppKit input context survive such a relaunch unless the view itself is replaced.

## Destruction and new-window effects

Destroying a `WebViewImpl` closes its page:

[`WebViewImpl::~WebViewImpl`, lines 1453–1481](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L1453-L1481).

Its ordinary C++ members are then destroyed, including both command/holding deques and the retained resent keyDown. The associated `WebPageProxy` is closed and its per-page event queue ceases to exist.

A new Safari window normally creates a new content `WKWebView`/`WebViewImpl`/`WebPageProxy` set and a new AppKit responder association. It therefore resets all three relevant scopes:

- the WKWebView’s AppKit input context;
- WebViewImpl interpretation/holding state;
- WebPageProxy IPC queue.

Closing or creating an `NSWindow` by itself is not what owns those WebKit queues. The diagnostic value comes from Safari constructing new content-view objects for the new window.

## Localization of the reported symptom

> All HTML inputs in one Safari window fail, the URL field does not, and a new Safari window fixes it.

This localizes most strongly to the **affected window’s content WKWebView boundary**, specifically its AppKit `NSTextInputContext` and/or `WebViewImpl` keyboard-interpretation state, with the per-`WebPageProxy` queue as the next adjacent candidate.

Why:

1. **All HTML inputs share one content text-input client.**  
   Switching between `<input>`, `<textarea>`, and `contenteditable` elements changes DOM focus but continues through the same `WKWebView`, `WebViewImpl`, input context, and usually `WebPageProxy`. A fault in any of those objects naturally follows every HTML editor in that content view.

2. **The URL field is Safari chrome, not the page’s `WKWebView`.**  
   It has a different native AppKit text client/input context and does not enter `WebViewImpl::interpretKeyEvent` or the page’s `WebPageProxy::keyEventQueue`. Its success rules out a system-wide inability to type Unicode and strongly argues against an application-wide event-tap failure at that moment.

3. **A new window creates a fresh content pipeline.**  
   If the defect were process-global InputMethodKit or `NSApp` state, the new window should ordinarily inherit it. Recovery specifically with a new window instead matches replacement of the per-window content `WKWebView`/`WebViewImpl`/`WebPageProxy` and its AppKit context.

4. **The scope is broader than one DOM document or input.**  
   Because the failure follows all HTML editors, an individual DOM element, JavaScript handler, or editor composition object is too narrow. If ordinary navigation does not fix it, that further disfavors WebCore document state and favors the longer-lived UI-process view/context state.

5. **The malformed sequence targets down/up bookkeeping.**  
   WebKit explicitly serializes keyDown completion against held keyUps ([`WebViewImpl.mm` lines 5875–5913](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5875-L5913)). A synthetic Unicode pair inserted between a swallowed physical down and its surviving physical up violates that model in a way that can remain attached to one `WebViewImpl`.

### Practical ranking

1. **Most likely:** stale/corrupted AppKit input-method state associated with the affected content `WKWebView`, or its per-`WebViewImpl` `m_collectedKeypressCommands` / keyUp holding state.
2. **Possible adjacent layer:** that view’s `WebPageProxy::Internals::keyEventQueue`, especially if an asynchronous completion was lost or associated with the wrong native event.
3. **Unlikely:** per-DOM-input or page-script state, because every HTML editor is affected.
4. **Unlikely:** Safari/UI-process-global or input-source-global state, because the URL field and a fresh window remain healthy.
5. **Not literally per-`NSWindow`:** WebKit’s mutable queues are owned by the content view/page objects. The window boundary is diagnostically visible because Safari usually gives each window a separate content WebView pipeline.

content.text:
# Revised diagnosis: unmatched `keyUp` events likely poison Safari’s per-view input state

These observations strongly narrow the failure to Safari’s **web-content text-input pipeline**, not Zig or page JavaScript:

- Every normal HTML input is affected.
- Safari’s URL field remains healthy because it is a native AppKit control, outside WebKit.
- A new window creates a fresh `WKWebView`, `NSTextInputContext`, and keyboard-event queues, clearing the bad state.

## The concrete defect

Lex intercepts physical `keyDown` but not `keyUp`, because [`event_mask`](macos/Lex.swift#L454-L468) excludes `.keyUp`.

For every physical letter, Safari receives:

```text
synthetic keyDown
synthetic keyUp
physical keyUp       ← no corresponding physical keyDown
```

For example, the final `x` in `hoanx` produces:

```text
Backspace down/up
Backspace down/up
KeyA down/up, characters="ãn"
physical KeyX up
```

Therefore every intercepted letter contributes one more `keyUp` than `keyDown`.

## Why this can persist until the window closes

Current WebKit’s macOS input path interprets keydowns asynchronously. While keydowns are outstanding, keyups are placed in a holding queue owned by that particular `WebViewImpl`.

The relevant WebKit behavior is:

1. Every keydown creates one outstanding command queue.
2. Any keyup arriving while a keydown is outstanding is added to a holding queue.
3. Each keydown completion releases exactly **one** held keyup.
4. Matching is FIFO only—WebKit does not verify that key codes correspond.
5. Surplus keyups are not automatically drained when no keydown remains.

With Lex’s malformed sequence:

```text
D1 = synthetic KeyA down
U1 = synthetic KeyA up
P1 = unmatched physical key up
```

WebKit can reach:

```text
outstanding keydowns: [D1]
held keyups:          [U1, P1]

D1 completes:
    releases U1

remaining held keyups:
    [P1]
```

The next synthetic keydown may then release stale `P1` rather than its own keyup. Because Lex contributes another surplus physical keyup with every letter, the queue can become increasingly skewed.

This logic is visible in WebKit’s [`WebViewImpl::interpretKeyEvent`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5875-L5913), with only one queued event released per keydown completion in the [completion paths](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.mm#L5982-L6006).

The associated command and holding queues are members of each [`WebViewImpl`](https://github.com/WebKit/WebKit/blob/main/Source/WebKit/UIProcess/mac/WebViewImpl.h#L1153-L1167). Closing the window destroys that view and its retained queue state. A new window starts clean, but Lex can eventually produce the imbalance again—explaining why recovery is only intermittent.

The exact queue implementation depends on the installed Safari/WebKit version, but the unmatched down/up lifecycle is invalid on every version.

## Updated confidence

**High confidence:**

- The problem is in the Safari web-content input path.
- Lex sends unmatched physical keyups.
- The state is scoped to a WebKit content view rather than the browser globally.
- New-window recovery is consistent with destruction of that per-view input state.

**Most likely specific mechanism:**

- Surplus physical keyups corrupt or skew WebKit’s asynchronous input-method bookkeeping.
- Backspace/insertion commands subsequently become associated with stale key lifecycle state, producing the apparent late deletion.

**Now unlikely:**

- Website JavaScript—the issue affects plain inputs generally.
- Autocomplete—the URL field is unaffected.
- Zig arithmetic—the planned edits remain correct.
- Event-tap timeout or local-event suppression—neither explains per-window persistence and exact suffix corruption.

## Decisive confirmation

The smallest diagnostic build would:

1. Add `.keyUp` to the tap mask.
2. Record which physical alphabetic keydowns Lex consumes.
3. Suppress only the matching physical keyups.
4. Continue passing Lex’s tagged synthetic keydown/keyups through.

Safari would then receive balanced event lifecycles:

```text
synthetic keyDown
synthetic keyUp
```

instead of:

```text
synthetic keyDown
synthetic keyUp
unmatched physical keyUp
```

If prolonged rapid typing no longer poisons HTML inputs in the same window, this confirms the primary cause. The non-atomic Backspace/replacement design remains fragile, but the unmatched physical keyup is now the strongest explanation for why the failure accumulates per Safari window and disappears when that window is recreated.
Fix the issue in a clean, minimal way that follow the current coding style.

## What OpenKey actually does

OpenKey’s current code does **not distinguish Safari HTML inputs from Safari’s URL bar**. Both belong to the same process and therefore expose the same bundle identifier, `com.apple.Safari`; the branch only examines the frontmost application’s bundle ID ([`OpenKey.mm` L15](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L15-L18)).

Safari is implicitly included in the general “autocomplete” workaround because:

- the workaround is enabled for every application unless explicitly disabled;
- the only disabled application is Spotlight;
- Safari is also covered by the `com.apple.` prefix in the separate Unicode-Compound compatibility list.

See [`OpenKey.mm` L56-L60](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L56-L60) and [`OpenKey.mm` L169-L198](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L169-L198).

Consequently, **OpenKey provides no evidence for using Shift+Left specifically in Safari HTML fields while retaining Backspace in Safari’s URL bar**. A CGEventTap process-level implementation cannot infer that distinction from `FRONT_APP`; doing so would require focused accessibility-role/DOM information or an explicit user mode.

## Default Safari replacement strategy

With “Autocorrect fixed” (`vFixRecommendBrowser`) enabled, the normal Safari path is:

1. Insert one invisible Unicode character, normally **U+202F NARROW NO-BREAK SPACE**.
2. Increase the requested deletion count by one.
3. Send that many Backspace down/up pairs.
4. Insert the complete replacement as one Unicode keyboard-event down/up pair.
5. Suppress the original physical key-down by returning `NULL`.

The controlling branch is [`OpenKey.mm` L739-L790](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L739-L790):

```text
U+202F down
U+202F up
(backspace down, backspace up) × (N + 1)
replacement-string down
replacement-string up
```

The extra character is explicitly described as the autocomplete fix:

- [`SendEmptyCharacter`, L339-L356](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L339-L356)
- increment of `backspaceCount`, [`L741-L754`](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L741-L754)
- deletion and insertion, [`L763-L778`](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L763-L778)

Its apparent purpose is to disturb/commit the browser’s recommendation or autocorrection state before replacing text. The source labels it only as `//fix autocomplete`; it does not document the WebKit mechanism. For macros it applies the same pattern: insert the invisible character, increment the deletion count, delete, then insert macro text ([`OpenKey.mm` L544-L569](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L544-L569)).

This is **not** the clean workaround for the reported trailing-Backspace race: it still places synthetic Backspace events immediately before Unicode insertion and has no synchronization or delay.

## Selection-based replacement

OpenKey contains a Shift+Left implementation:

```text
Left Arrow down with Shift flag
Left Arrow up with Shift flag
```

See [`SendShiftAndLeftArrow`, L384-L406](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L384-L406).

However, in current master it is selected only for Spotlight:

- `shouldUseSelectionReplacement()` returns true when Spotlight is visible or its bundle ID is active ([`L178-L198`](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L178-L198)).
- It sends Shift+Left `backspaceCount` times, then sets `backspaceCount = 0`, so the subsequent Backspace loop is skipped ([`L756-L768`](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L756-L768)).

The resulting clean minimal sequence is:

```text
(Shift+Left down, Shift+Left up) × N
replacement-string down
replacement-string up
```

Because typing replaces the selection atomically, there are **no synthetic Backspaces capable of arriving after insertion**. This is the minimal OpenKey-derived workaround applicable to the described Safari HTML-input symptom, but applying it selectively to HTML fields rather than the URL bar is an adaptation—not an existing Safari branch in OpenKey.

Commit [`a582ac4`](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/commit/a582ac4d6f6ee3589895f217c3aafb5083498449), **“Fix macOS UI and Spotlight composition”** (2026-06-01), introduced:

- the workaround-disabled app list;
- Spotlight detection;
- `shouldUseRecommendWorkaround`;
- `shouldUseSelectionReplacement`;
- conversion of Spotlight replacement from Backspaces to Shift+Left selection.

That commit is the repository’s strongest direct evidence that selection-first replacement is the project’s workaround when ordinary synthetic replacement causes composition problems.

## Chromium-only Shift+Left branch

There is another, older Shift+Left branch, controlled by the optional `vFixChromiumBrowser` setting:

```objc
if (vFixChromiumBrowser && [_unicodeCompoundApp containsObject:FRONT_APP])
```

It preselects one character before the ordinary deletion path ([`OpenKey.mm` L741-L754](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L741-L754)). Because `_unicodeCompoundApp` is tested with exact `containsObject:` here, Safari does **not** match the `@"com.apple."` prefix entry. This branch therefore targets listed Chromium bundle IDs, not Safari.

It is also not full selection replacement: generally it selects one character and then sends the remaining Backspaces. If the count was one, it decrements the count to zero.

## Delays

There are **no `sleep`, `usleep`, dispatch delays, timestamp spacing, or acknowledgements** in the current replacement path. Calls to `CGEventTapPostEvent` are made consecutively. OpenKey’s workaround is structural—dummy character or selection—not timing-based.

Therefore the minimal proven structural change for this symptom is not “add a few milliseconds”; it is:

```text
select old UTF-16/code-point units with Shift+Left
insert replacement Unicode string
```

Care is needed for surrogate pairs, combining marks, and grapheme clusters: one Left Arrow corresponds to the target editor’s cursor unit, not necessarily one UTF-16 code unit.

## Event-posting API and event shape

### Posting API

Current OpenKey exclusively uses **`CGEventTapPostEvent(_proxy, event)`**, not `CGEventPost`, throughout these helpers:

- Unicode and physical-key sending: [`OpenKey.mm` L253-L337](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L253-L337)
- Backspace and Shift+Left: [`L358-L406`](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L358-L406)
- whole-string insertion: [`L496-L503`](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L496-L503)

The callback saves its supplied proxy in `_proxy` before processing ([`L663-L670`](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L663-L670)).

Commit [`303222d`](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/commit/303222d09d28124229351102126985783d127d26), **“fix issue #63 #60 #57 #59”** (2019-08-12), changed macOS injection from `CGEventPost(kCGHIDEventTap/‌kCGSessionEventTap, ...)` to `CGEventTapPostEvent(_proxy, ...)`.

### Unicode virtual key

Unicode events are created with **virtual key code `0`**:

```objc
CGEventCreateKeyboardEvent(myEventSource, 0, true);
CGEventCreateKeyboardEvent(myEventSource, 0, false);
```

The Unicode string is then attached with `CGEventKeyboardSetUnicodeString`. See:

- single character: [`L253-L261`](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L253-L261)
- complete replacement string: [`L496-L503`](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L496-L503)

Virtual key `0` happens to be the physical ANSI `A` key, but here OpenKey uses it as the carrier event and overrides its textual payload with `CGEventKeyboardSetUnicodeString`.

### Key-down only versus down/up

Current OpenKey attaches the Unicode string to **both the key-down and key-up events**, then posts both:

```text
Unicode keyDown, virtual key 0, string attached
Unicode keyUp,   virtual key 0, same string attached
```

That applies to single characters, the invisible character, compound Unicode, and complete replacement strings ([`OpenKey.mm` L253-L261](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L253-L261), [`L321-L333`](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L321-L333), [`L339-L356`](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L339-L356), [`L496-L503`](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L496-L503)).

Commit [`590bf93`](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/commit/590bf9327617dfa582079674b9170176327b4ef3), **“[macOS] correct sendkey.”** (2019-11-06), changed the previous key-down-only Unicode injection to explicit key-down plus key-up, with the Unicode payload on both.

## Practical conclusion

For Safari HTML inputs exhibiting a delayed synthetic Backspace, the minimal clean sequence suggested by OpenKey’s later composition fix is:

```text
1. Suppress the triggering physical key-down.
2. Post Shift+Left down/up N times to select the old text.
3. Post one virtual-key-0 Unicode key-down containing the replacement string.
4. Post one matching virtual-key-0 Unicode key-up containing the same string.
```

Use `CGEventTapPostEvent` when injecting from inside the event-tap callback. Do not post synthetic Backspaces and no delay is required by this strategy.

For Safari’s URL bar, retain the ordinary Backspace-and-insert path only if it is known to be reliable there. OpenKey itself does **not** implement that HTML-versus-URL-bar discrimination; it treats all Safari focus locations alike.

## Findings

### 1. OpenKey is the only inspected repository with auditable macOS event-tap replacement code

OpenKey installs an active `kCGSessionEventTap` at `kCGHeadInsertEventTap`, listens to keyboard and mouse events, and runs it in common run-loop modes: [`OpenKeyManager.m` L37-L75](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKeyManager.m#L37-L75).

Its replacement flow is:

1. Consume the user's transformation key.
2. Optionally disrupt browser autocomplete.
3. Delete or select the preceding characters.
4. Inject the complete replacement string—or inject it one character at a time.
5. Return `NULL` for the original event.

See the main path in [`OpenKey.mm` L712-L790](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L712-L790).

### 2. Its closest “atomic replacement” technique is Shift+Left selection, then one Unicode event pair

OpenKey implements Shift+Left by creating Left Arrow down/up events, applying the Shift flag to both, and posting them through the current event-tap proxy: [`OpenKey.mm` L384-L406](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L384-L406).

It can repeat that operation for every character that otherwise would have been backspaced, set `backspaceCount = 0`, and then send the replacement: [`OpenKey.mm` L756-L777](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L756-L777).

The replacement string is placed in **one synthetic key-down and key-up pair** with `CGEventKeyboardSetUnicodeString`, rather than separate delete and insertion transactions: [`OpenKey.mm` L423-L503](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L423-L503).

This is the strongest direct precedent for the Safari failure described: WebKit sees a conventional selected range being overwritten, rather than having to serialize a series of Backspace events followed immediately by unrelated Unicode events.

**Important qualification:** current upstream enables full selection replacement specifically for Spotlight, not Safari. That behavior was added in the 2026 commit [“Fix macOS UI and Spotlight composition”](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/commit/a582ac4d6f6ee3589895f217c3aafb5083498449). Nevertheless, it is a mature event-tap implementation of exactly the replacement primitive applicable to Safari.

### 3. OpenKey’s browser workaround is normally sentinel insertion + extra Backspace

For browser autocomplete/recommendation problems, OpenKey sends a non-visible character before deletion:

- normally `U+202F NARROW NO-BREAK SPACE`;
- `U+200C ZERO WIDTH NON-JOINER` for listed applications.

The implementation is in [`OpenKey.mm` L339-L356](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L339-L356).

During a normal transformation it sends the sentinel and increments `backspaceCount`, ensuring that sentinel is deleted along with the prior text: [`OpenKey.mm` L741-L768](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L741-L768). The same method is used for macro replacement: [`OpenKey.mm` L544-L568](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L544-L568).

The option defaults enabled on macOS (`vFixRecommendBrowser = 1`): [`AppDelegate.m`](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/AppDelegate.m). OpenKey’s documentation explicitly describes this feature as fixing autocorrect in Chrome, Safari, Firefox and Excel: [`README.md`](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/README.md).

This workaround addresses autocomplete/composition interference, but it still depends on delete-then-insert ordering. It is therefore less directly suited to an intermittent WebKit transaction-ordering failure than selection replacement.

### 4. Per-character insertion is a compatibility fallback, not OpenKey’s default

OpenKey exposes “Send key step by step.” When disabled, it uses the single Unicode-string event pair; when enabled, it loops over the replacement and calls `SendKeyCode` for every character: [`OpenKey.mm` L770-L785](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L770-L785).

`SendKeyCode` synthesizes both key-down and key-up, including for Unicode characters: [`OpenKey.mm` L267-L337](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L267-L337). This down/up symmetry was deliberately added by the historical [“correct sendkey” commit](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/commit/590bf9327617dfa582079674b9170176327b4ef3).

The project’s changelog says bulk send is the faster default and per-key sending should be enabled for incompatible applications: [`CHANGELOG.md` L33-L39](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md#L33-L39).

Per-character sends may improve applications that reject multi-character Unicode payloads, but they create more WebKit event boundaries and do not make deletion plus insertion atomic.

### 5. Event source and posting location are deliberate

OpenKey creates its events from a **private event source**:

[`OpenKey.mm` L117-L121](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L117-L121)

```objective-c
myEventSource = CGEventSourceCreate(kCGEventSourceStatePrivate);
```

It then posts generated events via `CGEventTapPostEvent(_proxy, ...)`, not a separate global `CGEventPost` call. The 2019 compatibility change that introduced bulk sending also changed injected events from HID/session global posting to tap-proxy posting; see commit [`303222d`](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/commit/303222d09d28124229351102126985783d127d26).

Synthetic events are recognized by comparing their source-state ID against the private source and are ignored by OpenKey’s own callback: [`OpenKey.mm` L601-L605](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L601-L605).

For physical-key-style output, OpenKey also sets `kCGEventFlagMaskNonCoalesced`: [`OpenKey.mm` L267-L287](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L267-L287).

These choices are low-risk refinements worth matching, but there is no source evidence that merely changing source type fixes Safari replacement ordering.

### 6. No delay-based synchronization in the replacement path

There is no `usleep`, sleep, timer, or `dispatch_after` between selection/deletion and Unicode insertion in the audited OpenKey path. All events are posted synchronously through the tap proxy.

Thus, mature OpenKey evidence supports **changing the editing operation**, not adding arbitrary latency.

### 7. Clipboard code exists, but it is unrelated to live typing

OpenKey uses `NSPasteboard` only for its explicit text-conversion feature, reading and rewriting clipboard contents: [`OpenKeyManager.m` L108-L132](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKeyManager.m#L108-L132).

Its live replacement path does not copy, cut, paste, or restore the clipboard. `SendCutKey` exists but has no production caller: [`OpenKey.mm` L408-L421](https://github.com/tuyenvm/OpenKey/blob/master/Sources/OpenKey/macOS/ModernKey/OpenKey.mm#L408-L421).

A clipboard workaround would therefore not follow OpenKey’s typing architecture and would introduce clipboard races, formatting effects, paste permission/UI behavior, and restoration complexity.

### 8. No accessibility text mutation

OpenKey requires Accessibility permission because of its active event tap, but its typing code contains no `AXUIElement`, selected-text-range mutation, or accessibility value assignment. The only inspected accessibility-related source handles authorization/UI concerns, not text replacement.

For HTML inputs, AX text mutation would also vary by WebKit element exposure and would be a materially larger architectural change.

## EVKey and GoTiengViet limitations

- The public [EVKey repository](https://github.com/lamquangminh/EVKey) contains Windows source, website material, and downloadable macOS binaries, but not the macOS implementation source. Its website links `EVKeyMac.zip` and identifies macOS version 3.3.10: [`header.html` L72-L76](https://github.com/lamquangminh/EVKey/blob/master/docs/_includes/header.html#L72-L76). Consequently, no Safari event-injection mechanism can be responsibly attributed to EVKey from this repository.
- Searches did not locate a mature, publicly auditable macOS GoTiengViet event-tap implementation. Repositories with that name were unrelated, web extensions, empty, or non-macOS code.

Accordingly, OpenKey provides the only concrete source-backed comparison among the named products. Claims about EVKey or legacy GoTiengViet internals would require reverse engineering binaries rather than open-source citation.

## Ranked approaches for this patch

| Rank | Approach | Safari/WebKit compatibility | Patch minimality | Assessment |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| **1** | **Safari-only repeated Shift+Left, then one bulk Unicode down/up pair** | High | High | Best fit. It converts two logically separate operations into ordinary selected-text replacement while preserving the existing event tap and Unicode emitter. Directly modeled by OpenKey’s selection loop and bulk sender. |
| **2** | **Shift+Left, then per-character Unicode down/up pairs** | Medium–high | High | Use only if Safari rejects the bulk Unicode payload. Selection still solves the deletion race, but multiple insertion events are less atomic. |
| **3** | **Sentinel character, extra Backspace, then bulk Unicode** | Medium | Very high | OpenKey’s established browser-autocomplete workaround. Minimal, but still relies on the ordering that is already intermittent in the reported Safari case. |
| **4** | **Private `CGEventSource` + `CGEventTapPostEvent(proxy, ...)` + proper key-up events** | Medium as supporting changes | High | Good hygiene and proven by OpenKey. Apply alongside ranks 1–3 if the current implementation uses global posting, a shared source, or key-down-only Unicode events. Not sufficient evidence as a standalone Safari fix. |
| **5** | **Small delay between deletion and insertion** | Uncertain | High | Easy but timing-dependent, adds latency, and has no mature OpenKey precedent. A last-resort diagnostic rather than a robust fix. |
| **6** | **Clipboard paste with save/restore** | Medium | Low | Often reaches web inputs, but causes clipboard races, formatting/paste semantics, and possible privacy prompts. No live-typing precedent in OpenKey. |
| **7** | **Accessibility selected-range/value mutation** | Variable | Very low | Potentially direct, but HTML accessibility trees and custom editors vary. Requires focus/element discovery and error handling; incompatible with the “minimal event-tap patch” constraint. |

## Recommended minimal change

For `com.apple.Safari` and, if testing confirms it, other WebKit-hosting bundle IDs:

1. Suppress the original transformation keystroke as today.
2. Emit one Shift+Left down/up pair per preceding UTF-16/user-visible character being replaced.
3. Emit the replacement with one `CGEventKeyboardSetUnicodeString` key-down/key-up pair.
4. Use the callback’s `CGEventTapProxy` for all posts.
5. Create events from a private `CGEventSource`.
6. Ignore self-generated events by source-state ID.
7. Keep existing Backspace behavior for native applications.

This copies OpenKey’s mature primitives while limiting behavioral change to Safari/WebKit. It avoids clipboard and AX dependencies and does not add arbitrary delays. Care is required for surrogate pairs and combining sequences: selection count should correspond to the target application’s cursor movement units, not blindly to UTF-8 bytes.

Old Safari sequence:
Backspace × N → insert replacement

New Safari sequence:
Shift+Left × N → insert replacement over selection

This structurally removes the operation that matched the failure: a Backspace can no longer execute after insertion and delete part of the replacement.

The behavior is restricted to `com.apple.Safari`; other applications retain the existing Backspace-based path. This follows the selection-replacement technique used by mature event-tap input methods for problematic macOS text clients.

# Replaced the ordering strategy

The Shift-Left workaround has been removed.

The callback now:

1. Posts the required synthetic Backspaces.
2. Rewrites the original physical `keyDown` with the UTF-16 replacement.
3. Returns that modified event instead of posting a separate synthetic insertion.

Quartz explicitly guarantees that events posted through the callback proxy enter the stream before the event returned by the callback. The resulting sequence is therefore:

```text
synthetic Backspace(s)
returned replacement keyDown
physical matching keyUp
```

For `nguyee`:

```text
nguye → nguy → nguyê
```

This also removes the synthetic `virtualKey: 0` insertion pair and preserves the physical key identity/down-up lifecycle.

Implementation: [`Lex.swift`](macos/Lex.swift#L852-L890)

# Select Text in Webkit applications via macOS accessibility API
Ask Question
Asked 4 years ago
Modified [4 years ago](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/72478435/select-text-in-webkit-applications-via-macos-accessibility-api?lastactivity "2022-06-03 17:19:36Z")
Viewed 1k times
4
I need to select text in a WebKit view of another application (Apple Mail) using accessibility APIs.
For regular text fields, I do something like this:
```
func selectText(withRange range: CFRange) throws {
    var range = range
    guard let newValue: AXValue = AXValueCreate(AXValueType.cfRange, &range) else { return }
    AXUIElementSetAttributeValue(self, kAXSelectedTextRangeAttribute as CFString, newValue)
}
```
However, in the composing window of Apple Mail every text seems to be of type `Static Text` which doesn't come with the necessary `AXSelectedTextRange`

...

## 1 Answer 1
```
func getTextMarker(forIndex index: CFIndex) throws -> AXTextMarker? {
        var textMarker: AnyObject?
        guard AXUIElementCopyParameterizedAttributeValue(self,"AXTextMarkerForIndex" as CFString, index as AnyObject, &textMarker) == .success else { return nil }
        return textMarker as! AXTextMarker
}

func selectStaticText(withRange range: CFRange) throws {
        guard let textMarkerStart = try? getTextMarker(forIndex: range.location) else { return }
        guard let textMarkerEnd = try? getTextMarker(forIndex: range.location + range.length) else { return }
        let textMarkerRange = AXTextMarkerRangeCreate(kCFAllocatorDefault, textMarkerStart, textMarkerEnd)

        AXUIElementSetAttributeValue(self, "AXSelectedTextMarkerRange" as CFString, textMarkerRange)
}
```

summary.summary:
## Active task

Fix an intermittent Safari web-content typing bug in the macOS event-tap Telex app. The user has tested multiple proposed fixes on macOS; all have failed. Continue investigating and implement another clean, minimal fix following the existing coding style.

Repository:

- `lex`
- Current HEAD: `8345d9e` (`lex: fix could not type Vietnamese on Safari.`)
- Current working tree was clean at the latest inspection.
- Linux sandbox; no `swiftc` or macOS runtime testing.
- `zig build test` has consistently passed.

## Confirmed behavior

Original failures in Safari website inputs:

- `nguyee` should become `nguyê`, but becomes `nguye`; `ê` briefly appears and disappears.
- `hoanx` should become `hoãn`, but becomes `hoaã`.
- Affects ordinary HTML `<input>` fields, not just JS-heavy controls.
- Safari URL field is unaffected.
- Closing the Safari window and opening another may temporarily clear it.
- Native applications work.

The Zig engine is correct:

- `nguyee`: requests one deletion and replacement `ê`.
- `hoanx`: requests two deletions and replacement `ãn`.
- Tests pass and replacement arithmetic is correct.

The target-side effective ordering is consistently insertion before the final retrospective edit, despite the low-level event posting order.

## Failed fixes — do not retry unchanged

### 1. Suppressing unmatched physical keyups

Added `.keyUp` to the tap, tracked consumed key codes, and suppressed matching physical keyups. User reported no improvement.

Conclusion: unmatched physical keyups may be malformed but are not the effective cause.

This fix was rolled back in later commits.

### 2. Safari-only Shift+Left selection replacement

Changed Safari edits from:

```text
Backspace × N → insert replacement
```

to:

```text
Shift+Left × N → insert replacement over selection
```

User observed:

```text
nguyeê
```

with `ê` highlighted.

This proves Safari effectively inserted `ê` first, then processed Shift+Left, selecting the newly inserted character. Do not retry selection via separately injected keyboard events.

### 3. Post Backspaces, return modified original keyDown

Removed synthetic insertion and instead:

1. Posted synthetic Backspace events via `tapPostEvent`.
2. Replaced the original physical event’s Unicode text.
3. Returned that event from the tap callback.

This preserves the physical key identity/down-up lifecycle and uses Quartz’s guarantee that proxy-posted events enter before the callback-returned event.

User still observed the original failure:

```text
nguye → nguyeê briefly → nguye
```

Therefore Quartz/event-tap insertion order is not the issue. Safari/AppKit/WebKit processes the resulting editing commands asynchronously and applies deletion after insertion.

The current HEAD `8345d9e` contains this failed strategy and is clean/committed.

## Current implementation area

Main callback:

```bash
nl -ba macos/Lex.swift | sed -n '704,914p'
```

Current replacement path is around lines 830–890:

- Engine computes `backspace_count`.
- Posts Backspace down/up pairs.
- Calls `event.keyboardSetUnicodeString(...)` on the physical keydown.
- Returns the modified original event.

Event tap setup:

```bash
nl -ba macos/Lex.swift | sed -n '444,480p'
```

Zig engine details:

```bash
nl -ba src/lex.zig | sed -n '600,735p'
nl -ba src/lex.zig | sed -n '1768,1815p'
nl -ba src/lex.zig | sed -n '3850,4028p'
```

## Strongest current diagnosis

Safari’s web-content text pipeline interprets separate deletion/navigation and insertion keyboard commands asynchronously. Even when CGEvents enter in the intended order, the insertion can be committed before a prior Backspace or Shift+Left command.

Evidence:

- Backspace approach: inserted `ê` flashes, then late deletion removes it.
- Shift+Left approach: inserted `ê` appears, then late Shift+Left highlights it.
- Returning insertion from the callback rather than posting it does not help.
- URL field is native AppKit and unaffected; HTML inputs use WebKit.
- Recreating a Safari window resets relevant per-view/input-context state.

A fix based on any separate synthetic “move/delete first, insert second” keyboard sequence is therefore unlikely to be reliable.

## Best next direction: avoid multiple keyboard commands

Investigate a Safari-only atomic replacement using macOS Accessibility APIs, since the app already requires Accessibility permission.

Candidate flow:

1. Get the system-wide focused UI element:
   - `AXUIElementCreateSystemWide()`
   - `kAXFocusedUIElementAttribute`
2. Read its `kAXSelectedTextRangeAttribute`.
3. Build an `AXValue` range covering the preceding `backspace_count` UTF-16 units.
4. Set that selected range.
5. Set `kAXSelectedTextAttribute` to the engine replacement.

This avoids Backspace/Shift+Left keyboard interpretation. Determine before implementation:

- Whether Safari HTML inputs expose/set:
  - `kAXSelectedTextRangeAttribute`
  - `kAXSelectedTextAttribute`
- Whether setting selected text causes normal DOM `beforeinput`/`input` events.
- Whether calls are synchronous enough to avoid the race.
- Behavior in password fields and contenteditable.
- Whether calling AX synchronously inside the event-tap callback risks deadlock or timeout.
- Range units: likely `CFRange`/UTF-16, but verify. Current Vietnamese precomposed BMP characters and ASCII are one UTF-16 unit each, matching engine backspace counts in reported cases.

Avoid replacing the entire `kAXValueAttribute` unless necessary; it can break caret position, event semantics, controlled inputs, and password fields.

If direct AX selected-text replacement is unsupported/unreliable, the next fallback is asynchronous serialization with an explicit delay/completion boundary. That requires careful queueing of subsequent physical input, so it is less minimal and should not be attempted casually.

## Interrupted research state

The latest searches attempted to research WebKit’s AX implementation and external use of `kAXSelectedTextAttribute`, but both `librarian` calls failed due to the daily free limit. A generic web search returned Apple’s `AXUIElementSetAttributeValue` documentation but no decisive result.

Do not depend on librarian immediately; use:

- Apple docs via web page fetch.
- WebKit source via GitHub/raw URLs or a shallow clone.
- Shell `curl`/`git grep` if network access permits.

Useful WebKit searches:

```text
kAXSelectedTextAttribute
NSAccessibilitySelectedTextAttribute
accessibilitySetSelectedText
setSelectedTextRange
AXSelectedTextRange
```

Look under WebKit macOS accessibility classes for `WKWebView`/`WebAccessibilityObjectWrapperMac`.

## Prior external research

OpenKey was inspected as a mature event-tap Vietnamese input method. It uses Shift+Left selection replacement in some compatibility paths, but this app’s real Safari test proved that separately injected Shift+Left and insertion are still reordered. Do not copy that workaround unchanged.

InputMethodKit / `NSTextInputClient` replacement remains the architecturally robust long-term solution, but the user requested a clean minimal fix in the current app, so first assess Safari-only AX selected-text replacement.

## Immediate continuation plan

1. Confirm clean state and inspect current committed diff relative to original baseline:

```bash
cd .
git status --short
git diff acbc467..HEAD -- macos/Lex.swift
```

2. Research WebKit/Apple AX selected-text replacement semantics from source/docs.
3. If viable, replace the current failed Safari path with a minimal Safari-only AX helper while retaining existing event injection for other applications.
4. Ensure failure fallback is safe:
   - If focused element or AX attributes are unavailable, reset engine and preferably pass through or use the existing behavior deliberately.
   - Do not silently advance engine state without applying the edit.
5. Run:

```bash
git diff --check
zig build test
git status --short
```

6. Clearly state that macOS runtime validation must be performed by the user.

You have to assign the pointer to the variable with the _in-out operator_ `&`
```
var position : CFTypeRef?
let res : AXError = AXUIElementCopyAttributeValue(windowAccessibilityElem, 
                    kAXPositionAttribute as CFString, 
                    &position)
```
* `res` contains the error on failure.
* `position` contains the position on success.
In the [documentation](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/applicationservices/1462085-axuielementcopyattributevalue) an in-out parameter is indicated by _On return, ..._

input.task: Review the current uncommitted macOS Safari fix in @macos/Lex.swift. Intent: Safari web-content controls asynchronously reorder separate synthetic Backspace/Shift+Left commands and insertion, so for Safari only we synchronously set kAXSelectedTextRangeAttribute to cover the preceding engine backspace count, then return the physical keyDown with its Unicode text changed to the replacement; non-Safari behavior is restored to the pre-fix synthetic sequence. User-observed failures from prior attempts: insertion flashes then a late Backspace deletes it; Shift+Left runs late and highlights the insertion. The engine produces one deletion + ê for `nguyee` and two deletions + ãn for `hoanx`. Review git diff against acbc467. Focus on whether the Accessibility range approach is sound for Safari HTML input/contenteditable, Swift/CoreFoundation API correctness, event-tap deadlock/timeout risks, selection/caret and UTF-16 range correctness, and whether a smaller or safer fallback is needed. Ignore style except where it affects compile/correctness. Output: high-confidence blockers first, then non-blocking risks, and the smallest concrete corrections.

run.result:
`Recommendation:` The Safari-only AX-selection + rewrite-the-physical-keyDown design is sound and correctly fixes the reordering failures (selection is applied via synchronous AX IPC before the tap returns the keyDown, so within one keystroke the ordering is guaranteed). One blocker-level robustness fix is needed before shipping; the rest are documented risks with safe degradation.

## Verified facts the review rests on

- Diff vs `acbc467` confirmed: non-Safari path is byte-identical to the pre-fix synthetic sequence (backspaces + text posted via `tapPostEvent`, physical event swallowed with `return nil`).
- [lex.zig `compose_utf16_string_replacement`](src/lex.zig#L1794-L1816): each `Span.to_utf16()` emits exactly **one** UTF-16 code unit (precomposed BMP), and `replacement_count` is always ≥ 1 after `add`. Consequences: (a) `backspace_count` equals the UTF-16 length of the text Lex previously inserted, so `CFRange(location - backspace_count, backspace_count)` is unit-correct; (b) the "empty replacement leaves raw char over an active selection" hazard cannot occur.
- CF/AX API usage in `select_previous_characters` is correct: `CFGetTypeID` guards before `as!`, `AXValueGetType == .cfRange` before `AXValueGetValue`, `AXValueCreate(.cfRange, &range)` correct. Mutating the tapped event with `keyboardSetUnicodeString` and returning `passUnretained(event)` is the documented CGEventTapCallBack contract for modified events. `import Carbon` transitively provides the AX symbols — compiles.
- Relative-offset math (get location, subtract, set on the same element) is robust to whether Safari reports the range relative to a text field's value or the whole web area.

## Blocker

**1. No AX messaging timeout — a busy Safari WebContent process freezes session-wide keyboard input.**
`select_previous_characters` makes up to 3 synchronous AX IPC calls per keystroke inside the event-tap callback (a `.cgSessionEventTap`, so it blocks keyboard delivery to *every* app). The default AX messaging timeout is 6 s. A WebContent process stuck in a JS busy-loop/GC means: keyboard frozen for seconds, then `tapDisabledByTimeout`, engine reset, raw passthrough. Smallest fix (S, <1h): create the system-wide element once in `AppDelegate`, set a short timeout, and reuse it:

```swift
// AppDelegate init/launch:
let system_wide_element = AXUIElementCreateSystemWide()
AXUIElementSetMessagingTimeout(system_wide_element, 0.1) // seconds; on the
// system-wide element this sets the global timeout for this process's AX calls.
```

Pass or expose that cached element to `select_previous_characters` instead of creating it per keystroke. On timeout the calls return an error, the existing `return false → reset → passthrough` fallback fires, and the tap stays healthy.

## Non-blocking risks

**2. Stale-selection race under key repeat / fast bursts on a slow page.**
The AX read reflects Safari's *processed* state, but the previous modified keyDown is delivered asynchronously after the tap returns. If keystroke N+1's callback runs before WebContent applied keystroke N's insertion, the read location is stale; the guards (`length == 0`, `location >= character_count`) can still pass, and the wrong range gets selected/replaced. Assumption I could not verify locally: WebKit's isolated AX tree serves reads from a snapshot off the main thread, so the read does **not** serialize behind pending key events. At human typing speed this is rare; key autorepeat over a telex modifier (holding `e` on "e…") on a loaded page is the realistic trigger. Two mitigations, smallest first:
- S: in the Safari branch, bail (reset + passthrough) when `event.getIntegerValueField(.keyboardEventAutorepeat) != 0` and `backspace_count > 0`.
- M (1–3h, follow-up): before setting the selection, read `kAXStringForRangeParameterizedAttribute` for the candidate range and compare against the text the engine expects to replace (`buffer_effective[modification_index..buffer_length_previous]` — needs a small C-ABI addition, which per AGENTS.md means updating `lex.h` too). Mismatch → reset + passthrough. This closes the race almost entirely.

**3. Fields where the selection isn't settable degrade safely — accept as-is.**
Settable `AXSelectedTextRange` works for Safari's native-backed fields (URL bar) and standard HTML `input`/`textarea`/contenteditable via WebKit's AX text API (the same path VoiceOver uses). Custom editors that fake text editing (Google Docs, Monaco/canvas editors) will fail the get or set; the fallback (reset + raw char) yields literal input, not corruption. That is the correct degraded behavior. Optionally log the failure once for diagnosability.

**4. Bundle-ID scope.** `com.apple.Safari` excludes Safari Technology Preview (`com.apple.SafariTechnologyPreview`) and other WebKit apps that presumably share the reordering bug. Trivially widened later; not needed now.

**5. Unit mismatch only if the replaced text wasn't inserted by Lex.** Since the engine resets on space, delete-sync, mouse clicks, modifiers, and non-alphabetic keys (arrow keys land in the F700 private-use range → reset), the replaced range should always be Lex-inserted precomposed BMP text. If a page normalizes the DOM to NFD behind Lex's back, the UTF-16 math breaks — no practical guard; the M mitigation in #2 also catches this.

**6. Minor.** `NSWorkspace.shared.frontmostApplication` can lag an app switch by one keystroke (misrouted branch, safe either way). A slightly more robust discriminator is `AXUIElementGetPid` on the focused element you already fetch, compared against Safari's PID — optional.

## Smallest concrete change set

1. Cache the system-wide `AXUIElement` in `AppDelegate`, call `AXUIElementSetMessagingTimeout(_, 0.1)` once, use it in `select_previous_characters`. (Blocker, S)
2. Add the autorepeat bail-out in the Safari branch. (Risk #2 cheap mitigation, S)
3. Follow-up, not required to ship: engine-side "expected replaced text" export + `kAXStringForRange` verification. (M)

No other correctness issues found; I specifically checked the empty-replacement hazard, CFRange/UTF-16 unit consistency, the compose-after-select ordering (safe given `replacement_count >= 1`), the CGEventTap modified-event return contract, and that the non-Safari path is an exact restoration of the pre-fix behavior.

# AXUIElement Set Messaging Timeout(_: _:)
Sets the timeout value used in the accessibility API.
macOS 10.4+
```
func AXUIElementSetMessagingTimeout (
     _ element :  AXUIElement ,
     _ timeoutInSeconds :  Float 
) ->  AXError
```

## Parameters
`element`
The AXUIElementRef representing an accessibility object. `timeoutInSeconds`
The number of seconds for the new timeout value.

## Return Value
If unsuccessful, `AXUIElement Set Messaging Timeout` may return one of the following error codes, among others:
`k AXError Illegal Argument`
One or more of the arguments is an illegal value (timeout values must be positive). `k AXError Invalid UIElement`
The AXUIElementRef is invalid.

## Discussion
Pass the system-wide accessibility object (see `AXUIElement Create System Wide()` ) if you want to set the timeout globally for this process. Setting the timeout on another accessibility object sets it only for that object, not for other accessibility objects that are equal to it.
Setting `timeout In Seconds` to 0 for the system-wide accessibility object resets the global timeout to its default value. Setting `timeout In Seconds` to 0 for any other accessibility object makes that element use the current global timeout value.

##### Discussion

##### Discussion
Pass the system-wide accessibility object (see AXUIElementCreateSystemWide ) if you want to set the timeout globally for this process.

## Implemented a different Safari path

- Restored the original synthetic-event behavior for non-Safari applications.
- Safari no longer receives separate synthetic Backspace or Shift+Left events.
- Lex synchronously selects the preceding characters through macOS Accessibility, then returns one modified physical key event that replaces the selection.
- Added a 100 ms Accessibility timeout to prevent an unresponsive Safari process from blocking the global event tap.
- If Safari does not expose a writable text selection, Lex safely passes through the original character instead of risking text deletion.

This specifically avoids the asynchronous WebKit ordering that caused `ê` to appear briefly and then disappear.

`zig build test` passes. Swift/macOS runtime compilation and Safari behavior cannot be tested in the Linux sandbox.

+# The Safari text box that ate Vietnamese characters
+
+Lex had a bug with an unusually specific appetite. Sometimes it ate Vietnamese characters, but
+only inside web pages in Safari.
+
+Typing `nguyee` should produce `nguyê`. Instead, the input briefly showed `nguyeê`, then settled on
+`nguye`. The `ê` was inserted and immediately deleted. Another sequence, `hoanx`, should produce
+`hoãn`, but could produce `hoaã` instead.
+
+The Zig input engine was returning the right edit. The macOS event tap was posting events in the
+right order. Safari was still applying them in the wrong order.
+
+This is the story of how all three statements can be true at once.
+
+## The clues pointed inside Safari
+
+The failure was intermittent, but its boundary was unusually sharp:
+
+- It affected ordinary HTML `<input>` elements, not just JavaScript-heavy editors.
+- It affected Safari website content, but not Safari's URL field.
+- Other macOS applications worked normally.
+- Closing a Safari window and opening another one could make the problem disappear.
+
+That last clue initially looked like random browser weirdness. Together, the clues separated two
+text systems that happen to be drawn in the same window. Safari's URL field is a native AppKit text
+control. A website input is edited through WebKit and, usually, a separate Web Content process.
+
+The problem was therefore unlikely to be the Vietnamese rules in
+[`src/lex.zig`](src/lex.zig). It was more likely to be the boundary between the global keyboard event
+tap and WebKit's text editor.
+
+## How Lex normally edits text
+
+Lex observes physical key-down events with a Quartz event tap. The event is sent to the Zig engine,
+which returns a retrospective edit: remove some characters immediately before the caret, then insert
+a replacement string.
+
+For example:
+
+| Typed input | Existing text | Engine edit            | Result  |
+| ----------- | ------------- | ---------------------- | ------- |
+| `nguyee`    | `nguye`       | delete 1, insert `ê`   | `nguyê` |
+| `hoanx`     | `hoan`        | delete 2, insert `ãn`  | `hoãn`  |
+
+Historically, [`macos/Lex.swift`](macos/Lex.swift) implemented that edit as a sequence of synthetic
+keyboard events:
+
+```text
+Backspace × N → insert replacement
+```
+
+This works in native macOS text controls. It also looks sensible: post the deletion events first,
+post the replacement second, and the application should see them in that order.
+
+Safari demonstrated the dangerous word in that sentence: "should."
+
+## Events can arrive in order and take effect out of order
+
+Several attempted fixes made the behavior easier to understand.
+
+First, Lex also intercepted key-up events and suppressed physical key-ups corresponding to consumed
+key-downs. This fixed a suspicious event lifecycle, but did not change the Safari failure. The
+unmatched key-up was untidy, not causal.
+
+Next, Lex tried replacing Backspace with selection:
+
+```text
+Shift+Left × N → insert replacement over the selection
+```
+
+Typing `nguyee` then produced `nguyeê` with the new `ê` highlighted. This was useful evidence. Safari
+had inserted the replacement first and applied Shift+Left afterward, even though Lex had posted the
+selection events first.
+
+The third attempt removed the synthetic insertion event. Lex posted Backspace through the event-tap
+proxy, changed the Unicode text carried by the original physical key-down, and returned that event
+from the callback. Quartz guarantees that proxy-posted events enter the event stream before the event
+returned by the callback.
+
+The bug remained. `ê` appeared, then the earlier Backspace removed it.
+
+At this point the low-level ordering was no longer the interesting ordering. Quartz was delivering
+events correctly. Safari's web-content editing pipeline was interpreting the deletion and insertion
+as separate commands and committing their effects asynchronously. Ordering at the CGEvent boundary
+did not guarantee ordering at the WebKit editing boundary.
+
+No rearrangement of separate Backspace, navigation, and insertion events could make that contract
+reliable. Adding a delay would only turn the race into a slower race while blocking the global
+keyboard event tap.
+
+## The fix: select synchronously, then perform one edit
+
+The working fix avoids sending Safari a separate keyboard deletion command.
+
+When the frontmost application is Safari, Lex now:
+
+1. Gets the focused accessibility element with `kAXFocusedUIElementAttribute`.
+2. Reads its `kAXSelectedTextRangeAttribute` as a `CFRange`.
+3. Moves the start of that range backward by the engine's deletion count.
+4. Sets the resulting range through the Accessibility API.
+5. Changes the Unicode text of the original physical key-down to the engine's replacement.
+6. Returns that one key-down to Safari.
+
+The essential operation looks like this:
+
+```text
+caret:       nguy[e|]
+AX selection nguy[e]
+key-down:        ê
+result:      nguyê
+```
+
+The Accessibility range update is synchronous. By the time the event-tap callback returns, the old
+text is already selected. Safari then receives one keyboard editing command: insert the replacement
+at the current selection. There is no synthetic Backspace or late Shift+Left command left for WebKit
+to reorder.
+
+Lex deliberately does not assign the field's entire value through Accessibility. Returning a real
+key event lets Safari perform the replacement through its normal input path, which is important for
+web pages that observe keyboard and input events. It also avoids rebuilding the field value and
+manually restoring its caret.
+
+## Failure needs to be boring
+
+Accessibility support is not identical across every editable element. Password fields and custom
+canvas-based editors may not expose a writable selected-text range. The fix therefore has narrow
+guards:
+
+- The special path is used only for Safari. Other applications keep the established synthetic-event
+  behavior.
+- The reported accessibility values must have the expected `AXUIElement`, `AXValue`, and `CFRange`
+  types.
+- The caret must be a zero-length selection and must have enough preceding characters to cover the
+  requested edit.
+- If any check fails, Lex resets its engine state and passes through the physical character instead
+  of guessing and deleting user text.
+
+Accessibility calls are synchronous inter-process calls, which introduces another less exciting
+failure mode: an unresponsive Safari process could block the event-tap callback. macOS normally gives
+Accessibility messaging a timeout measured in seconds. That is far too long for code sitting in the
+global keyboard path, so Lex sets the process-wide Accessibility timeout to 100 milliseconds. A
+timeout becomes a harmless literal keystroke instead of a frozen keyboard.
+
+## What actually fixed the bug
+
+The final change was not "send the same events in a better order." Every version of that approach
+still depended on WebKit honoring the semantic order of independent keyboard commands.
+
+The fix was to stop expressing one logical replacement as multiple keyboard commands. Accessibility
+establishes the range synchronously, and a single returned key-down performs the edit.
+
+After that change:
+
+```text
+nguyee → nguyê
+hoanx  → hoãn
+```
+
+The broader lesson is small but useful: event-stream order and application-state order are different
+things. When a boundary processes commands asynchronously, correctness usually comes from reducing
+the number of commands crossing that boundary, not from becoming more creative about their timing.
*** End Patch
